KUALA LUMPUR: Vantris Energy Bhd has launched a year-long coral reef restoration programme off Pulau Lang Tengah, Terengganu, planting 246 coral fragments.
Carried out with conservation organisation Coralku, the initiative saw 15 staff volunteers attach the fragments to 15 modular structures known as Reef Stars.
These frames provide corals with a stable base on which to attach and grow.
The team will monitor and maintain the site for 12 months to track coral health and survival rates.
Vantris said the project draws on coral resilience research, selecting colonies with a higher natural tolerance for warmer waters.

Nhakhorn Somchit, Vantris vice-president of quality, health, safety, security, sustainability and environment, said the programme allows staff to directly participate in marine conservation beyond the initial planting phase.
Coralku co-founder and director Dr Natasha Zulaikha Zahirudin said corporate backing is vital to sustain conservation, provided efforts remain guided by science and monitoring.
Coral reefs cover less than 0.1 per cent of the ocean floor but support about 25 per cent of marine species.
They also protect coastlines and support the livelihoods and food security of more than one billion people worldwide.
The project builds on Vantris's previous marine work, including Thailand's first Rigs-to-Reefs project in 2020.
The group's heavy-lift vessel, Sapura 3000, relocated seven retired offshore platform jackets to a reefing site near Koh Pha-ngan.
The structures now provide habitats and shelter for marine life, and Thailand's Department of Marine and Coastal Resources has since designated the site a protected area.
e30bfc7a062a2185: ROME: Atalanta rescued an extraordinary late 4-4 draw against Inter Milan on Sunday as the champions fell three points off the Serie A title pace despite Francesco Pio Esposito’s hattrick, while AC Milan and Juventus claimed big wins.

Inter looked comfortable in Bergamo when Petar Sucic’s penalty gave them a two-goal cushion in the 76th minute after Esposito’s treble, but Charles De Ketelaere’s second goal of the night and a stoppage-time Franck Kessie penalty salvaged a point for La Dea.
It marked only the third time Inter have dropped points in the league this season but kept Cristian Chivu’s side in third place, one point behind Roma and three adrift of leaders Lazio.

Esposito struck twice in the first half, pouncing on a deflected ball in the box to sweep home the opener before doubling Inter’s lead by heading home from a corner.

De Ketelaere proved the catalyst for Atalanta’s fightback, pulling a goal back with a header and firing home a powerful finish either side of Sucic’s spot kick.

65fdc0a4de4d47b7: LIVERPOOL: Mauricio Pochettino endured a nightmare start as Manchester United manager with a 4-0 defeat at Liverpool that left the Red Devils still rooted in the Premier League relegation zone.
United never recovered from Leny Yoro's controversial red card after just eight minutes as Dominik Szoboszlai and Florian Wirtz quickly made Liverpool's man advantage count.
Teenager Rio Ngumoha rounded off a stunning individual with Liverpool's third before Victor Munoz completed the rout.
Defeat leaves United second bottom of the table and gave Pochettino an early indication of the huge job he has ahead to restore the 20-time English champions to their former glories.

"We feel pain for that defeat, but we need to keep the head up and translate that anger to an energy to start to work from tomorrow for the next game," said Pochettino, who was furious at the decision to dismiss Yoro.
"I need to defend my club and say what I feel. I feel like that was an action that everyone who plays football can see was clearly not a red card.."
Liverpool climb into the top four and within seven points of leaders Arsenal to rekindle faint hopes of challenging for the title.
"We could have scored more," said Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola.
"In other games you will remember those chances, but today we've controlled the game and everything was happening around the (United) box."
Pochettino answered United's call after Michael Carrick was sacked last week after winning just one of the Red Devils' first 10 league games in charge.
The Argentine has been linked with a move to Old Trafford for a decade, but failed to make a strong first impression on the United fans.
- EUROPE'S WORST DEFENCE -
Pochettino's bold team selection backfired with the centre-back pairing of Matthijs de Ligt and Yoro at fault for the game's decisive moment.
De Ligt, on his first Premier League start for nearly a year, let a long ball down the middle and go and allowed Alexander Isak to bear down on goal.
The Swedish striker took a heavy touch before he was clipped by Yoro, but referee Sam Barrott still deemed the French defender had denied a clear goalscoring opportunity and produced a red card.
Szoboszlai rubbed salt into United wounds by drilling home the resulting free-kick from the edge of the box.
Moments later Ngumoha skipped past Diogo Dalot and crossed for Wirtz to hook a shot in off the underside of the bar.
Having relegated Harry Maguire to the bench, Pochettino was forced to turn to the veteran centre-back just 22 minutes in to try and stem the bleeding.
United lost 7-0 at Anfield three years ago and a switch to a back five helped avoid similar damage, albeit with the help of some wayward Liverpool finishing.
Maguire made a brilliant block to deny Isak a third goal just before half-time.
Bradley Barcola and Isak were guilty of wasting huge chances early in the second half.
But Barcola's blistering speed created Liverpool's third just after the hour mark.
The French international destroyed Lisandro Martinez for pace before picking out Ngumoha to slot home.

Wirtz rounded off one of his best Liverpool displays since a £100 million (US$131 million) move from Bayer Leverkusen last year with the assist for Munoz to crash home the fourth goal eight minutes from time.
Liverpool fans rejoiced in their rivals' pain with chants of "you are going down."
United have not been relegated since 1974 but find themselves in a battle for survival despite still enjoying one of the biggest revenues in world football.
The 34 goals they have conceded in all competitions is the worst defensive record of any team in Europe's top five leagues this season.--AFP

3f6c01b8c8b47c7d: JUBA: A weekend attack by opposition forces in volatile South Sudan killed 24 civilians, including seven children, local authorities said Sunday.
The world’s youngest country, which gained independence in 2011, has been torn apart by violence between rival political factions, often linked to ethnicity or cattle rustling.

An area called Bol Bol Boma in the country's northwest was targeted in an attack between Saturday night and Sunday morning, Machuei Bith, acting commissioner of Tonj East County in Warrap State, told AFP.
He said the attackers came from the neighbouring Unity State and were part of the SPLA-IO forces loyal to former vice president Riek Machar, who has been under house arrest since March 2025.
Twenty-four civilians, including herders, were killed, Bith told AFP on Sunday evening, raising the previous toll of 15 dead.
The victims included seven children and six women.
Four armed attackers "wearing SPLA-IO uniforms" were also killed, he had said earlier.
A local police officer confirmed this on condition of anonymity.
The toll could rise, and a team is to be sent to the scene, he told AFP.
Last week, two groups from two districts of Warrap State clashed in a market in the town of Makuach, leaving 17 dead and 23 injured, according to local authorities.
Last month, at least 72 people were killed in intercommunal violence on the border between Warrap State and Unity State.
The region has been trapped for years in a cycle of revenge killings, cattle raids, and fighting for control of territory, exacerbated by the proliferation of firearms.
The East African country endured a bloody civil war between 2013 and 2018 between troops loyal to president Salva Kiir and those loyal to Machar, which claimed more than 400,000 lives.
Clashes have intensified in recent months between forces loyal to the two men in the country, where the humanitarian situation is catastrophic in many areas.

SEOUL: South Korea's education minister resigned yesterday over an artificial intelligence-assisted cheating scandal that erupted ahead of the country's key college entrance exams last week.

The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial college entrance exam known as the Suneung.
The annual nine-hour Suneung is widely seen as a ticket to prestigious universities, well-paid jobs and even better marriage prospects in the highly competitive country.
The confession sent officials scrambling to roll out a slew of preventive measures, including blocking public Wi-Fi in testing areas and placing stickers over clothing buttons,
However, education minister Choi Kyo-jin struggled to reassure the public, particularly after remarks he made three days before the exam.

"The exam concluded without any major incidents. However, as the minister in charge, I do not believe I am immune from public criticism that we failed to prepare adequately in advance," Choi wrote on X.
"Now that the exam is over, I take full responsibility and hereby offer my resignation."
President Lee Jae-myung had accepted his resignation, the presidential office said.

Asked during a parliamentary hearing last Monday whether he was confident that authorities could catch would-be cheaters on exam day, the 72-year-old replied: "Due to my age, I am not confident I could."
His response quickly drew public backlash.
Choi did not appear at press conferences in the days leading up to Thursday's exam, where a vice-minister instead announced the preventive measures.

Officials said 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices were identified during Thursday's exam, nearly half of which were detected through three emergency alerts sent by the government to identify smartphones that test takers had failed to hand over. — AFP

b8511cf66f373ef3: ISTANBUL: Several thousand people marched through Istanbul on Sunday to protest a growing crackdown on opposition and independent media outlets.
The protest was called by the main opposition, Yeni Parti, days after police raided Sozcu TV, installing a government-appointed trustee and arresting senior staff members.
It was the third such takeover in a year after similar moves against Tele1, Halk TV, Turkey's most-watched news channel and leading digital news website T24.

Press freedom has come under sustained pressure over the past decade through prosecutions, digital censorship and government accusations that journalists are spreading "fake news", prompting criticism from rights groups at home and abroad.

Carrying a huge banner reading: "We want freedom of thought, freedom of the press and freedom for journalists," protesters marched through the Besiktas neighbourhood, chanting, cheering and whistling, an AFP journalist said.
As they reached the shores of the Bosphorus, several voiced concern at the narrowing space for voices perceived as critical of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his government.
"Our press has been silenced, all opposition channels have been silenced!" a 64-year-old protester called Tunay told AFPTV, without giving her surname.
"All our freedoms are on the verge of being restricted," she sighed. "As a country, we are very unhappy. We are anxious about the future."
The direction Turkey was heading in was "not good", agreed another demonstrator called Koksal, also 64.
"We are living through a period in which all democratic rights have disappeared," he told AFP.
"All democratic journalists and opposition television channels are being shut down, blacked out!" he explained, saying that he, like many others, was being forced to get their news from social media.
"But they are shutting down social media too – all forms of it that are effective."
Over the past two months, Turkey has arrested several journalists over their coverage of a multi-billion-dollar investment fund scandal, at least two of whom remain in pre-trial detention.
Twenty-five journalists are currently behind bars in Turkey, according to figures from the MLSA media rights group.

VIETNAM has withdrawn a proposal allowing children aged 15 to 17 to donate their organs after death, following public criticism in a country where deceased donor transplants remain limited.
The country began kidney transplants in 1992 and performs the most annual transplants in the region, according to state media.
However, the vast majority of transplants in Vietnam rely on living donors.
Transplants in many other nations mostly use organs from deceased donors, expanding their donor pool.
Officials in Vietnam say they are seeking to update a 2006 law on organ and tissue donation, aiming to increase life-saving transplants while safeguarding donors.
A draft submitted to the National Assembly proposed allowing 15- to 17-year-olds to donate their tissues, organs or bodies after death, provided the child's parent or legal representative consented.

But after online backlash, officials removed the under-18 donor provision from a revised draft, with the government saying it had accepted recommendations from lawmakers that only legal adults should be permitted to donate their organs.
Dissent is heavily restricted in communist Vietnam, but opposition centred on whether parental consent could adequately protect child donors from pressure or exploitation.
Criticism also focused on a survey of schoolchildren as young as 7 conducted last month to gather feedback on the draft law.
The po ll prompted questions about whether minors could understand complex medical, legal and ethical issues, state outlet Tuoi Tre News said.
It said "the provision allowing minors to register as posthumous organ donors prompted considerable controversy and differing opinions among the public".
"Taking these concerns into account, the government has revised the draft", stipulating that only people aged 18 or older may donate their organs, Tuoi Tre said.
National Assembly deputy Pham Khanh Phong Lan urged lawmakers to oppose allowing child organ donors, saying: "You cannot sacrifice one child to save another."
The newly revised draft still allows living minors to donate regenerative tissue, for bone marrow or stem cell transplants, to family members when no suitable adult donor is available.
The procedure would require health assessments, counselling and consent from both the child and their legal representative. — AFP

5e6993cec7ee3fbc: WASHINGTON: Americans should expect more technology outages and disruptions as companies and government agencies replace ageing systems, the top US intelligence official said on Sunday.

"And as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, and interruptions in service," director of national intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN's "State of the Union" programme. "That is going to happen."

Clayton was interviewed on the Sunday morning news programmes days after President Donald Trump attributed a recent spate of technology failures to upgrades of companies' technology systems. Clayton said the upgrades were necessary to improve performance and cybersecurity as technological advances strain older systems.

A string of technology failures this month disrupted critical US systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services, a technical glitch that affected several major banks and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network.

Speaking on the ABC program "This Week", Clayton reiterated his previous statements that those outages were not the result of coordinated or state-sponsored actions, attributing them to technical upgrades.
Clayton declined to discuss specifics of separate reports of cyberattacks on the FBI and the department of agriculture, saying he expects investigators to provide answers "in due course".
38c1fc7daef1ddac: KINGSTON UPON HULL: Hull striker Oli McBurnie damaged Brighton's Premier League title challenge with a pair of stoppage-time goals to seal a 2-0 win after an inspired display from Tigers goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis.
Brighton were left to rue Tzolakis's incredible performance and their lack of a ruthless touch in front of goal at the MKM Stadium on Sunday.
Crucially, the Seagulls finished with 10 men after Costinha was sent off for a second booking in the closing minutes.
McBurnie ensured Hull took advantage of Costinha's dismissal as the Scotland international struck twice in the final seconds.
Arsenal's 2-2 draw at Newcastle and Manchester City's 1-1 draw with Fulham on Saturday had given Brighton the chance to accelerate their title challenge.
Brighton have already beaten Arsenal and City this season to emphasise their ability to trade blows with the Premier League's heavyweights.
But their failure to kill off Hull suggested it remains unlikely they can keep pace with champions Arsenal over the course of an entire season.
Fabian Hurzler's side remain in second place but trail Arsenal by six points after their third league defeat in 11 games.
After opening the season with successive victories against Manchester United and Coventry, Hull had gone eight league games without a win to spark fears of an immediate return to the Championship.
Their gritty victory lifted them to 11th place to ease those concerns.
In the first meeting between the sides since 2016, Brighton should have taken a 10th-minute lead when Maxim De Cuyper's low cross reached Diego Gomez in the six-yard box.
Gomez looked certain to score but Tzolakis produced a superb save to claw away the sliding midfielder's shot.
Brighton wasted another good chance moments later as Pascal Gross hooked De Cuyper's cross to Costinha, who somehow scuffed wide with the goal at his mercy.
Yasin Ayari blasted against the crossbar from the edge of the area before the Hull 'keeper stopped Georginio Rutter's close-range shot from the rebound.
Tzolakis came to Hull's rescue yet again in first half stoppage-time.
De Cuyper's cross caused panic in the Hull area and Gomez pulled the trigger with a powerful strike, but Tzolakis was equal to it, sticking out a boot to save.
Tzolakis pushed away Gross's curler immediately after half-time, while Gomez lashed narrowly wide from an acute angle.
Even when Brighton finally got the ball past Tzolakis, they ended up frustrated as Regan Slater headed Charalampos Kostoulas's chip off the line.
The turning point came in the 89th minute when Costinha dragged down Sorba Thomas to stop a breakaway, earning a second yellow card that gave Hull the chance to steal the points.
They did exactly that two minutes into stoppage-time as McBurnie poked home from close-range after Slater and Lucas Gourna-Douath cut through the Brighton defence.
Brighton were shattered and McBurnie rubbed salt into their wounds with another tap-in from Mohamed Belloumi's pass with virtually the last kick of the game.--AFP

PORTIMAO: Marco Bezzecchi won the Portuguese MotoGP sprint race on Saturday as overall leader Marc Marquez slid off his bike when it seemed he was poised to wrap up the championship.
Marquez came to grief on the wet track in the penultimate lap on turn seven while in third place.
The 33-year-old Spaniard will have to wait to claim a joint-record eighth world championship crown in the premier class of motorcycling.
"The important thing is that I'm physically fine," Marquez said.
"Bezzecchi won, he did his job, but tomorrow we'll try to close out the championship."
Raul Fernandez and Marc's younger brother Alex Marquez came second and third, respectively, behind Aprilia rider Bezzecchi, who won his first sprint of the season.
Marc Marquez has a 55-point lead in the overall standings over Jorge Martin, who finished fifth in the sprint, with Bezzecchi third.
"I'm so happy, the sprint has been a torture for me until now, many thanks to the team," said Bezzecchi, who is 62 points adrift of Marquez.
Italian Bezzecchi started on pole and secured a dominant victory, comfortably holding off Fernandez.
Marc Marquez provided the drama, looking almost certain to claim the title from third place but then slipping up in the rain to keep the battle going into Sunday's Grand Prix. — AFP
e6b62dae6f80dcae: LOS ANGELES: "Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping", the sixth film based on Suzanne Collins's hit book series, vanquished the competition in its debut weekend at the North American box office, industry estimates showed Sunday.

With a haul of US$120 million, according to Exhibitor Relations, the Lionsgate film almost tripled the opening weekend of the last entry in the dystopian action franchise, 2023's "Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes".
Analyst David A. Gross called the opening weekend figure "sensational" and "an excellent return" for the series, which revolves around a fight-to-the-death tournament of youths.
"Sunrise of the Reaping" is set more than 30 years after "Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" and over two decades before the blockbuster first quartet of movies starring Jennifer Lawrence.
Joseph Zada, McKenna Grace and Whitney Peak star in the film, which has cameos from Lawrence and original series co-stars Josh Hutcherson and Woody Harrelson.
With US$9.3 million, second place went to "I Play Rocky", a biopic from MGM about Sylvester Stallone's tough road to make the original Oscar-winning "Rocky" – released 50 years ago this weekend.
Anthony Ippolito stars as Stallone, with Oscar-winning director Peter Farrelly ("Green Book") at the helm.
"This is an outstanding wide release for a fall-Awards film," said Gross, who estimates it will be "very profitable" given its "reasonable" US$28 million budget.
Third place went to Paramount's "Ebenezer", starring Johnny Depp as Charles Dickens's iconic misanthrope.
After debuting in first place last weekend, the film took in an additional US$7.7 million, for a total domestic haul of US$32.5 million.
Warner Bros.' "The Cat in the Hat", an animated film with comedian Bill Hader voicing Dr Seuss's famed feline, came in fourth with US$6.9 million, upping its domestic total to US$47.1 million.
Fifth place went to "Godzilla Minus Zero", the sequel to Takashi Yamazaki's visually stunning, Oscar-winning "Godzilla Minus One".
This time, Godzilla reemerges to fight against another iconic monster, the three-headed dragon King Ghidorah.
The film, distributed by GKIDS, took in US$2.7 million for a total domestic haul of US$54.6 million.
700a6d0b858a220c: ROME: AC Milan returned to the Serie A top four as Goncalo Ramos ended his goal drought in a 5-1 thrashing of Frosinone on Sunday, while Juventus hammered Venezia 4-0 to go sixth.
Ruben Amorim's side sealed back-to-back wins for the first time in over a month to go fourth, five points behind leaders Lazio, as club record signing Ramos broke a five-match goalless streak.

Frosinone have been one of the surprise packages of the season since winning promotion from Serie B but dropped to seventh behind Juventus after Luciano Spalletti's side extended their unbeaten run to four matches with a big win in Turin.

"We knew with the pace we have with (Adrien) Rabiot, (Diego) Moreira, (Christian) Pulisic and Ramos, we could make transitions. We changed a little bit the way we play the game because of the opponent, and it was a good night for us."
Milan got off to a flying start with a Gabriele Calvani own goal and a composed Ramos strike inside 19 minutes.

Amorim accused his players of "not helping Ramos" ahead of the game after the Portugal international scored just twice in his first 11 league games following a €74 million (US$86 million) summer move from Paris Saint-Germain.

His third goal of the season was met with a loud roar from the San Siro crowd after he was teed up by France international Rabiot, who became the first Milan midfielder since Kaka in 2004 to notch a goal or assist in seven consecutive league games.

The visitors soon hit back through Patrizio Masini, but Milan pulled clear in the second half with some lethal counter-attacking as substitutes Ardon Jashari and Alphadjo Cisse struck before Pulisic's dinked finish completed the biggest victory of the Amorim era.
Goals from Nick Woltemade, Teun Koopmeiners, Juan Cabal and Randal Kolo Muani moved Juve up to sixth place thanks to a second-half surge in Turin.

Juve coach Spalletti faced scrutiny after an underwhelming start to the season, with Antonio Conte linked with a return to his former club during the international break. But Spalletti celebrated becoming just the sixth coach to reach 600 Serie A games with a resounding win, despite his team being booed off at the break following a goalless first half.
"In the first half, we gave the ball away too much, nobody moved or followed up a pass. It was crucial the players recognised that something was missing," Spalletti told DAZN.
"In the second half, the players were decisive and more relaxed."

Woltemade's introduction after the break sparked the game into life as he pounced on a loose ball to smash home his second league goal in two games before turning provider for Koopmeiners's whipped finish.
Cabal headed home Juve's third before Kolo Muani won and converted a penalty to complete the rout, with all four goals coming between the 53rd and 71st minutes.
Elsewhere, Milutin Osmajic scored a double in a 2-0 win for Genoa at Sassuolo and Bologna were held to a 1-1 draw by Udinese.
Champions Inter visit Atalanta in the final game on Sunday.

b9f5fde4140bfb2f: LIVERPOOL: Mauricio Pochettino said Manchester United must harness the pain from a 4-0 thrashing by Liverpool on Sunday into positive change despite feeling aggrieved by Leny Yoro's eighth-minute red card.
Pochettino's reign got off to a nightmare start when Yoro was controversially sent off for bringing down Alexander Isak.
United never recovered as Liverpool instantly took advantage when Dominik Szoboszlai smashed home the resulting free-kick.
Defeat leaves United still second bottom of the Premier League and at risk of relegation from the English top flight for the first time since 1974.
"It's so painful, we feel pain for that defeat, but we need to keep the head up and translate that anger to an energy to start to work from tomorrow for the next game," said Pochettino.

"I'm not going to change what happened and being respectful is always important," added Pochettino.

5ba05a0599fee523: HERZLIYA: The parties of caretaker Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot concluded a new round of talks on Sunday without reaching an agreement on a possible coalition government, which would require concessions from both sides.
Delegations from Eisenkot's Yashar party and Netanyahu's Likud met for four hours at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, following a first round of discussions last Sunday.

"The latest round of coalition talks... has concluded. The two sides outlined their positions on a range of substantive issues and discussed them in detail," the two parties said in a joint statement.
"A follow-up meeting will be held," they added, without specifying a date or revealing any other details.
A former army chief of staff, Eisenkot has until Dec 6 to form a government, with the possibility of a 14‑day extension, after October elections failed to give either camp an absolute majority.

His 48-member bloc, which needs 61 lawmakers to reach a majority, remains divided over whether to build a coalition through an alliance with ultra‑Orthodox parties, a rapprochement with Arab parties, or a national unity government with Likud.
Netanyahu is pushing for a national unity government, which could see a rotation of the premiership between the two men, a mechanism already tried in Israel.

Such an arrangement could allow Netanyahu to keep his political protection against the corruption charges he faces, as well as continue to oppose the creation of an independent commission of inquiry into the security failures that preceded the Hamas attack of Oct 7, 2023.
But that prospect runs up against Eisenkot's refusal to serve in a cabinet led by Netanyahu, against whom he centred his campaign.
His ally Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister, also reiterated on Saturday his refusal to join a coalition with "Netanyahu or his bloc, under any circumstances".
National 'unity'?
On Saturday, Yashar presented the resumption of talks as "a genuine commitment to forming the broadest possible government", saying that Eisenkot had asked his representatives to explore all options.
But Likud immediately laid down several conditions for its participation in a unity government, a formula backed by Netanyahu.
Among other things, it demands an end to "all personal attacks and incitement to hatred" targeting Netanyahu and his government.
It also called for bringing together "all the parties that support the existence of the State of Israel as the nation‑state of the Jewish people", without the participation of Arab parties.
Netanyahu and his allies regularly target Arab parties, which secured a record 19 seats in the legislature and are opposed to Netanyahu remaining in power.

Likud is also demanding agreement on several major policy positions, notably rejecting the creation of a Palestinian state, maintaining Israeli control over territories in Syria, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip.
It is also pushing for a compromise on conscription of ultra‑Orthodox Jews, a particularly sensitive issue in Israel.
On Friday, Eisenkot warned that he would not allow the talks to drag on, saying he was ready to submit to parliament an "emergency national government".
Although he did not spell out how, his statements suggest a two‑stage plan: the swift formation of a minority government based on the core opposition parties and then broadening it.

A minority of the Eisenkot government could receive support from the 19 Arab party lawmakers, but Eisenkot's right-wing ally Avigdor Liberman rejects working with them and instead advocates an alliance with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.

9869285f83fd61de: KINGSTON UPON HULL: Hull striker Oli McBurnie damaged Brighton's Premier League title challenge with a pair of stoppage-time goals to seal a 2-0 win after an inspired display from Tigers goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis.

69e60cb7b73cece8: GENEVA: The head of the World Health Organization on Sunday pleaded for peace in the epicentre of the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak that has killed nearly 5,700 people.

85d164d808c7484e: TURIN: Carlos Alcaraz won the ATP Finals with a 6-2, 7-6 (9/7) victory over world No 1 Alexander Zverev in the title match in Turin on Sunday.

After becoming the youngest man to complete a career Grand Slam at the start of the season with victory in the Australian Open, the 23-year-old has bookended an up-and-down year with a first title at the season-ending showpiece tournament.
Alongside Roger Federer, Andre Agassi and Novak Djokovic, Alcaraz now forms part of an exclusive list of men to have won all four majors and the ATP Finals.
With his illustrious compatriot Rafael Nadal never managing to win the season-ending tournament, Alcaraz became the first Spanish champion since Alex Corretja in 1998.
"It's been an amazing week. I couldn't finish the week in a better way, so I'm really proud," Alcaraz said after capturing his sixth title of the year.

"I've been through really difficult moments with myself, with my team, and we could go through everything. I'm playing great tennis, so for me, lifting this trophy is something that I've been chasing for a really long time. It means the world to me," he added of the hamstring issue he suffered earlier in the tournament.
A wrist injury had caused Alcaraz to miss a good chunk of the middle of the season and following that victory in Melbourne he failed to add to his seven major titles.

But since returning in August, he has enjoyed a blistering end to the year, winning his last 14 matches to capture trophies at the Vienna Open, the Paris Masters for the first time and now the elusive ATP Finals.
He lost in the season-ender's final to Jannik Sinner last year, but with the injured Italian having curtailed his season, Alcaraz found himself again in the Turin title match against a world No 1.
Zverev, a two-time ATP Finals champion, broke his Grand Slam duck this season by claiming the French and US Opens, catapulting him above Alcaraz and Sinner to the top of the rankings.
Topsy-turvy
The top two seeds in Italy, Alcaraz and Zverev were a cut above the rest all throughout the tournament, both topping their respective pools with three wins from three.
The first set of Alcaraz's semi-final win over Ben Shelton was the only frame either player had dropped all week.

Indeed Zverev had marched into the final without dropping a service game, but he was mightily tested straight out of the traps by Alcaraz as the world number three forced three break points in the very first game before the German dug in to hold.
Alcaraz was not so wasteful two games later, however, as he broke Zverev to love when the 29-year-old overcooked a mid-court forehand.
Zverev forced break-back points in the next game but, after failing to convert, he was left to rue his luck even further as the Spaniard broke to 30 to grow his lead to 4-1.

Zverev wiped out one break but Alcaraz was nonetheless firmly in the ascendancy and pounced for a third time on the Hamburg native's serve in an entertaining seventh game which saw Zverev dejectedly chuck his racquet to the floor after netting a smash from an Alcaraz tweener lob.
A netted backhand by Zverev - his 19th unforced error of the match - on Alcaraz's first set point then brought an end to a surprisingly sloppy opening frame.
Both players exchanged breaks in the second set as it went the distance.
The Murcian took a 3-0 lead in the tie-break before Zverev won the next six points to bring up three set points.
But the Spaniard struck back to wipe them out before getting a mini-break to bring up championship point on his own serve.
The first went begging when he whipped a forehand into the tramlines but he brought up a second with a drop-shot and sealed the title with a backhand.
b1b00e7b8735c384: ANTALYA: The COP31 climate talks ended in failure Sunday as a contentious deal collapsed over fossil fuels and the summit in Turkey stretched into record overtime.
The final agreement was rejected in a chaotic finale to a UN climate summit that ran two days over schedule, underscoring the strains on diplomacy in an increasingly fractured world.
UN secretary-general Antonio Guterres, who urged nations to send fossil fuels "the way of the dinosaurs" during a fiery appearance at the talks, expressed deep dismay.
"I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands," the outgoing UN chief said in a statement.
COP31 negotiations chair Chris Bowen, who unsuccessfully sought to broker consensus among nearly 200 nations, conceded he could not overcome what he called "unbridgeable red lines".
"Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision... And that's disappointing. Very disappointing," Bowen, who is Australia's climate minister, told a throng of reporters.
More than 49 hours after the summit was supposed to end, COP31 president and Turkish environment minister Murat Kurum banged the gavel to conclude the marathon talks.
Calls for reform

Bowen said the summit backdrop was "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory", as soaring energy prices and fallout from the Middle East war complicated the search for unity.
Under pressure to show progress in a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Nepal, Bowen sought an overarching "cover decision" to prove countries were still united in tackling the crisis.
But his plan unravelled as familiar fault lines emerged over fossil fuels, with the EU and Saudi Arabia locking horns over the pace of the shift away from coal, oil and gas.
The negotiations stalled as oil-producing states blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels in the final deal.

"We will not endorse a cover decision... that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change," said Ireland's climate minister, Darragh O'Brien, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency.
"And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels."
Panama, Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands also objected, and as the deal imploded, COP31 became the longest climate summit on record.
Former US vice-president and climate advocate Al Gore said it was "outrageous that a handful of petrostates have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels".
The COP process is "in need of significant reform", Gore said on X, as most countries sought "to move forward in good faith."
Falling short
The outcome revived memories of the failed Copenhagen summit of 2009 and raised fresh doubts about the effectiveness of climate diplomacy.
"It certainly fell short today," said UN climate chief Simon Stiell, describing progress over the marathon fortnight of negotiations in Antalya as "limited".
"The world cannot afford a repeat," he said.
Frustrated by the inertia, countries are pushing ahead outside the COP process.
Around 60 countries joined a first-of-its-kind conference in April on phasing out fossil fuels while several nations at COP31 unveiled their own plans to exit coal, oil and gas.
In a last-ditch bid for compromise, COP31 co-hosts Turkey and Australia could only muster a veiled reference to fossil fuels in the final text.
But the pact also took fire for retaining a call to expand carbon capture – a costly technology championed by the fossil fuel industry.
"We believe that climate change requires all solutions on the table," said Mohammad Ayoub, a climate negotiator for oil giant Saudi Arabia.
Facing blowback over the fossil fuels omission, the co-host nations tried to rally support behind a global goal to electrify the world economy.
They said "electrification" could cut heat-trapping emissions and bolster energy security, but the target was ultimately torpedoed, along with the rest of the doomed Antalya Pact.
'Profound disappointment'
Countries lamented a missed opportunity to reinforce the Paris agreement's 1.5°C target, which scientists expect the world to overshoot in a few years as carbon-cutting goals fall short.
The summit also widened fault lines over science, with a fight over the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) spilling into the negotiations.
"We are profoundly disappointed by the substance of the cover decision," said UK climate negotiator Kate Hughes.
"It moves us backwards on the science... It is a lowest common denominator where it should have been, instead, presenting bold collective ambition on climate action."
As always, the summit laid bare the divide between major polluters driving climate change and smaller nations bearing the brunt of its impact.
Developing nations pushed for a US$120 billion target climate goal, which disappeared from the failed deal.

c94e0f4ef392c3ff: The computerization of cars comes at a price to US consumers, according to the Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), which says that software fees and other charges faced by mechanics push up garage costs.

An investigation by the non-profit consumer group estimates that car repair costs for Americans have been inflated by $12 billion each year, as vehicles integrate more computerized functions. Its report, Closing Shop, is available online.

To find a failed sensor, release an electronic parking brake, or perform diagnostics, a technician has to first connect a laptop or tablet to the vehicle. To so this, the repair shop has to have the right software tools, and that means paying the vehicle manufacturer subscription charges and other fees, in order to get the information they need to complete the job.

If smaller independent repair shops can’t afford all the necessary software or subscriptions, they may be forced to steer customers to authorized dealerships for some fixes – about one in five jobs – and this allows the latter to charge more.

PIRG claims that drivers pay for this through their insurance premiums, even if they never need to get their car fixed, because higher repair costs mean higher insurance claims. It says the price of auto insurance has risen three times as fast as the rest of the US economy since 2012.

Even if mechanics do choose to pay for the software, they spend an estimated collective 83 million hours a year buying, downloading, logging in, and waiting. At typical repair rates, that adds up to $12 billion.

A separate report from the PIRG Education Fund claims that a two-tiered repair model now exists, where independent sites conduct repairs with less information, less powerful diagnostic tools, and higher associated costs than the authorized dealerships.

The advocacy group wants to see legislators take this issue in hand, and has a number of recommendations for them. One is to stop manufacturers from locking out independent mechanics from simple repair jobs like changing brake pads, and require them to support a standard protocol for authenticating independent diagnostic tools.

Another is to give owners control over their vehicle’s data via a standardized platform for accessing telematics repair information, so that the owner can give access to an independent repair shop. Car firms can use the vehicle data to tell owners that a repair is needed and to take it to an approved repair shop, without even disclosing what the issue is.

DIY repairers should be able to get everything they need to fix their own cars. Service information and basic diagnostic software should be free, and PIRG also wants a cap on the license fees manufacturers charge for their official software tools.
“We’ve allowed car manufacturers to build a toll road between the mechanic and the repair,” says Nathan Proctor, leader of PIRG’s Right to Repair campaign and co-author on the report.

“We have a plethora of tolls on the road – subscriptions you need for manuals, diagnostic tools, secure access and more. Not only are all these tolls expensive, they also create traffic jams, slowing down the whole process, which adds to the costs for consumers.” ®

"The unrest has also seriously affected the long-term image, reliability and future prospects of Bangladesh's garment industry in the global market," he said.

00b8a82ccaeac1db: ONE of the most distinctive and colourful aspects of Malaysian multiculturalism is that syncretic amalgam of the Chinese, more specifically Hokkien, way of life infused with Malay cultural elements that is the Peranakan heritage of the Babas and Nyonyas.

The adoption of the sarong in the Nyonya way of dressing and Malay cooking style and ingredients — complete with Nyonya ceramic table wares — have made Peranakan architecture and restaurants a mainstay of tourist attractions, particularly in the former Straits settlements of Penang and Melaka.

Alas, like many things that have become an integral part of Malaysian heritage and folklore, the Peranakan way of life has become quaint and dated. Penang Chief Minister Chow Kon Yeow has just sounded the alarm about its threat of extinction. Speaking at the opening of the 37th International Baba Nyonya Convention in George Town on Saturday, Nov 21, he revealed that there were now only about 1,000 active practitioners of this way of life in the state.

"A language can fade in one generation if parents stop using it at home. A beading technique can vanish when the last person who knows it puts down her needle," Chow had said. If this is the reality, one must wonder if anything can be done this late in the day to try to reverse the decline and ultimate death of the Peranakan way as a living facet of the overall Malaysian social and cultural fabric.

If such a distinct and unique culture way of life is fast dying, can anything really be done to preserve it? Apparently, the Penang government is doing its bit. Chow spoke of gazetting Penang Dondang Sayang and the Penang Hokkien dialect as official State Heritage on Oct 10. A total of RM25 million has also been channelled through the George Town World Heritage Incorporated since 2024 to conserve historical buildings and assets, including Peranakan townhouses and temples.

However, there is only so much official intervention can do to arrest a culture on its death throes unless the community itself does its bit to keep it alive. The spirit is obviously willing, as the convention which brought together delegates from Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and Australia attests.

The delegates must themselves come up with concrete proposals to popularise Peranakan language and other cultural elements among the community's younger generation from the Baba and Nyonya community. The fate of such a unique way of life ultimately rests with the community itself and the steps it must commit to take to perpetuate it within each Baba and Nyonya family unit.

It will be a sad day indeed if only the physical aspects of the Peranakan culture live on one day in museums and heritage buildings as mere tourist attractions instead of it living and breathing as part of the Malaysian cultural mosaic. It will be a most tragic irony if the Peranakan culture continues to thrive as cultural relics instead of remaining as a lived-in tradition.

748a437d0a4c7254: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi got a cold reception in her first outing to China, but Beijing's "blatant" snub — including a visibly scaled-down welcome — could galvanise her conservative base, experts said.

Her trip to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit marked the first time she met Chinese President Xi Jinping face-to-face since her comments about Taiwan last year plunged relations between the two major Asian powers to historic lows.

Takaichi suggested that Tokyo could intervene militarily in the event that China attacked Taiwan, and a furious China, which views the democratic island as part of its territory, retaliated with trade restrictions and warned its citizens not to travel to Japan.

That backdrop meant "there was little she could expect" from the trip, and "little was indeed achieved in terms of Japan-China relations", Noriyuki Kawamura, a professor emeritus at Nagoya University of Foreign Studies, said.
Takaichi, as expected, failed to secure a formal sit-down with Xi on the Apec sidelines.

She was greeted by relatively low-ranking officials on arrival in Shenzhen and without the elaborate performances that welcomed other world leaders, prompting headlines at home about China's "blatant" snub.
Takaichi was also seen struggling to step off her plane because of what appeared to be an unusually large gap between the plane's door and the top of the boarding stairs.
That prompted online speculation it had been done intentionally by Beijing to embarrass her.
Japan's top government spokesman Minoru Kihara told reporters on Friday that they had been aware of the gap.

"Since we had received that information in advance at the site, we took appropriate measures to ensure safety," Kihara said, without specifying whether the Japanese or Chinese side had provided the information.
"As a result, Prime Minister Takaichi disembarked from the aircraft safely," he said.

A mostly expressionless Xi twice exchanged handshakes with Takaichi during the two-day forum — first very briefly and then for about 10 seconds as he listened to her speak with a beaming smile on her face.
However, experts say the cold shoulder might not be all bad news for her domestically, potentially stoking support from the most hardcore of pro-Takaichi voters.
"The way they see it, she didn't give in to the snub she got, but shook hands with (Xi) as many as two times with dignity," Kawamura said.

Yu Uchiyama, a political science professor at the University of Tokyo, also said that China's chilly reception was unlikely to cost her popularity at home, pointing out that public support for her didn't wane even after her Taiwan statement a year ago.
"I wouldn't be surprised to see her loyal supporters become upset by the way she was mocked and grow more resentful toward China," Uchiyama said.
A day after the summit ended, China again said Japan's "most urgent task is to correct its wrong words and actions on the Taiwan issue as soon as possible", according to a foreign ministry spokesman.
Takaichi's critics at home, however, saw the Apec summit as proof of Japan's diminished global standing under her stewardship and her lack of diplomatic acumen.
Footage circulated widely online of Takaichi approaching President Donald Trump after a group photo and patting him on the back, only to be ignored by the US leader who instead walked away with Xi.
That viral image, coupled with Trump's historic trilateral summit with Xi and Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin, fed social media narratives that she is not taken seriously on the global stage.
"Since when did Japan become such a shameful country? The whole world is laughing at us," one post on X said.
Still, concerns for Japan's global reputation could easily be swept aside by a recent surge in distrust towards foreigners that will ultimately help sustain Takaichi's popularity, Uchiyama said.

Complaints about overtourism and soaring land prices linked to foreign investment have sparked Takaichi's push for tighter control of visa rules, prompting voters sceptical on immigration to coalesce around her policies.

On the back of this simmering sentiment "resembling xenophobia", Uchiyama said, it is possible that "people will start to think, 'why is Takaichi treated so badly overseas when she works so hard in her own country?'"

6575265caeb90001: ANTALYA: UN climate talks collapsed on Sunday as the European Union and others rejected a final draft deal put forward by COP31 presidents Turkiye and Australia, saying it was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.

The failed talks reflect world governments' struggle this year to muster ambitious action to address the worsening consequences of climate change, as wars, economic pressures and other crises compete for their attention.

After more than two weeks of negotiations that spilled two days into overtime — making it the longest COP on record — Turkiye's conference president Murat Kurum said at the closing plenary that he could see there was no agreement and confirmed he would not advance any new text.
"There is nothing to do, we did all that we could," he said. "There will be no new text from now on."
He later left the stage in the midst of speeches being delivered by country representatives.
Australia's COP31 president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, called the outcome "very disappointing" and said disagreements over fuels and climate finance were the dealbreakers.
The last time UN climate talks failed to get a deal adopted by all was in Copenhagen in 2009.

Ireland's Environment Minister Darragh O'Brien said the European Union could not support the proposed deal in part because it made no mention of the fossil fuels that scientists say drive global warming.
"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels," he said.
Saudi Arabia and other big oil producer countries had lobbied hard to keep their mention out of the text, according to observers at the summit.
Panama also said it could not support the text because it failed to address the scale and urgency of the climate crisis.

This year's COP is the first since the UN's environmental body in October confirmed the rise in global temperature was set to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), a threshold countries agreed at Paris climate talks over a decade ago to try not to exceed, and beyond which extreme weather impacts intensify.
Belgium's Climate Minister Jean-Luc Crucke said the failure of the deal was a difficult outcome, but appropriate.
"It's not the end of multilateralism, but there has to be courage to say no," he said.

While a blow to efforts to ratchet up international action, the failure to agree a political declaration in Antalya does not erase the obligations agreed by previous UN conferences or remove the technical and legal frameworks governing multilateral action against climate change.
PRESSURE FROM SAUDI ARABIA AND OTHER OIL PRODUCERS
The failed deal had acknowledged the planet's projected temperature overshoot and called for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse it.
That was a big ask from oil-producing countries.

While scientists say removing carbon from the atmosphere — when paired with steep emissions cuts — is vital to avoiding the worst impacts of climate change, critics of the proposed deal said they worried the carbon removal language would be used as a licence to keep pumping oil.

A representative for the Saudi delegation, which supported the deal's mention of carbon removal, told the summit at the closing plenary that he was surprised at the resistance to technology, which he said offered a concrete solution.

Developing countries had also criticised the deal for not providing sufficient new climate finance to help them adapt to a warming planet. The deal had called for a tripling of such finance, but did not specify from what baseline.
The failed deal had also included a goal put forward by Turkiye to expand electricity's share of total final world energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035, from around 23 per cent now.

Proponents of that pledge said it could cut greenhouse gas emissions by speeding the transition away from fuel-powered cars, furnaces, and other equipment. But critics said it could force more costs onto poor nations without providing a clear path away from fossil fuels.

The COP process is the main vehicle through which countries coordinate their efforts to curb global warming. Its annual meeting provides an opportunity for nations to signal they are willing to work together to find solutions and help finance the problems rising temperatures cause.

93931ec690232a48: ARTIFICIAL intelligence is increasingly shaping the fortunes of the US dollar, or at least the investment race surrounding it. The only problem is currency experts cannot agree whether that's for better or worse.
Estimates vary, but many analysts say AI is directly or indirectly responsible for at least a third of US gross domestic product expansion this year.
That alone seems straightforward, but the extent to which the dollar's value is AI-linked is more nuanced.

At its most basic, the lift to US growth, inflation and interest rate expectations from the AI boom is clearly dollar positive — as long as the United States retains its edge and the lion's share of the investment being ploughed into it.
While that may change as the early US investment surge slows, we're not there yet in most people's eyes.

The dollar is clearly reflecting expectations that the Federal Reserve may hike rates aggressively to cool an AI-fuelled boom and rein in inflation, with investors convinced the economy can take it while other central banks hesitate.
Since the Iran war began at the end of February, the US economy has brushed aside the related fuel-price shock with ease, and the AI story seems largely responsible.

US economic surprise indexes compiled by Citi have hit their most positive level in three years this month, contrasting starkly with euro zone equivalents, which have turned negative again for the first time in four months.
Little surprise, then, that euro/dollar has fallen below US$1.10 this week for the first time since March last year, while the broader dollar index has hit its best level in more than 19 months.

But wait. This dollar surge is happening just as Big Tech investors get the jitters over AI valuations and on fear of a capital expenditure slowdown after Democratic victories in the midterm elections prompt calls for at least some data-centre pushback.
The scale of the shakeout in AI-linked stocks has been withering for six weeks, seeing almost 30 per cent wiped off the US Philadelphia Semiconductor Index since early October.
So, why hasn't the fabled "AI dollar" gone with it?
Is the greenback simply lagging, or staying laser-focused on pumped-up Fed rate-rise expectations? Or maybe it's getting a safety bid from worries about equity-market turbulence?
Barclays FX strategists this week reckoned their bullish "AI dollar" view remains very much intact for next year.

Their take hinges on the fact the dollar is mainly tracking AI capex numbers that have been driving GDP outperformance, forcing the Fed to rethink the level of slack left in the economy and where neutral interest rates lie.
But there are as many questions in that as there are answers.
Bank of America's November survey of global fund managers offers some insight.
The poll showed asset managers this month cut tech allocations by the most in 20 years, with a record net near 40 per cent of respondents saying companies are "over-investing".
Perhaps most telling, more than half of the funds expect at least one hyperscaler to cut capex in the next six months.
So AI capex can still be your lodestar, but it may not mean the "AI dollar" is the slam dunk for 2027 that markets have recently rushed to price.
However, there's another way to view the nexus between AI and the dollar.
Deutsche Bank introduces its idea of "chipdollars", akin to the petrodollars of old.
World chip trade now exceeds oil and gas for the first time in history, it says, suggesting a less favourable outlook for the dollar.
The gist of Deutsche's view is that most US-designed chips are made outside the US, mainly in Asia.

As chip demand has soared and prices have risen, huge surpluses have built up in these countries. Much of that cash has been recycled into US capital markets, mostly equities rather than Treasury debt as in the past.
However, a big problem is that equities are three times more volatile than Treasuries, and tech stocks up to 10 times more so.
"Growing dollar dependence on inherently riskier capital should spill into higher US dollar volatility over time," Deutsche strategist Mallika Sachdeva wrote.
There's no doubt the "AI dollar" is now a thing. It's just that it could go either way next year — not unlike its analog predecessor.
The writer is from Reuters

7681ceab9b8dd97b: NEW YORK: For the second time this year, Wall Street bankers and lawyers took home a massive paycheck from a record-setting initial public offering (IPO).
For the second time this year, some of them came out of it complaining in private about how the process was riddled with complications and unlike any they had worked on before.

With SpaceX’s IPO in June, in which banks earned half a billion dollars in fees, bankers chafed over how tightly the Elon Musk-led company controlled the months-long process and kept financial and other information private, making it hard for advisers to do their jobs.

As Anthropic’s IPO, dubbed internally “Project Lantern”, eclipsed SpaceX on Thursday and bankers took home more than half a billion dollars in fees, several people close to the process listed a litany of problems that had plagued the offering process: a compressed timeline, marred by last-minute changes and delays in sharing financial projections; rushed document approvals; and highly unusual restrictions on bankers and concern about leaks — especially after Reuters reported many details from a draft IPO filing weeks before it was made public.

Anthropic, for example, instructed some of its 22 IPO underwriters to limit the number of bankers working on the deal to four, asking the firms to make sure they were senior staff, several people familiar with the matter said.
One of the people said the restriction likely came out of fear that information would leak, and that the banks found a way to work around it anyway.
Underlying these complaints is a new power dynamic between technology companies and Wall Street.

Companies such as SpaceX, Anthropic — and potentially also OpenAI in the future — have come to wield enormous power as the transformative potential of artificial intelligence creates a frenzied demand for their shares, and they are wielding it to do things their way.
That is upsetting some bankers. But banks and investors appear to have little choice but to play along.

“These companies certainly did have some market power to tell underwriters that it’s not going to be business as usual,” said Jay Ritter, a University of Florida professor emeritus who researches IPOs.
“But the big Wall Street firms, I suspect, are still going to be doing things as business as usual for all but maybe OpenAI (after these two deals),” Ritter said.

Ritter added that both SpaceX and Anthropic had negotiated to pay underwriters nothing on the additional shares sold through the greenshoe option. “I don't think most companies are going to be able to demand zero spread on overallotment shares,” he said.
Anthropic, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, the two lead underwriters on the two IPOs, declined to comment.
SpaceX and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment.
Both SpaceX and Anthropic debuted successfully, raising record amounts of money, and their shares rallied initially.
A key part of the underwriters’ job is to market the securities. Thanks to the demand for AI, that was an easy sell — both companies had order books oversubscribed many times over.
After an initial burst in shares, the trajectories of the two big AI firms diverged.
SpaceX climbed to a post-listing peak of US$201.80 on June 16 before retreating below its US$135 IPO price for the first time in mid-July.

Anthropic’s shares closed down 8.5% on Friday after a 17% first-day pop, as a dramatic unraveling of the AI trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector.
Unusual non-competes and restrictions

In the case of SpaceX’s IPO, the people close to the process said Musk’s team dictated terms at every stage. Musk's team told the largest and most powerful US banks — including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley — how to market SpaceX's stock and to whom.
It told some banks the specific order sizes they needed to “fill” — in some cases a few billion dollars — and gave them instructions on what types of investors to bring.
"Banks signed on to underwrite the IPO without being told what they would be paid," the people said.
The underlying current running through Anthropic’s IPO process was what several of the people who spoke to Reuters interpreted as a sense of extreme caution.

Anthropic asked some senior officers at banks working on its IPO to sign legal documents restricting core members of the transaction team from working with rival companies, including OpenAI, Cursor, DeepSeek and Hugging Face, for six months after it went public, according to the people.
Banks routinely manage conflicts and protect client confidentiality. But bankers and lawyers said it is rare for an IPO to impose exclusivity this broad, particularly on individual bankers.

In previous head-to-head IPOs such as those of ridesharing rivals Uber and Lyft, or real estate companies Trulia and Zillow, banks could simply pick a side, in part because the deals were smaller and required fewer banks.
Anthropic, by contrast, needed a broad syndicate to raise the enormous amount of capital it was seeking.
That, some of the people said, explained why Anthropic sought to bind individual bankers with these restrictions.

One banker who declined to sign on to the agreement said it was a challenge to find people who could promise not to actively cover or engage with Anthropic’s peers, especially as several of those companies pursue their own initial or secondary offerings.
Information leaks and late nights
Some of the restrictions were meant to control leaks of information.

Nearly four weeks before Anthropic’s filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), called Form S-1, was made public, Reuters reported on it, revealing details of the company’s financials, risk factors, dealings with other tech companies and other information.
Anthropic also used a product called NetRoadshow to share information, instead of regular PDFs, with most of the banks underwriting the deal.
NetRoadshow logs access details, including information such as who has seen the document and looked at which page. Documents on NetRoadshow also had individual bankers’ names as watermarks.
Leaks continued to surface in the press, but using NetRoadshow complicated bankers' work, including because the platform would not let them save copies of documents, one of the people said.
Anthropic planned to file an updated securities filing, called an S-1A, with the SEC with the price range and to launch the marketing on Nov 10.
To do so, it needed to send a draft to all the banks in its syndicate for them to sign off on it.
The night before it was to happen, a law firm on the deal sent a PDF to the banks about the sale of shares in Canada.
However, it was soon followed by another email asking them to disregard it, saying it “contains incorrect price range and share information,” according to the email, which was seen by Reuters.
The correct S-1A was then sent via the NetRoadshow platform around 2am New York time.
Banks were told they had several hours to sign off on it before it was filed with the SEC.

"This cooperation between the Pahang government, the Fisheries Department and the Pahang Youth Council should continue to strengthen community involvement, particularly among youths and the angling community, in efforts to conserve fisheries resources and protect inland aquatic biodiversity," he said.

He the threat posed by invasive fish species should not be taken lightly, as their presence could disrupt food chains, trigger competition for habitats and threaten the survival of local fish species.

"The Fisheries Department will continue to intensify efforts to monitor and control the populations of invasive fish species, while raising public awareness against releasing non-local fish into public waters.

b000e14618976563: CHUCK Schumer led Senate Democrats through November's midterm elections that gave them a decisive 56-seat majority.
Progressives responded with a collective "thank you, next," arguing he should now make way for a successor.
Critics say Schumer's decades in Washington, his age and his close ties to the party establishment make him ill-suited to lead a caucus increasingly shaped by younger, anti-establishment lawmakers.

"We write first to thank you," leaders of the populist Working Families Party, which backs like-minded Democratic candidates in elections, said in a Nov 13 letter to Schumer that called for a generational leadership change.
"If you step aside at the height of a victory you helped secure, you would show voters that the Democratic Party heeded their call for change.
"The new majority can begin its work united and focused on fighting for the people who elected them."
The top Democrat in the Senate for the past decade, Schumer, who turns 76 on Monday, has projected confidence that his colleagues will choose to keep him as their leader in a secret vote on Dec 1.
"I will be elected majority leader," Schumer, who is strongly favored to win, told reporters matter-of-factly last week.
But in the first contested Senate Democratic leadership race since 1994, the New York senator faces a challenge from Senator Chris Van Hollen, 67.
While only modestly younger than Schumer, the Maryland lawmaker and his progressive allies outside the Capitol have cast him as an agent of change.

Van Hollen has said the 2026 results show voters are demanding the party break with the status quo and adopt a bolder approach that gives new voices, including incoming progressive lawmakers, more influence in the caucus.
The Maryland Democrat has run an increasingly public campaign, though the outcome will be determined in private by 56 Senate Democrats.
At least 16 Democrats have publicly committed to backing Schumer, while only six have said they will vote for Van Hollen.
"I'm in this to win it," Van Hollen said on Thursday.

"That's my goal. I think if we want to move forward on an ambitious agenda like this, we need new leadership. We need to change the culture of the Democratic caucus. People need to have more input. Our new members need to be at the table."
Democrats flipped nine Senate seats in November, including in several states President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024.
Many of the incoming freshmen said during their campaigns that they would oppose Schumer for Democratic leader.
"Do I like Chuck Schumer?" asked Senator-elect Troy Jackson of Maine. "He's been great, but I do think it's time for new ideas."

In an interview last week on CNN's "State of the Union," Van Hollen cited a "hunger for change" among Senate Democrats and said two incoming senators won despite Schumer's efforts to back their primary opponents.
He criticised Schumer for aligning with powerful pro-Israel and cryptocurrency interests in those races.

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said Van Hollen stands out because he understands how Washington and the Senate work as a past chair of House and Senate Democrats' respective campaign arms, and he's willing to take risks.

"Those two things are what we need right now, and we need to rethink the way we legislate," he said, pointing to Van Hollen's trips to advocate for a wrongly deported migrant and to draw attention to Israel's war in Gaza as examples of his willingness to take risks.
Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia suggested the leadership fight reflected a healthy discussion within the caucus about its future direction. "And there's nothing wrong with that," he told Reuters.
Senate Democratic leader is the only unresolved role among Congress' top four positions.

House Democrats last week nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker in the next Congress, where John Thune will continue to lead Senate Republicans and Representative Jim Jordan will succeed Speaker Mike Johnson as the top House Republican.

Schumer is up for reelection in 2028, and losing the leadership race could make him a more vulnerable target, as ambitious Democrats such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez consider running for his seat.
A memo from Ocasio-Cortez's campaign acknowledged she could run for president, Senate or reelection to the House in 2028.
For his part, Schumer has swatted down questions about his future beyond the leadership election.
"I'm focused on 2027 and delivering for the American people," he said on Wednesday.
* The writer is from Reuters
