cb5543f7243bb1fa: SYDNEY, Nov 22 — A man who heroically tackled a gunman at a Jewish festival on Bondi Beach said his wounds still ache as he issued a plea for unity almost a year after Australia’s worst mass shooting in decades.
Fruit seller Ahmed al Ahmed, who was born in Syria and moved to Australia in 2006, was visiting the Sydney beach with his cousin on a Sunday afternoon last December when he heard shots ring out.
He rushed to tackle one of the gunmen as they fired round after round into a crowd of men, women and children.
“I didn’t think about it,” he told AFP.
“Because to save people’s lives, there’s no need to think, when you hear the kids and the women and old people and men and everyone asking for help.”
“Every human has a secret courage in his heart. It comes in the time when needed, when it’s asked.
“I heard people asking, and I did it.”
Fifteen people were killed and dozens were wounded on December 14, 2025, as crowds gathered at the world-famous beach to celebrate Hanukkah.
An elderly woman also died this month from complications linked to her wounds.
Ahmed’s actions have been credited with stopping many more from dying after video of his act of bravery taken by a bystander went viral.
The father of two was lauded as a “true Australian hero” by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, and a fundraising campaign raised millions of dollars.
But Ahmed said much of the initial fame passed him by — he was too focused on recovering from the devastating wounds he suffered.
Face to face with a killer
Tackling the gunman and wrestling the rifle from his hands, Ahmed said he found himself face to face with the killer — a memory that still haunts him “day by day, night by night”.
“He was thinking he’s a god, and no one can touch him,” he said.
In that moment Ahmed was aiming the gun at the shooter.
“I asked him: ‘leave, leave’,” he said.
“I don’t wanna shoot.”
The shooter retreated, leaving Ahmed to take cover behind a tree, where he came under fire.
“I start feeling my whole clothes get wet, you know, similar like someone taking a bucket of blood and threw it on you,” he said.
“And then I start feeling: ‘Oh, I’m gonna die. Oh my God, my kids, my family, my wife. What’s happened?’”
The man he tackled, Sajid Akram, was killed by police at the scene.
His son, Naveed, remains in custody facing a total of 78 charges, including terrorism and murder. He has yet to enter a plea.
Two of the five bullets that struck Ahmed that day are still inside him.
He is on medication for nerve pain and to help him sleep, with the mobility of his left hand still limited.
“I’m still suffering,” said Ahmed, who focused his energies on writing a book — “Light Will Win” — that was released this month.
He is also setting up a foundation to help women and children trapped in violence, inspired by his own difficult upbringing as the son of a police officer in Syria.
He told AFP he wouldn’t do it any differently if he relived that fateful day, despite his wounds.
“I’ve been chosen. God chose me for that and to lead our community not to be divided,” Ahmed said.
‘We are human beings’
The Bondi shooting — one of the worst attacks on Jews worldwide since the October 7 killings by Hamas in Israel — changed Australia forever.
The ruling Labour Party announced a crackdown on gun ownership and new laws allowing them to ban extremist political groups.
However, Australia has also since seen a surge in support for Pauline Hanson’s far-right One Nation party, which has vowed sweeping cuts to immigration, especially from “radical Islamic countries”.
For Ahmed — a Muslim and an immigrant — such politics have no place in the country he calls home.
“I’m a proud Aussie,” he said.
“One Nation — it’s wrong, wrong, wrong, wrong.”
“We have to respect each other. We have to care about each other.”

“You know, we are human beings. No matter where you come from, no matter what your colour, what you are, what’s your religion, we have to treat each other with respect, and don’t judge and blame others.”
“Australia is multicultural.”
Equating the actions of the two shooters at Bondi with his religion — as many have — is unthinkable for Ahmed.
“This is not a Muslim,” he said. “I’m a Muslim, and I put my life in danger.”
“I never heard my religion say to kill innocent people. That’s not right.”
“We are human beings. This is me, Ahmed al Ahmed.” — AFP
e71f7b2677b26408: ANTALYA, Nov 22 — The COP31 presidency proposed an eleventh-hour deal today that again fails to mention fossil fuels — an omission that deepened a tense standoff at the UN climate talks.

The latest offering by summit co-hosts Turkiye and Australia published deep into overtime leaves unresolved tensions over planet-heating fossil fuels but retains a much-sought goal to electrify the global economy.
The proposal needs consensus approval from nearly 200 nations at a closing session today but they have struggled to bridge differences during two weeks of grinding negotiations.
The European Union and other nations have pushed for strong language on transitioning away from fossil fuels, a call that has faced resistance from oil-rich Saudi Arabia.
An EU official told AFP the latest proposal was a “backwards” step, warning there was a “very real possibility” that COP31 ends with no deal.
“I am more pessimistic today than I was yesterday,” the official said on condition of anonymity.
“The situation is difficult, and the outcome is uncertain. The oil-producing countries are putting up a fierce fight,” a German official said.
A Saudi official declined to comment when approached by AFP.
Fossil fuels are a flashpoint at the climate talks and the summit comes against a difficult backdrop of soaring energy prices and geopolitical tensions stemming from the war in Iran.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase out of fossil fuels but a second, pared-down version released Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas.
Threats of a walkout prompted Turkiye and Australia to convene a hurried meeting between the European Union and Saudi Arabia in a bid to broker a compromise.
The latest text introduces a reference to a previous global deal in 2023 to shift the world away from fossil fuels — but stops short of naming them explicitly.
And it retains a contentious push to expand carbon capture and storage, a technology championed by the fossil fuel industry but criticised as costly and ineffective in cutting emissions.
“We are very disappointed with how the text looks,” the environment minister of Antigua and Barbuda, Michael Joseph, told AFP after leaving the COP31 presidency’s offices.
“I can’t honestly say that I’m okay with it passing” in its current state, Joseph said, adding that the draft was “quite silent” on fossil fuels.
Goal to electrify
The draft also calls for global efforts to boost the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 and the expansion of “clean energy”.
The summit had been under pressure to show progress in tackling soaring greenhouse gas emissions in a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Nepal and Indonesia.
Facing blowback over fossil fuels, Turkiye and Australia pointed to “electrification” as a way to cut heat-trapping emissions and bolster energy security.
This works by replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels directly—like diesel cars and gas heating—with electric alternatives.
But some nations had demanded an explicitly “clean” target to ensure the electrification push was powered by renewable energy and not fossil fuels.
Around one-third of global electricity is produced using coal and another fifth using fossil gas.

Attempts by Saudi Arabia, India and Kenya meanwhile to delay the next set of reports by the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) have been another major source of friction at the talks.
The draft text “highlights the importance” of these reports for an upcoming stocktake of global carbon-cutting efforts in 2028.
Dozens of countries across Europe, Africa and the Pacific want these assessments by the global scientific authority on climate change published in time for that crucial stocktake.
Countries have also disagreed at COP31 over how to respond to the looming breach of the 1.5C warming target set under the Paris climate accord.
The latest draft expressed “deep concern” that global warming would cross 1.5C above pre-industrial levels in the next few years.
The talks also jammed over long-running complaints that rich nations are shirking their obligations to help developing nations confront climate change.
The removal of a US$120 billion (RM493 billion) target for climate adaptation angered developing nations. — AFP
fe2a2d2b2f8f1f80: LOS ANGELES, Nov 22 — Airlines carried almost as many passengers last year as cinemas sold tickets worldwide, turning in-flight entertainment into a major market for Hollywood.

Some 4.98 billion movie tickets were sold in 2025, according to the European Audiovisual Observatory, while the International Air Transport Association (IATA) counted around 4.97 billion air passengers.

“The airlines take this very seriously, as do the film companies. It’s a serious market for them,” Terry Steiner, president of Terry Steiner International, the largest independent distributor of in-flight entertainment, told AFP.
When Steiner founded her company in 1993, airlines mostly screened a handful of films on a shared screen at the front of the cabin.
Since then, “things have become so much more personalised due to advances in technology,” she said.
With seatback screens and menus packed with films, TV shows, music and games, the airplane movie has become an almost essential part of flying.
“People watch movies on airlines for different real reasons,” said Steiner, who spent years in advertising and the film industry.

“Sometimes people will watch the same movie over and over again because it makes them feel good. But then there are people who want something new, and they’ll say, ‘Oh, I missed that at the box office. I really want to go see that.’”

Her company acts as the link between studios and airlines, supplying some 100 carriers as well as other non-theatrical markets, including hospitals, prisons, cruise ships, universities and the US military.
Each airline has its own personality, she explained, and her job is to find the films that suit each one best.
‘Around for a long time’
The in-flight entertainment and connectivity market has expanded from US$2.85 billion (RM11.7 billion) in 2015 to a projected US$9.5 billion this year, according to research firm MarketsandMarkets.
One of the drivers, the firm says, is airlines’ growing shift to wireless technology.
With free Wi-Fi and the option to download content, passengers can now turn to streaming platforms to catch up on their shows or discover a documentary.
Steiner acknowledges the parallel with movie theatres, which had to adapt when streaming took off.
But “it’s not a competition at all,” she said. “It’s not stopping the business.”

“There’s a difference between what they can watch there and what we are offering,” added Steiner, who just received the APEX Lifetime Achievement Award, honouring her decades of innovation, leadership and lasting contributions to the global aviation industry.
“We are offering new products, new releases, and you can’t really see them at the same time in streaming,” she said.
“It’s not going anywhere, and it’s going to be around for a long time.”
What to watch on a plane?
Passengers can choose from a wide range of genres and productions from around the world, subtitled and edited for the in-flight format.
So what makes a good airplane movie?
“Horror and thrillers are not so good. Plane crashes are a big no-no,” Steiner said with a smile.
Blockbusters remain a staple, along with “comedies, rom-coms, dramas of a certain sort.”
But the market can be unpredictable.
“You could have a tiny little art film, and it will catch on, or just a few airlines will book it, and it feels great,” she said.
“Or you could have a huge theatrical hit, but it might not be right for the airlines due to violence, sexuality, subject matter or whatever.”
Airplane movies have even become a cultural subgenre of their own, with blogs and specialised websites regularly updating their guides to what to watch at 30,000 feet.
“A long flight is the perfect excuse to finally watch that classic you’ve been putting off,” Harper’s Bazaar wrote in September, recommending, among others, Casablanca, the 1942 Oscar winner.
As for Steiner, she knows exactly what she’ll pick when she flies: “I’ll watch something I have not seen before, for sure.”
Could airplane movies one day get their own category at the Academy Awards?
“Wouldn’t that be great?” she laughed. “I would love that.” — AFP
a0498f6699102af8: TANJONG MALIM, Nov 22 — Witnessing first-hand the difficulties faced by patients in getting to hospitals for regular treatment due to a lack of suitable transportation has prompted Muhammad Anuar Abdul Aziz to establish an ambulance service in the Muallim district here to address the gap.

Interestingly, although operating commercially, AMM Muallim Ambulance, which has been in operation for the past two years, places strong emphasis on empathy and compassion, extending assistance to underprivileged groups.

“In this district, many patients are senior citizens and those suffering from chronic illnesses who require regular follow-up treatment at hospitals but face transportation constraints, particularly those without family members to assist them.

“Hence, this service was established to provide a more accessible medical transportation alternative, especially for patients who need assistance travelling between their homes and hospitals,” Muhammad Anuar told Bernama when met at the AMM Muallim Ambulance office here.

The 32-year-old entrepreneur said that although government ambulance services were available, they generally prioritised emergency cases requiring immediate transportation to hospitals rather than patients attending regular follow-up appointments.

Elaborating further, Muhammad Anuar, who is also a Civil Defence Force (APM) volunteer, said that despite operating as a profit-making business, AMM Muallim Ambulance continued to prioritise cases involving social assistance.

“I admit that as a private company, we are in business to make a profit. However, when we go out into the field and witness first-hand the difficulties these patients face in their daily lives, it makes us realise that we cannot simply turn a blind eye to their plight.

“So far, we have provided free services to some patients for hospital appointments and treatment. They include cancer patients and those who have lost their livelihoods due to health problems,” he said.
The Tanjong Malim native, who is also a father of two, said he started AMM Muallim Ambulance in early 2024 with just one ambulance before expanding the operation to four units.

In addition to five permanent staff members, the company’s operations are supported by part-time personnel comprising doctors, nurses and medical assistants, particularly when field services are required.

Muhammad Anuar said all five permanent staff members had obtained Basic Life Support (BLS) certification to ensure they possessed the essential skills to provide basic assistance and care to patients in the field.

In terms of its scope of operations, AMM Muallim Ambulance offers various services, including non-emergency patient transfers to government or private hospitals, transportation for patients discharged from hospital, as well as medical standby services for various programmes and events.

“We also provide follow-up treatment at patients’ homes, including wound care and dressing, to assist those who have difficulty moving around. These services require the involvement of medical officers, nurses and medical assistants,” he explained.
On charges, he said the fees depended on the travel distance and the patient’s medical requirements, ranging from RM100 to RM300 for journeys within the Muallim district.

“For interstate transportation or patient transfers to destinations throughout Peninsular Malaysia, the estimated charges range from RM800 to more than RM3,000, depending on the distance and the level of medical support required,” he said.
In terms of demand, Muhammad Anuar said his company recorded an average of 20 trips daily.

Looking ahead, he hopes to realise the Ambulans Prihatin Muallim (Muallim Compassionate Ambulance) programme within the next five years through strategic collaboration with the state government to expand free transportation assistance for the B40 and asnaf communities in the district.

“We are currently in the process of completing the proposal paper before submitting it to the relevant authorities. I hope this initiative can be realised to help ensure the healthcare needs of the people in Tanjong Malim are met,” he said. — Bernama

737f2c05f64b962c: SINGAPORE, Nov 22 — Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong will make an official visit to Australia’s Canberra and Sydney from November 23 to 25 for the 11th Singapore-Australia annual leaders’ meeting.
He will arrive at the Western Sydney International Airport (WSI) onboard Singapore Airlines’ inaugural flight to WSI, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said today.
Opened by Australia Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on October 25, the new 24-hour airport received its first passengers on the same day.

The new route, together with the national carrier’s prior services from Sydney Kingsford Smith International Airport, means Singapore Airlines will have five daily flights between Singapore and Sydney.
While in Canberra, the Australian prime minister will host a private breakfast for PM Wong, following which, they will co-chair the 11th annual leaders’ meeting.
PM Wong is also scheduled to meet Leader of the Opposition Angus Taylor.
In Sydney, he will meet New South Wales Premier Chris Minns and call on Governor-General Sam Mostyn, as well as meet with overseas Singaporeans at a reception.

PM Wong will be accompanied by his wife, Loo Tze Lui, Minister for Foreign Affairs Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, Minister for Sustainability and the Environment and Minister-in-charge of Trade Relations Grace Fu, Minister for Transport and Second Minister for Finance Jeffrey Siow, Members of Parliament Alex Yeo and Dr Hamid Razak, and officials.
During PM Wong’s absence, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade) Gan Kim Yong will be the Acting Prime Minister.
The upcoming meeting between Albanese and PM Wong will be their fourth this year.
They met in April when the Australian prime minister made an official visit to Singapore, where the two leaders issued a joint statement on economic resilience and trade essential supplies.
More recently, the two leaders met at the Asean-Australia Summit and on the sidelines of the 33rd Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting.
Singapore is Australia’s sixth largest trading partner and the sixth largest source of foreign direct investment as at 2023.
The two countries upgraded bilateral relations on the 60th year of diplomatic ties during PM Wong’s visit to Australia in October last year.

Dubbed CSP 2.0, Singapore and Australia agreed to deepen partnerships across six existing key pillars — economics and trade, defence and foreign affairs, people-to-people, science and innovation, digital economy, and green economy — while covering new and emerging areas such as cyber, digital, space and artificial intelligence.

Singapore, as the fifth-largest refinery and export hub in the world, and among the top 10 exporters of petrochemicals, is one of the major sources of Australia’s oil, accounting for 26 per cent of refined fuel imports, 55 per cent of petrol imports, about 23 per cent of jet fuel, and 16 per cent of diesel.
Meanwhile, Australia, as the world’s second largest exporter of liquefied natural gas (LNG), is a key source for Singapore, supplying about a third of the city state’s needs. — AsiaOne

d0fe4915832dd827: GEORGE TOWN, Nov 22 — Penang is not required to make any payments to Perak before water supply under the Bulk Water Supply Agreement (BWSA) begins, Chief Minister Chow Kon Yeow said, dismissing claims that the state would have to pay RM210 million annually for 40 years despite receiving no water.

522d710dd7f24c0a: Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be. All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of sexism. But one of the tragedies of Labour’s 18 long years of exile from power and the climactic defeat of organised labour in the miners’ strike was the fact that they opened the way for the wholesale reinvention of work and watershed developments that we seem to be only just waking up to. 03465a8e3093a278: BANGKOK: Thailand plans to ban exports and transit shipments of chemicals used in rare-earth mining following the detection of elevated arsenic levels in rivers in the northern part of the country and will work with China and Myanmar in addressing the pollution.

Thai officials will meet with representatives from both countries on Nov 24, followed by a Thai-Myanmar working group meeting on Nov 25–26, deputy prime minister Yodchanan Wongsawat told a briefing in Bangkok on Saturday.

Thai foreign minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said earlier this month that the government will seek urgent action from Myanmar over suspected mining pollution in the cross-border Kok and Sai rivers after arsenic levels surged to as much as 30 times the Thai standard, threatening public health and farmland in the country’s north.

A poll by the prominent Suan Dusit University in Bangkok released on Sunday found that 89.2% of respondents were concerned about river contamination, while 85.9% had little or no confidence in the government’s ability to address it.

Thailand will seek permission to install four water monitoring stations in Myanmar, with another four on the Thai side to ensure consistent readings, natural resources and environment minister Suchart Chomklin said at the same briefing.
The government also plans to designate a stretch of the Kok River as a pollution control zone from Dec 2 to tackle cross-border water contamination, Yodchanan said.
"Authorities are reviewing regulations on the restrictions for the shipments of chemicals to limit the impact on other industries," he added.
The proposed pollution control zone would cover more than 150km of the Kok River within Thailand.
Authorities also plan to install about 20 monitoring points along affected rivers and tributaries, alongside laboratories in Chiang Mai and Chiang Rai to speed up testing, according to Suchart.
"Officials have identified 10 groundwater sources in Chiang Rai and are preparing 14 village water supply systems to provide clean water to nearly 20,000 people," Suchart said.

Prime minister Anutin Charnvirakul said on Saturday that he raised the issue with Chinese president Xi Jinping on Nov 20 and that Beijing had pledged to cooperate and provide technical support to improve monitoring of water quality.

Anutin said Thailand would also raise the pollution issue at the Ayeyawady-Chao Phraya-Mekong Economic Cooperation Strategy meeting that includes representatives from Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and Vietnam on Nov 28 and a Mekong-Lancang leaders’ meeting in China in late December.
3044158d781bb872: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 22 — Containing medical insurance premiums alone will not resolve rising healthcare costs, as the underlying cost of care must also be addressed, Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) Governor Datuk Seri Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said.
He said rising medical costs, escalating insurance claims and higher premiums are important vital signs indicating pressure on the healthcare system.

Private spending on healthcare, including insurance and out-of-pocket expenditure, is now almost on par with public spending, while medical plan payouts have increased more than 13-fold from less than RM1 billion in 2003.

“For some families, maintaining meaningful medical protection is becoming more difficult,” he said in his keynote address at the 103rd Reunion Dinner of the Alumni Association of King Edward VII College of Medicine and University of Malaya and University of Singapore in Petaling Jaya last night.
The text of his speech was released today.
Abdul Rasheed said that as part of efforts to make medical protection more accessible, MediAsas, a base medical insurance and takaful plan, is scheduled for launch in January 2027.
“(The plan) will undergo periodic reviews by an independent MediAsas board to ensure its benefits and pricing remain relevant,” he said.
Other reform measures include greater transparency in medical treatment costs, he said, noting that treatment costs for the most common procedures have already been published, alongside drug prices.
Abdul Rasheed said there is also a need to progressively move from volume-based to value-based healthcare, rewarding care that works rather than simply the amount of care delivered.
BNM, together with the Health Ministry, is developing payment approaches that make costs more predictable while creating stronger incentives for appropriate, efficient treatment, he said.
“Through MediAsas, this includes steps towards diagnosis-related payment approaches (to) make costs more predictable while rewarding providers for greater efficiency.
“When costs are predictable, coverage can be too,” he added.
On digital healthcare, Abdul Rasheed said interoperable electronic medical records (EMR) are now available, with pilot testing underway across public hospitals and selected private hospital groups.

He also highlighted the Healthcare Partners Protocol and Solutions Committee, which brings doctors, hospitals and insurers together to strengthen collaboration, resolve claims-related issues and clarify protocols.
Emphasising the role of medical professionals, Abdul Rasheed said doctors are central to ensuring patients received appropriate treatment and healthcare resources are used effectively.
“Value-based healthcare cannot simply be a financing concept or regulatory programme. It has to become part of how we think about good healthcare.
“Not less care for the sake of reducing cost. But the right amount of care. At the right time. For the right patient. With the right outcome,” he added. — Bernama

a4baa541b572244c: BAE Systems is developing a passive radar system it claims could track airborne threats at a fraction of the cost of conventional radar, using existing broadcasts rather than transmitting signals that could reveal its position.

The defense biz says its covert radar technology detects reflections of television, radio, and mobile network transmissions from airborne objects. That lets it monitor airspace without broadcasting its own radar signal.

Conventional active radar transmits radio waves and measures their reflections to locate objects. But broadcasting like this is the equivalent of using a powerful searchlight to see in the dark, making the radar station itself highly visible to anyone monitoring the same radio frequencies.

Passive radar is not new, but BAE says its use of commercial off-the-shelf equipment brings the cost down to as little as a tenth that of comparable active systems. The equipment is compact enough to deploy from an SUV.

BAE says it can track targets ranging from small drones to larger aircraft and provides a clear 3D air picture with data such as target speed, heading, range and altitude. This could make it suitable for law enforcement agencies and for guarding critical national infrastructure, as well as military users.

BAE pitches the system for sites such as airports, where avoiding interference with existing equipment matters. Because it doesn't transmit its own radar signal, passive radar avoids adding another broadcast to the mix.

"While people are sat at home watching TV, our new radar technology can use transmissions from those TV and radio broadcasts without disturbance to keep crucial infrastructure such as power stations and air force bases safe from drone attacks. It also provides a boost for armed forces, allowing a soldier to monitor the battlefield undetected," says BAE's product manager for Counter-Uncrewed Systems (CUxS) Chris Shepherd.
The system will undergo live trials throughout 2027 with potential law enforcement, defense, and critical infrastructure customers, BAE says.

Elsewhere at BAE Systems, the news is less rosy: The Financial Times reports that it plans to shed more than 1,000 jobs at its head office and air division in the UK. The company says the cuts will help it become more agile and meet government demands for "greater speed and efficiency" in delivering critical defense products. ®

e8f0a058f0614b39: Web hosting might seem like an unlikely on-ramp to supercomputer administration, but it set Mark O'Shea on his way to running some of Australia's most powerful machines.
O'Shea is team leader for supercomputing operations and senior supercomputing systems administrator at Australia's Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.

Pawsey is home to Setonix, an HPE Cray EX supercomputer with more than 200,000 AMD EPYC CPU cores and hundreds of AMD Instinct MI250X accelerators. Its GPU partition ranks 87th in the November TOP500 and 37th in the Green500, which measures computational performance per watt.

"Working in web hosting wasn't much different to what I was doing a few years later with supercomputers," O'Shea tells The Register. "Datacenters are essentially several thousand computers, as are supercomputers.
"So, we essentially had the same problems," he says, especially as regards cooling and power management.
There's no single formal route into supercomputer administration in Australia, O'Shea says. He picked up the necessary skills over time.

Andrew Underwood, Dell's chief technology officer for high-performance computing and artificial intelligence across the Asia-Pacific, Japan, and China, says that lack of formal training means some supercomputer admins start in academia.

He's observed that many HPC admins emerge from the sciences, catching the computing bug during their studies. A biologist working with a massive genomics database, for example, might discover a taste for running the systems behind it.
"The biologist might decide they want to be someone working in IT helping other biologists transform their industry," Underwood says.
"One of the things I really admire about people who work in the supercomputing field is they take it so seriously," Underwood adds. "It's almost a passion, a hobby, more so than it is a job."
"They want to play that real supporting and foundational role of assisting and engaging with scientists to help them use the technology to solve the problems the world faces."

O'Shea agrees, noting that many people who get into supercomputer admin are PhD graduates who stick around their universities after they graduate. Some of them gravitate toward running the departmental computers and then wind up in supercomputing.

"There are many roles around universities allowing people to be introduced to [supercomputer administration] while still doing enterprise-style or more departmental admin for researchers and system administration," O'Shea says.
Regardless of how a supercomputer admin gets their gig, both O'Shea and Underwood say the supersysadmin community is tight knit – which may not always be a good thing.

"As an industry in supercomputing, we need to be open to people from diverse backgrounds," Underwood says, "and we need to build these frameworks like the Student Cluster Competition, conferences like eResearch and the SC Conference, where students can get educated and systems admins get exposed to continual training."

Back at Pawsey, O'Shea notes that while the supercomputer systems admin job is interesting and challenging, there's one thing that always gives Setonix's admins a kick: seeing what scientists achieve with the machine.
One early highlight, O'Shea says, was producing a detailed image of a supernova remnant, crunching through a 43 TB dataset in the process.

402e4abf38c942a1: In South Asia, survivors of sexual and physical abuse are often met with judgment and stigma
Originally published on Global Voices
Photo via Pratistha Gautam. Used with permission.
Editorial note: This article contains mention of gender-based violence, sexual assault, violence against children, and child sexual abuse, which may be triggering for some readers.

November 25 to December 10, 2026, marks the UN’s 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence. However, even as gender-based violence gets more recognition globally, survivors are still struggling to access social or legal justice. South Asia is no exception to this. Global Voices sat down with one survivor of childhood abuse who uses her experience to fuel her advocacy work today.

South Asia is home to nearly one quarter of the world’s population, woven with a diverse, culture-driven fabric where women are often celebrated as goddesses. However, this veneration doesn’t necessarily mean South Asian women are safe or free from abuse.

In Nepal, there are far too many examples of crimes against women and girls. For instance, Nirmala Panta, 13, was found dead in a sugarcane field — a case which has remained unsolved since 2018. Bhagirathi Bhatta, 17, was choked to death when returning home from school in 2021, and Inisha BK, 16, was found unconscious in the Janagaran Community Forest in Surkhet in early 2026. A similar yet shocking case is that of a 3-year-old Garima, who was found dead inside an abandoned house in Jeetpur in southern Nepal. While these tragic rape and murder cases leave deep scars in Nepal’s national psyche, even more cases go unheard and unreported.

Sparking a nationwide outrage, such cases force the country to confront a collective shame. They raise questions around human morality, diminishing trust and affection in society, and breakdowns in the legal justice system. In the face of these atrocities, women took to the streets, demanding justice and accountability. But their calls fell on deaf ears.
Pratistha Gautam’s story

“I was 11 years old when I was sexually abused by my close maternal uncle for four days,” said Pratishtha Gautam in an online interview with Global Voices in November 2026. Opening up about this incident was a real challenge for her, yet she was committed to sharing her story.

Her childhood was by no means easy. She moved regularly as a child, and at seven years old, she was sent to her maternal uncle’s house for a year because her parents had to move away to address her younger brother’s health issues.
It was in this house that a monster took away her innocence.

After four days of abuse, she escaped on the fifth day with the help of her neighbors. Finally getting a chance to flee from her abuser, she “rushed to my room, quickly happened to lock the door by chance, thankfully, and began to scream out to my neighbors.” She had witnessed men mistreating women in her neighborhood growing up and feels lucky that her cries weren’t met with indifference.

She felt neglected growing up and believed her parents loved her younger brother more. This left her with a sense of detachment from her family. The abuse only compounded her challenges. As she says, “It was not easy at all.”

The experience has left her with scars: “I have been awakened with nightmares since that incident, making my sleep extremely difficult.” She also suffers from panic attacks when she sees material about sexual abuse. She describes feeling like her heart is swollen and being torn apart. When triggered, she often freezes up and dissociates.

According to research from the American Academy of Pediatrics journal, child sexual abuse can be incredibly detrimental to a person’s long-term mental well-being. Child abuse survivors are more likely to suffer from anxiety disorders, depression, eating disorders and disturbances, sleep disruption and insomnia, and dissociation, as well as adverse physical health conditions and attachment issues, according to the Center of Expertise on Child Sexual Abuse.

This highlights the immense scale of pain that many children experience when they are victims of sexual abuse. Not everyone is able to speak out about such abuses. This is particularly true in South Asia, where there is a social stigma around abuse, due to entrenched ideas around “purity.”

She resents suggestions that it is women’s responsibility to not “tempt” men or draw attention to themselves. “Why should we be the ones to cover ourselves up?” she asks. She refuses to hide and stay silent while her abuser “is living free somewhere.” She refuses to remain invisible.

Even as many countries make strides in gender equality, gender-based violence continues to be a major issue. In a 2023 report, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that nearly one in three (31.6 percent) of women worldwide have been subjected to either physical and/or sexual violence in their lifetime — roughly 840 million women and girls.

At the root of gender-based violence lies a belief in male superiority. Not all men would openly endorse this belief, yet many see themselves as protectors of the women in their lives: their sisters, mothers, girlfriends, and wives. But this notion of protection is deeply flawed, especially when it comes at the cost of women’s freedom, mobility, access to opportunities, dreams, and agency.

Gautam recognizes this notion in her own upbringing. She had dreams of her own and was ready to chase them, but her family had a different plan for her. They wanted “to get me married off,” she said. She kept her independence through stubbornness and determination.
A trauma that persists

Today, Gautam lives in Adelaide in South Australia. She suffers from complex PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) and works as a mental health clinician helping other survivors of abuse. She reflected, in a heavy tone, on being a thousand miles away from home but safe and independent.
Image via Pratistha Gautam. Used with permission.

PTSD and insomnia aren’t the only consequences of her abuse. While she was once married, she struggled to cope with her trauma, and it negatively impacted her relationship, eventually leading to divorce.

As part of her treatment, Gautam has met regularly with psychotherapists over the years. Eventually, even that wasn’t enough. She put everything on hold for a year and gave herself time and space to focus on her mental health. She believes she would have difficulty living a normal life and still struggles with relationships. “I hate men. I used to hate them and still have trust issues,” she said.

Even as she struggles to process her own trauma, she also works to help others recover from abuse and offers pro bono psychological counseling. Being part of the solution has in some ways helped her heal. Her passion as a mental health clinician goes beyond her own individual experiences to the collective — a reminder to be empathetic as humans first.

While she primarily works in Australia, she is also committed to helping women back in her home country of Nepal. She has collaborated with Rakshya Nepal, an organization in Nepal that protects women and girls from sexual exploitation and trafficking.
Reflecting back on the choices she made, she said, “I cannot imagine if I could afford this luxury of mental space if I were not in Australia.”

This is also a testament to how South Asia treats survivors of sexual and physical abuse — even if they gather the courage to speak the truth, too often they are met with judgment and scorn. Part of this is due to limited regard for mental health, but it’s also about entrenched gender roles and strong societal expectations. There is a popular saying in Nepal reflecting these persistent gender dynamics: “timi ta chori manche ho ni” and “chora manche vayera gari halchan ni,” which roughly translates to “you are a girl, and boys will be boys.”
Written by Susmita Aryal

6f2d9f153e249ab8: Following the 2026 state elections, many are predicting that Umno and Perikatan Nasional (PN) will team up and win power in the next general election (GE).

Most analysts see it as an almost certain clash between PH and a PAS-led PN in the peninsula. Some argue that GE16 will be fought primarily on traditional flashpoints: Malay rights, Islamic values, economic delivery, and non-Malay frustrations.
That may be true, but I think this election is more likely to boil down to a dramatic contest of political agility and manoeuvres between Ahmad Zahid Hamidi and Anwar Ibrahim.

While East Malaysia’s blocs in Sabah and Sarawak will—as always—play a decisive kingmaker role post-election to protect local autonomy, the battle to capture Putrajaya itself remains a peninsula-driven contest. Within that crucible, GE16 will essentially be a battle of wills and operational skill between two men who know how to survive at the top.

Zahid's core competency is political engineering. He treats relationships as leverage, public statements as bargaining signals, and possesses a feel for power dynamics that is probably unmatched in modern Malaysian politics.

Yet, while his "blue wave" narrative resonates powerfully with Malay voters, it does not travel cleanly to the urban, mixed, and non-Malay constituencies that ultimately decide a national majority—though Umno relies on its traditional Barisan Nasional coalition mechanisms to manage multi-ethnic seats.

Conversely, Anwar’s strength lies in policy, narrative, and survival. A reformist with international credibility and a coherent platform, Anwar has ridden the waves of triumph and defeat, navigated various crises, and risen to become prime minister.
He is waging a war of attrition, using his control over the national budget and administrative levers to delay the electoral clock while Zahid tries to force an early hand.
To understand why this duel will define GE16, we must look back at how their paths have intertwined over the last three decades.

When the bitter fallout between then-Umno president Mahathir Mohamad and his deputy Anwar erupted in the late 1990s, Zahid—serving as Umno Youth chief—initially backed Anwar. Yet, after Anwar’s sacking in 1998, Zahid quickly pivoted, reconciled with Mahathir, and demonstrated the classic Umno survival instinct: prioritising pragmatism over loyalty.

From that point, Zahid embarked on a meticulously calculated ascent: consolidating his base in Perak, building a formidable personal network, becoming Umno’s deputy president, and finally taking the top spot in 2018.

Following the 2022 humiliation when Umno won just 26 seats, calls for his resignation mounted. He weathered the storm, teamed up with Anwar to secure the post of deputy prime minister, and used his proximity to power to reassert Umno’s relevance.

Anwar, for his part, pursued his long game: forming PKR, driving the Reformasi movement, riding the 2008 opposition surge, and eventually making an uneasy truce with his arch-rival Mahathir to wrest power in 2018. But political betrayals caused Mahathir’s government to collapse, paving the way for short-lived administrations under Muhyiddin Yassin and Ismail Sabri Yaakob.

The inconclusive 2022 general election threw Anwar and Zahid together into an improbable partnership. Zahid secured ministerial perks and shared authority, and by December 2025, the Attorney General’s Chambers granted him a discharge not amounting to an acquittal (DNAA) on the 47 corruption charges involving the Yayasan Akalbudi fund.
Critics blasted the move as a classic manoeuvre to shield allies and buy loyalty, though it has consistently been denied.
Since then, Zahid has supercharged Umno's stature among Malay supporters by leaning into the reliable narrative of Malay unity and perceived threats to Malay dominance.

The resulting PAS-Umno tactical cooperation benefits both parties. This momentum was reflected in the 2026 state elections, though formulas varied: in Johor, BN swept 48 of 56 seats alone (while PN supporters were quietly instructed to back BN in uncontested seats), whereas in Negeri Sembilan and Melaka, BN and PN formally shared seats.
True to form, Zahid is keeping all options open by refusing to commit to a formal GE16 pact with PN, executing a masterstroke that forces both PH and PN to compete for Umno's favour.

Simultaneously, he has tightened his internal grip: the Umno Supreme Council has postponed party polls to a date no later than six months after GE16, and an "unconditional open-door" policy has welcomed back former rivals like Khairy Jamaluddin and Hishammuddin Hussein. Zahid is building a broad electoral coalition while keeping his own leadership uncontested.

Demonstrating his pragmatic ambition further, Zahid acknowledged Gabungan Parti Sarawak's (GPS) absolute regional dominance by confirming that BN would sit out the Sarawak state election to respect East Malaysian autonomy and keep the federal focus razor-sharp on the peninsula.

Conversely, Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan has been battling severe internal friction. PKR has suffered heavy blows: high-profile figures like Rafizi Ramli and Nik Nazmi Nik Ahmad departed to form Parti Bersama Malaysia, Nurul Izzah went on indefinite leave as deputy president, and the party suffered a major rout in Melaka.

Anwar's prospects now hinge heavily on timing. PH’s parliamentary term runs until December 2027, with GE16 legally due by February 2028. Every month of delay buys both sides different advantages: Zahid consolidates his machine, while Anwar attempts to deliver tangible economic relief.
If Anwar can produce visible improvements in the cost of living by late 2027 and push through more reforms, the votes will return.

Furthermore, PH retains a structural edge in the urban and mixed constituencies that decide a national majority. State elections are typically less diverse and more heavily Malay-majority, making the "blue wave" less effective on a national scale.

Moreover, non-Malay support for PH is driven less by uncritical loyalty and more by a structural fear of the alternative (a PAS-led PN). As the Malay vote consolidates behind BN-PN, non-Malay voters increasingly rally behind DAP and PH as a defensive counterweight, keeping PH viable nationally even as it bleeds support in heartland seats.
Also, as seat negotiations between Umno and PAS heat up, deep fractures in the Malay-Muslim vote will be exposed.

Yet, as these electoral calculations play out, Zahid carries a heavy legal overhang. The Court of Appeal allowed the Malaysian Bar's judicial review challenge in May 2026, the Federal Court granted Zahid and the AG leave to appeal in October 2026, and the High Court has slated case management for June 2027, with the full hearing deferred until the Federal Court appeal concludes. It is a sword of Damocles that is certain to become a major campaign issue.

Ultimately, GE16 will be a contest of political operators. The 2026 state elections suggest Zahid holds the momentum. However, Anwar’s control over the electoral timeline, his economic levers, and the structural divide between state and national electorates keep the race wide open.

What began as a clash between reform and patronage has evolved into a masterclass in machine politics versus institutional statecraft. The next general election will not be decided by slogans or promises alone—it will be decided by who plays the sharper game over the next six to twelve months.

52e6204978a8560b: The Najib Razak saga has, in many ways, eclipsed even Anwar Ibrahim’s ‘Reformasi’ struggles, which saw many of us old-timers go through some very harrowing times.
Both were deputy prime ministers and served under Dr Mahathir Mohamad.
Their parallels are striking. Anwar was sacked, charged, convicted and spent time in prison before being pardoned, later rising to become prime minister.
Najib took the opposite route. An Umno prime minister, no less, he lost power, was charged, convicted and served time, before being pardoned twice, albeit conditionally.

Despite the unbridled demonisation of the DAP and non-Malays as traitors out to wreck a nation, it must be stressed that it was a courageous Malay judge—a woman no less—who sent the former Umno president to jail.
Now, there are many “firsts” in this saga.

Najib went on trial in what became known as “the world’s largest kleptocracy case”, a notorious distinction that brought his party and the country the sort of international headlines it could have done without.
Secondly, Najib is the first prime minister to be incarcerated in Malaysia.
And thirdly, this is the first documented house arrest case in the country, even preceding a proposed new law that the government intends to introduce in Parliament.
Now there are many views about the former Pekan MP’s house arrest.
Among them is the perceived double-standard. Why is Najib allowed these perks, while other convicts are not?
There is also the matter of the king’s decision in Najib’s pardon application. Must the king adhere to the pardon board’s advice? And should the minutes have been declassified?
As for the king’s decision to allow Najib to be placed under house arrest, that is his prerogative, one that is enshrined in our Federal Constitution.
He has chosen to exercise it in Najib’s favour for reasons known only to him. Not being privy to that decision, and without any insights into his reasons, it would not be proper to comment on it.
But it has to be emphasised that there is no prefect constitution, no perfect rendition of history, and no perfect interpretation of religion.
Hence, we need to rely on the wisdom and experience of those who make such decisions with the nation’s best interests at heart.
The recent publication of the minutes of that meeting of the pardons board has given the public a rare insight into what transpired and the stance taken by each board member.
That said, the published document should not trigger a blame game.
Whatever one feels about the decision, it must be acknowledged that it went through due process.
If Malaysians believe that process should be improved or changed, the proper avenue is through their elected representatives in the Dewan Rakyat.
For my part, I am satisfied that due process has been observed and therefore respect and accept the decision reached.

Still, I find it comical that Umno has been so worked up over the declassification of the document simply because it was not accompanied by a royal decree, even arguing that the omission was somehow tantamount to disrespecting the Malay rulers.
Has that same respect been shown to Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir amid the seemingly unending constitutional crisis in Negeri Sembilan, a controversy that bears Umno's fingerprints all over it?
The time has come for us to put the brouhaha over Najib's house arrest to rest.
At the end of the day, Najib was convicted for a crime, served some time in jail, applied for a pardon, as allowed by law, and was granted one.
Placing him under house arrest does not erase his criminal conviction.
There is no value in bickering over the merits of the house arrest as it serves no purpose other than to instigate one party and weaponise the issue.
It is time we focused on the more important stuff, like the bread-and-butter issues affecting ordinary Malaysians. That is a far more worthy cause.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

9b6b75dea9243402: Tony Pua has apparently discovered a remarkable constitutional innovation: when the king grants clemency against objections, publish the objections and call it accountability. Yet the awkward question remains. Does displaying dissent explain the constitutional decision, or merely provide political cover for those embarrassed by its outcome?
On Nov 18, Pua circulated pages described as declassified minutes from the Sept 18 Federal Territories Pardons Board meeting concerning former prime minister Najib Razak.

According to news reports, Attorney-General Dusuki Mokhtar and federal territories minister Hannah Yeoh opposed house arrest. The king nevertheless approved a conditional pardon. These reported extracts warrant authentication and contextual examination; a Facebook upload is not itself a constitutional certificate.
Let us distinguish three matters politicians seem determined to blend: the right to disagree during deliberations, the authority to decide, and the legality of disclosing deliberations afterwards.

Article 42 establishes the constitutional pardoning framework. Recording objections does not confer a veto. Nor does royal authority automatically exempt officials from explaining how records were classified, accessed and released.

Pua’s intervention invites sharper scrutiny precisely because he presents disclosure as vindication. Vindication of what? That DAP representatives objected? The minutes reportedly establish that much. That the government’s political conscience is therefore spotless? That is a considerably longer leap, requiring evidence rather than screenshots and self-congratulation.

DAP cannot simultaneously celebrate constitutional procedure when it documents ministerial dissent and treat the resulting royal decision as someone else’s political inconvenience. A constitutional monarchy is not a buffet where parties select the minutes they enjoy and leave the decision behind. If dissent was properly recorded, publicly explain it. If the decision was lawful, respect it. Neither proposition requires surrendering criticism of corruption.

Umno is justified in demanding a clear account of the disclosure process. Its leaders have asked whether the documents were officially declassified, who authorised circulation, and whether the palace was consulted. Those are legitimate institutional questions, although assertions that publication necessarily constitutes an insult to the king require a specific legal and factual foundation. Defending royal dignity should strengthen constitutional precision, not replace it with outrage.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim faces the more uncomfortable examination. He has publicly defended every prisoner’s access to the pardon process and acknowledged the king’s constitutional role. Fine words. But was his administration’s handling of disclosure governed by a consistent rule, or by whichever political controversy happened to be burning that week? The public deserves an answer from Putrajaya, not another seminar on principles everyone claims to cherish.

The comparison with Anwar’s 2018 pardon is unavoidable. Wan Saiful Wan Jan has called for those Pardons Board minutes to be released, too. That demand does not prove irregularity in either pardon. It does expose the weakness of selective transparency. If publication serves public confidence today, what principled distinction governs disclosure of earlier proceedings? Privacy, privilege and national security may justify redactions; political convenience is not a constitutional doctrine.

There is an important qualification. Minutes capture deliberation, not necessarily every legal consideration or the full operative instrument. Readers should resist pretending five circulated pages settle all constitutional questions. Officials must establish authenticity, classification status, completeness, and applicable disclosure authority before political protagonists announce their preferred verdict.

My assessment is that this affair tests the government’s credibility more severely than Najib’s political fortunes. A government preaching institutional reform must demonstrate procedures that survive partisan advantage. Publish a reasoned disclosure policy, identify the competent authorising authority, and apply equivalent standards to comparable pardons. Where confidentiality is required, explain its legal basis without exposing protected deliberations.

And Pua? He is entitled to criticise Najib, challenge clemency and defend his former colleagues. He is not entitled to confuse proof of opposition with proof of governmental consistency. The former may fit neatly into a social media post; the latter demands accountability across administrations, personalities, and inconvenient precedents.
The king does not require politicians to manufacture unanimity. The Constitution requires institutions to understand their responsibilities.
Umno should defend that distinction firmly; DAP and PH should answer it without theatrical evasion; Anwar should insist upon rules rather than improvisation.
When constitutional records become partisan ammunition, the real scandal is not disagreement. It is a government unable to explain who loaded the weapon, under what authority, and why only now.
Azam Mohd is an FMT reader.

8f13969a68ed3f91: Having agreed to new peace talks with Ukrainian and American representatives earlier this month, Russian negotiators suddenly wanted to discuss the European security order, too.
It was an obvious attempt to divert attention from the urgent need, after almost five years, for a ceasefire in Russian president Vladimir Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine.
While the inept US negotiating duo of Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff seemed to go along with the Russian proposal, the Europeans saw right through it.
They pointed out that there is already an agreed European security order, to which Russia is a signatory. The only problem is that Russia is blatantly violating it. That is what must be discussed.

The European security order is basically no different from what the United Nations Charter established in 1945. Coming after two bitter, brutal world wars, the UN Charter codified the territorial integrity of all states, and identified the crime of aggression as the ultimate violation of international law.

But the European order that gradually emerged towards the end of the Cold War went further than this. Through the laborious negotiations leading up to the Helsinki Accords in 1975, and through the process that produced the Paris Charter of 1990, Europeans added provisions on democracy, human rights, and economic cooperation to the basic security architecture.

Of course, there were occasional disagreements about how to implement these agreements’ requirements, and in both Georgia and Moldova in the 2000s, Russia openly violated provisions barring the presence of a country’s armed forces on the territory of another without its consent.

These moves sparked bitter debates, with Russia eventually calling for revisions to the European security order. The Kremlin, for obvious reasons, objected to the provisions concerning human rights and elections, and demanded that they be deleted or substantially diluted.

It wasn’t difficult to see why. A series of “colour revolutions” had started to sweep through the region, most notably in Georgia and Ukraine, where protesters demanded democratic reforms, the rule of law, and closer links with democratic Europe.
Upon returning to the presidency after a brief stint as prime minister to circumvent constitutional limits, Putin himself was confronted with huge demonstrations in Moscow.

With a democratic wave sweeping much of the world at the time, the Kremlin understood that the colour revolutions in other countries had inspired pro-democracy demonstrations on its own streets. More to the point, it knew that pro-democratic forces could count on moral support from the West.

Russia tried to force new negotiations to suppress previously agreed commitments on democracy, but no one else would support such an effort. The order that had been established at the summits in Helsinki and Paris stood firm.

More recently, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov has called attention to a provision from a 1999 Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe document, which holds that signatories “will not strengthen their security at the expense of the security of other states”.

Yet he completely ignores another provision from the same document, which reaffirms “the inherent right of each and every participating state to be free to choose or change its security arrangements, including treaties of alliance”.
Such cynical cherry picking is dishonest even by Lavrov’s standards. Membership in Nato or the European Union clearly preserves peace and in no way threatens Russia.

Democratisation in other countries may well inspire those seeking democratic change inside Russia, but that is not the democratising countries’ fault or problem, nor does it endanger Russia’s security.
Putin is now left trying to roll back various European countries’ security choices, and thus their sovereignty. This is obviously a non-starter.

Finland and Sweden chose to enter Nato not to attack Russia, but because Russia had just launched a full-scale invasion of another European neighbour. No sane person is under any illusion about cause and effect.

One hopes that at some point there will be an opening to return to confidence-building and arms-control measures. But with Russian guns blazing and Russian bombs falling over another European country’s civilian centres, now is obviously not the time.

The European security order’s foundational principle is to reject aggression and respect other countries’ territorial integrity. There is no need to revise that order, only to wait for a Russian regime that is willing to accept it.
In the next round of talks, European representatives will demand an immediate end to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. Until that happens, there is nothing else to talk about.
Carl Bildt is a former prime minister and foreign minister of Sweden.

dc93da4cf6a361d8: Over 223,700 children have dropped out of school in Cameroon’s Northwest and Southwest regions, while 2,463 schools are non-operational
Originally published on Global Voices
A general view of Buea's OIC Market in the Southwest Region of Cameroon, where displaced families sell goods to support their livelihoods. Photo by Cynthia Ebot Takang. Used with permission.

For children displaced by Cameroon’s ongoing armed Anglophone conflict, reaching safety has not ended the struggle. In Buea, the capital of Cameroon’s Southwest region, some children are balancing school with market trading to help their families survive.

“At least here in Buea, there are no gunshots, and we do not have to hide in the bush,” says 11-year-old Lorane in an interview with Global Voices, describing the relative safety his family found after fleeing their home in Cameroon’s conflict-affected Southwest Region.

The move brought the children to a calmer environment where they could resume schooling and live with less fear of armed violence. But leaving their communities also meant losing homes, familiar surroundings, friendships and, for some, years of education. In Buea, the struggle to rebuild family livelihoods has introduced another responsibility to their lives: helping their parents earn a living.
A safer place, but a childhood reshaped by displacement

The Anglophone crisis in Cameroon began in 2016, when teachers and lawyers began protesting over the perceived marginalization of English-language education and common-law systems, which they say favored French. This escalated into wider demonstrations and a government crackdown. In 2017, the situation deteriorated into armed conflict between government forces and separatist groups seeking independence for the two English-speaking regions as a state commonly referred to as Ambazonia. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) estimates that between 2.1 and 2.2 million people have been displaced due to the violence and insecurity.

At Buea’s OIC Market, children from displaced families sell bleach, puff-puff, plantains, ginger, garlic, and oranges, particularly during weekends and before school. Some travel from neighboring communities to help their parents sell goods, while others work around family-owned stalls.

For 14-year-old Joy, this means traveling from Mutengene to Buea on weekends to sell sachets of bleach. Her mother buys the bleach in bulk and repackages it into smaller sachets, which Joy sells for CFA 100 (about USD 0.17) each. She says daily sales can reach CFA 10,000–15,000 (about USD 16.81–25.21), helping support the household and her siblings.

Joy has been working since her family fled their village when she was in Class Five. “They were shooting guns in my village, so my mum had to bring us here so we could continue school,” she says. She has since become used to the routine, which allows her to contribute to the family while continuing her education.

For 14-year-old Sidoine, displacement meant losing four years of schooling. Her family fled Ekona after their house was burned while they were away at the farm. She remembers hiding in the bushes when they heard attacks were coming, unsure what would happen next. Her family eventually left their hometown, Ekona, for Buea, joining thousands of others who have had to rebuild their lives away from their roots. A well-wisher eventually helped her enroll in school in Buea.
Although the family sometimes visits their farm to collect food, it has not been possible to return permanently. Sidoine misses her former home and friends.
Rebuilding a family livelihood

For younger children, displacement has also changed family routines. Twelve-year-old Michelle sells plantains while waiting for his mother to return from church. His 11-year-old cousin, Lorane, sometimes accompanies him. The two help their parents attract customers, particularly on weekends.
They also miss people they left behind in Ekona, including their grandmother, who died during a raid as a result of the crisis.

Susan Achuagoh, a mother of five whose house was burned during the conflict, has had to rebuild her livelihood as an orange seller in Buea. She gives her children small quantities of oranges to sell while she remains at her stall. This helps supplement their family income.
“I sell oranges; I give them small things to walk around with while I stay at the stall,” she shared in an interview with Global Voices. “If they do not help like that, it will not go at all.”

Her children’s education was interrupted for more than three years during the conflict. Another mother, Mami Blessing, says her children’s schooling was also disrupted and that they now help her at the market as the family struggles to make ends meet.
The cost of conflict

Godiva Ndang epse Limene, Education and Partnerships Officer at Street Child UK-Cameroon, says the prolonged crisis in the Northwest and Southwest has increasingly become a crisis of childhood, affecting education, protection, and development.

Children exposed to armed violence, displacement, and repeated insecurity may experience anxiety, difficulty concentrating, and social withdrawal. Taking on economic responsibilities can add to these pressures. Ndang says work that takes up time needed for learning, rest, and play can affect children’s cognitive, emotional, social, and physical development.

She stresses that helping in a family business is not automatically child labor. The distinction depends on the child’s age, the nature and duration of the activity, the risks involved, and whether it interferes with education, health, rest, or development.

The right to education is only one of the rights affected. Children also have a right to rest, leisure, and play, as well as protection from economic exploitation. For those uprooted from their communities, maintaining friendships, participating in cultural life, and developing a sense of belonging are also important parts of growing up.
Learning spaces offer a route back to education

The scale of the disruption remains significant. Figures from the Regional Delegations of Basic Education cited by UNICEF in September 2026 show that 223,749 children were completely out of school in the Northwest and Southwest, while 2,463 schools were non-operational. Of these, 2,005 were in the Northwest and 458 in the Southwest.

To educate children in conflict-affected communities, local partners including TeenAlive, the Foundation for Inclusive Education (FIED), Strategic Humanitarian Services (SHUMAS), and the Authentique Memorial Empowerment Foundation (AMEF) support Mobile Neighborhood Learning Corners and Satellite Learning Corners. These are established in accessible locations such as village chiefs’ homes, churches, schools, and community verandas.

The program has supported close to 100 learning corners across the two regions. Other education interventions include help with school enrollment, uniforms, and learning materials, as well as Teaching at the Right Level, a tutoring program.

Street Child also combines education with other forms of support. Its girls’ resilience and empowerment work provides displaced adolescent girls with life skills, literacy, and vocational training, alongside start-up kits and mental health assistance. Its Play for Peace initiative, supported by the FIFA Foundation, uses sports to promote peace, health, and education in conflict-affected communities.

Ndang says children also need psychosocial support, safe learning environments, and opportunities to play and interact with their peers. She adds that helping caregivers rebuild their livelihoods matters because reducing economic pressure on families can lessen the burden on children.
Ambition despite displacement
Despite interruptions to their education and the responsibilities they have taken on, the children interviewed for this story continue to speak about their goals and ambitions.

Eliot, 14, who helps his mother sell oranges on weekends, wants to become an engineer. Sidoine hopes to study law, although she worries about the years she lost in school. Vickians, 12, who fled Lebialem and now studies computer science, wants to become a computer engineer.
On weekends, Vickians sells miondo, a cassava-based delicacy, with her parents. Her family continues to make sacrifices to keep her in school, and she remains determined to pursue her education.

At the start of the 2026–2027 academic year, Southwest Governor Bernard Okalia Bilai said the authorities wanted children across the region to have equal access to education and learning facilities, despite differences in school attendance between urban and rural communities. His remarks, reported in this September 2026 interview on the reopening of schools, underline the challenge facing the region: ensuring that displacement and insecurity do not determine whether children can access education.

Reporting note: The names used for the children in this story are pseudonyms to protect their identities. No photographs of the children have been published. Consent was obtained from parents before the interviews were conducted.
Written by Cynthia Ebot Takang

61f2e8252c946f4b: My editor asked me this week "why is everything except AWS breaking?"

It's a great question! They haven't been in the headlines! In fact, as they are wont to do, AWS spokesperson Patrick Neighorn got salty to a reporter about how unreliable Downdetector is when it started showing them as impacted.

If you'll permit me a small digression, this stems from a misunderstanding of what Downdetector is for. Historically the AWS status site was so hilariously slow to reflect the lived customer experience that some jackass (me) built a rewriter that sits at stop.lying.cloud to make it a smidgen more realistic. As a result, the question people are really trying to answer when they visit Downdetector is "my app just broke; is it my crappy code or is there a global event going on?" There are mitigations for both, but they look nothing alike.

AWS view crowdsourced reports of the form "the internet is broken, must be AWS" as a stain upon their honor. In fact, it's a badge of their own success, as "the internet" and "AWS" have become inextricably linked in people's minds.
But back to my editor's question, "why didn't AWS go down?"
Easy: it did.
Everything breaks, all the time, including the narrative

AWS now has 34 generally available commercial regions, of which two are currently smoking craters due to the Iran conflict. Each of these has hundreds of services that AWS offers to customers, of which a dozen or so are high quality, if I'm being characteristically uncharitable. They experience degradation in various ways, and they go largely unnoticed.
But on November 15, AWS confirmed an incident that disrupted 11 of those ~12 good services in their oldest and most important region, us-east-1.

At 3:05 AM PST, they stated that they started seeing sign-up errors, authentication issues, and connectivity issues. Five minutes later engineers were engaged. Not to be outdone, their status page swung into action after a leisurely coffee, and posted its first indication of an incident 93 minutes later. (See previous comments on stop.lying.cloud). The all-clear showed up at 6:53 AM.

Every site has downtime. Sometimes it blows up publicly, other times nobody seems to notice. Heck, AWS said in September that it had experienced permanent data loss in its two smoking craters, but after that news cycle passed I haven't heard a thing about it. I do think it's patently unreasonable to blame them for this specific problem; "acts of war" are kinda hard to predict from the corporate planning meeting.
A few things combined to help AWS out on November 15. First, it was pre-dawn Pacific time on Sunday. Most of us slept through it; my kids aren't even up that early.
Further, the services that were most impacted (IAM Identity Center) were for engineers signing in to AWS accounts, not consumers staring at an app that stopped working.

Plus, the competition sucked all the oxygen out of the room: a day-plus Microsoft 365 364 outage and a four-hour nationwide air traffic ground stop had done a great job of level-setting what kind of outage was going to get attention, and "us-east-1 being weird but the apps still work" doesn't cut it.

Downdetector – which is owned by Accenture, so it's not like AWS doesn't have a throat to choke if they want to stop picking on reporters – measures consumer screaming. Originally, it was largely Twitter semantic analytics. This isn't a bad thing! As I said, I want to know if the internet is breaking. We can sort out exactly what part later.
The November 15 outage didn't produce that kind of screaming. Ironically, the tool that AWS is complaining about in the newspaper is the reason they skated by without notice on this outage.
Counterintuitively, Downdetector reports that outages have decreased since about 2022. Instead, what we're seeing is large-scale centralization.

Our companies don't run email systems internally anymore; we outsource to large technology companies who are almost universally better at fixing and resolving large-scale issues than we will be internally. And it feels unkind to dunk on those hard-working folks for their outages; would we want them to dunk on us for ours?
("Wait, don't you own stop.lying.cloud?" "Do as I say, not as I do.")

But whether anyone notices depends upon what layer broke, and when. If my company's email system broke on Monday, and your company's email system broke on Tuesday, the story would stop at "computers suck." But when everyone's email system goes down at once, the world takes notice.

Microsoft had to tell the whole world about a bug it mostly sat on since July. AWS hasn't had to tell anyone anything. My editor runs a tech publication that covers this stuff for a living and didn't know. You can't buy PR like this, and AWS didn't have to.
If I were AWS, I'd stop complaining about Downdetector and send it a fruit basket. ®
