480a8b723958aa8d: Modeling of complex, chaotic processes such as weather and climate patterns and turbulent flows in aviation or in ocean currents has advanced enormously in recent years. However, such models are still prone to drift into physically impossible predictions over time. Now, researchers with MIT’s Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS) have found a way to introduce physics-based restrictions on machine learning models that can ensure that such models never exceed realistic bounds, based on what is actually possible in the real world. This new approach, using information that is now being made freely available by the team, could significantly improve the usefulness and reliability of such models, which besides climate and weather are also used in a wide range of industrial processes, aeronautics, and hydrology. The new findings are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) in a paper by MIT graduate student Sunbochen Tang and MIT professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis.  “Lack of guarantees for a bounded response has always been a major obstacle on formulating data-driven models for complex nonlinear systems,” says Sapsis, a professor of mechanical engineering and LIDS affiliate. The approach the team has developed, he says, “paves the way for applying the most advanced machine-learning architectures for prediction and control in a plethora of real-world problems, even those characterized by intrinsic instabilities.” Developing reliable models for complex dynamical systems is important across many domains. In fluid dynamics, turbulent flows can disrupt air travel, reduce the efficiency of wind turbines, and affect fuel economy of vehicles. Similarly, in weather forecasting, the chaotic nature of atmospheric dynamics makes accurate long-term predictions difficult.  “Tiny differences in the starting conditions can lead to dramatically different outcomes in a chaotic system,” Azizan says. “That makes predicting its behavior far into the future extremely difficult.” And yet, there are always physical constraints on the kinds of changes that are possible in the real world. “Chaos does not mean anything can happen. These systems often remain bounded, and their models should, too.” But how to introduce those boundaries into the models has been a thorny problem, says Azizan, the Hayes Associate Professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering and the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society, and a principal investigator in LIDS. “A model can match the data over a short period and still fail when you let it run for a long time,” he says. “Small errors can accumulate until the simulation produces values that grow without limit,” producing predictions that could never actually occur in real systems. “It’s a fundamental problem with many of the existing machine learning models,” he says. “It’s a question that comes up frequently in different domains: how can we embed physical constraints into these models in a way that preserves their flexibility, but ensures physically meaningful outputs?” “We want to preserve the chaos without the artificial runaway behavior that the real system does not have,” he says. “Our approach gives the model room to learn complex dynamics while guaranteeing that its trajectories stay bounded.” This is the first work that establishes such formal guarantees for machine learning models of chaos. Previous attempts to prevent unrealistic results from such models have often been based on “imposing penalties or incentives during training,” says Tang, a doctoral student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and LIDS, using functions that are often designed based on privileged information about the system. But as these only apply during the training process for the model, “there’s no guarantee that the model will satisfy the underlying constraints intended by such incentives at test time” once it is dealing with new inputs when it is actually used. “The model could still produce unbounded predictions,” he says. To illustrate why simply imposing arbitrary limits would not be a satisfactory solution to the prediction stability issue, Tang explains, “you can cap the predictions, for example, by setting an arbitrary limit on physical quantities, such as 100 degrees for temperature. That’s one possible way to keep predictions bounded, but it could restrict the model from representing complex and nontrivial features that should be learned directly from the data.” He says that “what sets our approach apart is that we formulate energy-based constraints. We let the model learn an energy-like function,” based on real-world chaotic systems, where energy dissipation helps keep trajectories bounded despite their complex behaviors. “Specifically, the model learns an energy-like function, along with a boundary where its chaotic behavior should be confined to. We then add a projection layer, a component that adjusts how the model predicts the system will evolve, to enforce energy dissipation as a hard constraint. Outside this boundary, the energy-like quantity must decrease, so the simulated system is drawn toward the bounded region. That way, we can establish theoretical guarantees that the model prediction remains bounded over arbitrarily long forecast windows.” The team tested their approach on a variety of different well-known physical systems, ranging from simple textbook cases to highly complex multidimensional systems, and found that their approach closely matched the true outcomes, while conventional approaches soon deviated into impossible predictions. Azizan adds that “the fundamental difference between our approach and the existing approaches is what we call hard constraining versus soft constraining.” While many of the current approaches “try to incentivize the model to satisfy the constraints, they’re not treated as hard constraints. Our approach is based on the concept of hard-constrained neural networks,” so that what comes out “is always physically consistent, even if it’s a completely new case the model hasn’t seen.” “AI models shine in scenarios where there’s a large amount of data available,” Azizan says, for example with images or with text, both of which are abundantly available on the internet. However, he says, “for a lot of physical systems, data is not as abundant.” For such cases where the data is limited, he says, “these physics-constrained approaches can help a lot, because the physics of the problem is another source of information.” The new approach is broadly useful for any chaotic systems. “This is readily applicable to a wide range of neural network architectures,” Tang says. They plan to continue testing it on ever-larger systems. “We’re trying to see how well this would work on data-driven models of realistic weather systems.” “The projection layer is modular: it is model-agnostic and can work with different neural network architectures,” Azizan says. “We hope other researchers and practitioners will build on it and test it on larger and even more complex problems.” The paper, along with open-source code, is now accessible online at PNAS. A follow-up work this year by members of the team was presented at the Learning for Dynamics and Control conference. The paper won the conference’s Best Paper Award. “Trustworthy and reliable AI needs more than just evidence that a model usually works,” Azizan says. “For high-stakes applications, you need guarantees about the properties that must always hold. In this work, we established one such guarantee: boundedness. Our broader goal is to make principles part of how AI models are built, not just how they are tested.”
c4fcf3d7ab6e8c9f: A 'Saturday Night Live' parody commercial delivered a sobering message to America about a widespread problem. Alican Lazutti/iStock via Getty Images Plus“Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people. The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister. “Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains. I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story. A growing trend One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes. My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults. The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion. The “Sister” sketch on “Saturday Night Live” has launched a national conversation about caregiving. Warning: ‘Sister’ may break down Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price. Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people. That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.” Family caregivers pay a price Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour, totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460. But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones. Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits. Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one. AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities. ‘Sister’ lampoons gender roles in caring for aging family members. NBC A ‘daughterhood penalty’ Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “daughterhood penalty,” or tax. Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability. Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives. But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing. Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores. Patricia Smith is affiliated with the Ottawa County, MI Democratic Party.
00aa8aae69bf041d: The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.

Wireless industry lobby group CTIA said a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing:

The pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts.

CTIA said the pilot test shows "that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications."
f193d99c3cb1adeb: In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army announced Thursday that it would delay a plan to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week.

The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week.

"Public communication is essential to public trust," Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday. "Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information."
1aecbf9c5342cd9b: Each generation of Intel Xeons or AMD Epycs brings dozens of new SKUs: high-core count parts tuned for throughput, high-frequency ones optimized for latency, low-power chips designed for the edge, and everything in between.

But if you ask Ian Finder, who heads development of Nvidia’s datacenter CPUs, for the vast majority of use cases, all those SKUs are overkill. “There was sort of an overskewing, for many years on the other vendors side of things,” he told El Reg on the sidelines of Supercomputing 2026 this week.

Nvidia is a relative newcomer to the datacenter CPU space. The company’s first part, called Grace, launched in 2023, but didn’t see widespread deployment outside AI headnodes, high-end NICs, and a handful of standalone CPU deployments by hyperscalers like Meta.

We explored the chip in greater detail earlier this year, but the GPU slinger’s latest CPU, Vera, is a different beast. In addition to showing up as part of Nvidia’s Vera-Rubin superchips, the CPU will also be offered in standalone CPU racks, storage, and context memory systems. Just this week, Nvidia announced a new rack with 192 Vera CPUs aimed at high-performance computing (HPC) workloads, which don’t translate well to GPUs. And at least on paper, a single SKU with 88 cores clocking to 3.3 GHz powers all of them.
Historically, CPUs with different combinations of cores, clocks, I/O, and power have been used in these roles.

According to Finder, most datacenter CPUs haven’t been loaded that heavily, and as a result unloaded latency has been the optimization point. As a consequence, CPUs that rely on high core counts to boost throughput often suffer from elevated loaded latencies.

On the flip side, chipmakers can optimize for loaded latency, but this usually comes at the expense of throughput. We see this pretty clearly across AMD’s last few generations of Epycs, where it designed both space-efficient Zen-C cores that prioritize throughput and fatter frequency-optimized versions that prioritize latency.

“As more cores are up and running, your latency to memory gets higher because you have to deal with congestion on the connectivity buses,” More than Moore analyst Ian Cutress tells The Reg. “What Nvidia is saying is right. Sometimes, you do have to pick between core count and core latency.”
A balanced architecture

With Vera, Nvidia sought to thread that needle to design a balanced architecture that maintains low latencies and high throughput even when all 88 cores are loaded. This does mean making some compromises – in particular, the CPU's vector unit isn’t the beefiest. But if you’ve got GPUs capable of running vectorized code, that compromise starts to make a lot more sense – and if you’re buying Vera you almost certainly do.

“If you do a few things like that, you can actually get a part that, for the workloads people care about — knowledge agents for CI/CD, for software engineering, or databases and analytics — you can build a part that gets you the same performance per core as the frequency-optimized x86 parts at the same throughput per watt as the density-optimized parts,” Finder argued.

We should note that Nvidia isn’t unique in this line of thinking. Cloud providers have long passed on the highest core-count parts in Intel or AMD’s lineup in favor of parts they feel deliver the right mix of throughput, latency, memory bandwidth, and capacity.

The reason, in part, is that cloud providers don’t know exactly what their customers will actually be doing with those cores, and so it’s better to offer something that’s well-rounded than one that has the highest clocks or lowest latency. This same logic works pretty well for agent sandboxes.
“Nvidia is confident that it understands the market well enough that one chip will cover most use cases,” Cutress said. “You could argue that Nvidia just wants to corner that bulk market.”

Having said that, there are plenty of reasons to have multiple SKUs or product lines. Throughout much of AMD’s latest launch cycle, the House of Zen has argued its chips make for better agentic CPUs because agents aren’t one workload but many. Some may benefit from higher core counts while others may benefit from higher frequency, and AMD’s more diverse portfolio offers choice.

To that point, Vera does have one trick up its sleeve: a split personality. The processor is one of the few Arm chips that supports simultaneous multithreading (SMT), but the way it works differs wildly from what Intel would call Hyperthreading.

When enabled, SMT effectively bifurcates Vera’s Olympus cores. Eighty-eight cores turns into something that functionally looks more like 176 narrower cores. So if you need more throughput than 88 cores afford, or your workload doesn’t benefit materially from a wider core, Vera does offer some flexibility.

A broader SKU stack also helps with binning. Chip manufacturing isn’t a perfect process, and you’re going to run into defective cores from time to time. Binning allows chipmakers to sell these defective chips at a discount.
Cutress suspects that Nvidia is probably doing this for its customers and it’s just not advertising them as different SKUs the way Intel and AMD have the past few decades.
For instance, a hyperscaler might be happy to take a 72-core variant of Vera that clocks a little higher or delivers more memory bandwidth per core for the same amount of power.
But for now we have just the one, for the green lord on their green throne in the land of AI where the bots lie. ®
583b7a1c74131e15: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.

And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”

Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August, he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite.

Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.

Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR’s research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.

But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”

Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”

In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.

In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming.

It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”
59d932d229ff420e: Activists want to establish legal infrastructure to protect the environment and punish those responsible for defiling it
Originally published on Global Voices

An aerial view of the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico, the largest marine oil spill in history. Under the proposed ICC amendment, oil company executives could be held accountable in such cases. Image via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 2.0.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In September 2024, Vanuatu, Fiji, and Samoa filed an amendment request at the International Criminal Court (ICC) to get “ecocide” recognized as a crime under international law. The ICC currently recognizes four criminal categories: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression.

Over two years later, the amendment is still formally pending; but that does not mean environmental activists are waiting around — in fact, many are working both in the public eye and behind the scenes to establish legal infrastructure to protect the environment, combat the climate crisis, and punish those responsible for defiling the planet.

According to an independent expert panel convened by the Stop Ecocide Foundation, ecocide is legally defined as “unlawful or wanton acts committed with knowledge that there is a substantial likelihood of severe and either widespread or long-term damage to the environment being caused by those acts.”
For the countries that backed the proposal, the climate crisis is not an abstract threat; it is a real and present danger with active consequences for their people.

In 2021, Simon Kofe, Tuvalu’s Minister for Justice, Communication and Foreign Affairs, gave a presentation at the international COP26 conference on climate change while standing in knee-deep water to demonstrate how rising sea levels threaten low-lying island nations. Tuvaluan officials are also exploring ways to become the first “digital nation” as a backup plan in case rising sea levels submerge all livable land in the archipelago. In Fiji alone, six villages have already been relocated because of climate change, with others in progress and dozens more under assessment. As Vanuatu’s Special Envoy for Climate Change and Environment, Ralph Regenvanu, says, climate damage is “devastating our island economy, submerging our territory, and threatening livelihoods.”

Shortly after the amendment was submitted, it was also backed by the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which is experiencing increasingly deadly flooding as well as air quality issues related to exploitative mining operations.
Tuvulu’s Foreign Minister delivers an address to COP26, while standing in knee-deep water to illustrate how rising sea levels threaten Pacific nations. Image from Simon Kofe’s Facebook. Fair use.

It is not a coincidence that those who are pushing hardest for these legal mechanisms are those most affected by the climate crisis. These nations did little to cause the crisis, while major superpowers like the U.S., China, and Europe, as well as the corporations that bolster them, have made billions by exploiting and polluting the environment unchecked.

Meanwhile, those who suffer from the consequences of our eroding climate have limited legal recourse against the corporations and states most responsible. This juxtaposition is where the argument to make ecocide an international crime comes in.
Vanuatu was the first state to call for ecocide to be added to the ICC in 2019. In announcing the proposal, Regenvanu said:

“We are taking bold and necessary action to address these challenges and encourage other vulnerable states to take note of our newly tabled proposal to bring ecocide to the ICC. Legal recognition of severe and widespread environmental harm holds significant potential to ensure justice and, crucially, to deter further destruction.”
A protest poster against ecocide shaming oil giants at a climate protest in Maryland in 2017. Photo from Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 2.0.
Why reform the ICC?

The International Criminal Court was formally established in 2002 to prosecute individuals for grave international crimes (not to be confused with the International Court of Justice, which settles legal disputes between countries).

Environmental crimes are particularly tricky, as traditional legal accountability measures tend to rely on specific individuals or property that have been harmed in order to pursue legal action. In cases where polluters are contributing to a broader destructive pattern, the legal standing becomes murky. This theory has been tested numerous times as individuals have sought to sue fossil fuel companies in civil court for their destructive practices and malfeasance, with most cases largely unsuccessful.

Supporters say that if the proposed amendment were successful, it would give ICC prosecutors the power to hold individuals, such as the executives of large polluting companies or heads of state, responsible in cases like massive oil spills or the deforestation of essential rainforests.
As an editorial in The Global Witness notes:

While there have been a series of recent valiant attempts to sue fossil fuel corporations in civil court for covering up evidence that their activities were causing global warming, the defendants have largely been able to get away scot-free. … Criminalizing ecocide would fill this legal gap, and allow individuals (and companies in some jurisdictions) to be prosecuted for engaging in acts with knowledge that they are substantially likely to damage the environment, without the need to show harm to any individual person.

To add a crime to the Rome Statute, a proposal must win a two-thirds majority vote within the court’s Assembly of States Parties. Even then, an amendment to the statute’s crimes provisions would bind only the states that accept it, and the court could not prosecute nationals or territory of states that do not.

The Rome Statute has 123 signatory parties — a number that does not include China, India, or the U.S., the world’s three largest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions. The U.S., in particular, under current President Donald Trump’s administration, has backed away from climate commitments in recent years, including withdrawing from the UN’s 2015 Paris Climate Agreement. It has also become increasingly hostile toward the court itself, as the Trump administration imposed sanctions on individual ICC prosecutors and judges beginning in early 2025. Then, in a September 2026 address to the UN General Assembly, Trump urged all member states to withdraw from the treaty altogether, and, weeks later, in October 2026, he imposed sweeping sanctions on the court itself.

With the biggest emitters outside the court, and Washington working to undermine it, advocates are looking beyond The Hague and ICC reform. As legal watchdogs argue, the end goal is not merely to get the ICC to recognize ecocide — though that would be an excellent first step — rather, if the ICC were to establish a framework for prosecuting international environmental crimes, through an amendment or merely by adapting its existing policies, this could push ratifying states to update their domestic penal codes and adopt policies to protect and preserve their own ecosystems, and also prosecute those who violate them.
Existing provisions within the Rome Statute
The International Criminal Court (ICC) at The Hague. Photo via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY 2.0.
Even though the proposal has thus far not been adopted by the ICC, the court has not stood still.

In December 2025, ICC prosecutors published a policy paper on prosecuting environmental damage through the pre-existing mechanisms already laid out in the Rome Statute — the international treaty which established the ICC.

The Rome Statute mentions the environment exactly one time. Article 8(2)(b)(iv) makes it a war crime to launch an attack knowing it will cause “widespread, long-term and severe” damage to the environment. Traditionally, this article has applied only during armed conflict, and previous attempts to prosecute environmental destruction at the court have been unsuccessful.
Vanuatu’s ambassador to the UN, Odo Tevi, has argued that the reckless destruction of nature “can and does take place at any time, not just during conflict.”

The December 2025 policy, launched at the Assembly of States Parties, was co-hosted by Costa Rica, France, Germany, Panama, and the Marshall Islands. It explains how environmental destruction can be investigated and prosecuted within the four existing crime categories, for example, when pollution or the seizure of natural resources is used to commit a crime against humanity.

Analysts at the Conflict and Environment Observatory note that this policy paper does not address the ecocide proposal and that ambiguity in the war crime standard remains. Others point to limited resources at the prosecutor’s office.

In September 2026, ICC representatives said they had “moved into the implementation stage” to establish clearer parameters for prosecuting environmental crimes under the Rome Statute. In its statement, the office said it had received numerous communications about alleged crimes with an environmental dimension and was building a network of environmental law enforcement authorities, relevant organizations, expert groups, and civil society organizations to investigate.

But some jurisdictions are not waiting. As one recent study notes, “the substance of ecocide criminalization has advanced everywhere except through the amendment: an EU directive whose gravest offense is officially ‘comparable to “ecocide,”’ a Council of Europe convention, national codes in Belgium, France and Ukraine, and a completed OTP [ICC’s Office of the Prosecutor] policy that prosecutes environmental damage through the existing four crimes.”

Counts vary depending on how many states currently employ domestic laws against ecocide. Stop Ecocide International says twelve countries, including Belgium, France, and Ukraine, have adopted ecocide or equivalent offenses into domestic law. Mauritius became the most recent in April 2026, and legislation is progressing in countries including Brazil, Peru, Argentina, Mexico, Italy, and the Netherlands. As noted in the aforementioned study, the EU’s revised Environmental Crime Directive also covers conduct “comparable to ecocide,” and member states had to transpose it by May 2026.
What comes next

The next stage is procedural rather than dramatic: Whether states give the proposal a formal path forward at the Assembly of States Parties’ 25th session in The Hague, from November 30 to December 7, 2026. A vote would signal whether the Rome Statute can grow beyond the atrocities it was written for. A stall would leave the prosecutor’s policy and national laws as the main tools available.
The decision comes at a crucial time for the ICC, as some international stakeholders begin to question the legitimacy, power, and effectiveness of international ruling bodies.

For the nations that started this, the stakes are not abstract. They are asking the world to build infrastructure to prosecute and prevent harm that is already happening to them. Until that infrastructure is implemented, the burden of harm will continue to fall on those least responsible for causing this crisis.
Written by Sydney Allen

0be690a4d27ad801: Suspected Chinese spies deployed AI agents which worked autonomously to find a zero-day in an open source application and then abuse the flaw to break into university networks, gaining full control of a server, according to Amazon CISO CJ Moses.

The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance.

In this case, the agents found and exploited a zero-day MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application. Amazon notified the project's maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a security advisory.

On September 10, Amazon's Threat Intelligence Team found a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn that provided visibility into the campaign targeting universities in East Asia, outside Mainland China, Moses said in a Friday report shared with The Register.
The campaign occurred over a period of 48 hours beginning on September 8, and the prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, with timestamps in executed scripts configured to China Standard Time.

Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory.

None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools.

Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents.
"Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses wrote.
Then the AI agents found the zero-day path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label, and this time they were able to gain access to the server.

"The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server."
Later, the agents abused the same flaw to execute a Python reverse shell running as root.

In another session, after the agents discovered the zero-day, the human operator provided them with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network, and connected to a server running the same vulnerable code.

Amazon's discovery follows an earlier report by Gambit Security's threat intelligence team that also documented a Chinese operator using Cairn to carry out at least 105 attacks, and managing to compromise, "to varying degrees," at least 27 companies.

This campaign also occurred in September. In addition to Cairn, the attacker used two other open source AI harnesses to steal credit card records and other sensitive data from a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, a large private US industrial supplies distributor, and a US online fashion retailer, and other companies.
"Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations," Moses wrote. ®

b0d657d4bd72416f: The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has officially advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after safety tests revealed concerning behaviors beyond their controversial recording capabilities.

The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring issues, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed an interest in a minor.

In another case involving a cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) simulation, testers noted that one pair of glasses informed the wearer that emergency services had been called and were scheduled to arrive at the scene, despite no one having made the call.
Some glasses did not properly process safety warnings on children’s toys, others made mistakes when reading medication leaflets, and some misinterpreted warnings for extreme weather events.

The AP did not specify the models it tested, saying only that they tested six models ranging from under €100 ($110) to over €500 ($550), including two that "were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations where human safety played a key role."

A spokesperson also declined to match any specific behavior to a model by price point (minor dating advice linked to a €354 pair of glasses, for example), adding that the research was intended to highlight the risks of AI glasses in a broader sense.
"Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning. Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far," said Monique Verdier, vice chair at the AP.
"AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot currently be justified."

The warning issued this week follows the regulator's previous work on smart glasses. The AP reminded the public in September that everyone has the right to privacy and encouraged organizations to ban them where necessary.
The same warning mentioned the potential risks regarding data processing under the GDPR, as well as those related to the training of AI.

The AP doubled down on these earlier criticisms, saying the latest tests showed that the AI functions rely on processing data using servers mostly located outside of the European Union. Relatedly, it found that users were not given sufficient information about how the AI was processing the data they captured.

On a cybersecurity note, the tests threw up a range of issues, including the ability for people nearby the glasses-wearer to connect to the device without permission, view recordings, and in some cases operate the camera.
Further, the regulator echoed the pre-existing concerns about smart specs - those that helped give them their colloquial name “pervert glasses.”
Its tests found that with "virtually all of the camera glasses examined," the recording lights that are supposed to clearly show when a user is recording were dim and easily coverable.
The AP said that models could also be wangled into recording even when that light indicator was covered, which goes against what manufacturers so often claim.
"As a result, bystanders can barely see whether they are being filmed," it said.

The technology has a number of beneficial use cases, such as assisting the visually impaired, those with lower literacy levels, or for any number of other scenarios where people need help understanding the world around them
However, the watchdog's official stance on the technology, as it is today, deems smart glasses "unsafe… due to the risks to users and bystanders."
Verdier said politicians in the Netherlands and across Europe should take note of the results when developing AI policy.
"It is important that we, as a society, learn to deal with these types of high-risk AI products," she said.
"Simply banning everything provides some leeway in the beginning, but we cannot sustain that indefinitely. It is important that we collectively work on awareness, resilience, and ethical conscience."
Smart specs can't shake the hate
When DEF CON announced a no pervert glasses policy ahead of its event in August, the move was broadly welcomed by attendees.
"Love to see a ‘no pervert glasses’ policy at DEF CON," said Eva Galperin, EFF director of cybersecurity, at the time.

Several other organizations have implemented similar restrictions, including Monopoly Events, which manages UK Comic Cons, national treasure pub chain Wetherspoons, and even Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Most members of the general public will have at least come to terms with the fact that the smartphone generation, and their willingness to snap shots anywhere and everywhere, means there is no enshrined human right to privacy in public spaces.
Public video recording once carried an air of expectation or consideration for bystanders’ personal privacy, although smartphone users have slowly eradicated that over time.
Like it or not, it's generally understood that a smartphone is usually recording something - or someone - at any given time, especially in urban areas.
On paper, the fact that smart glasses can record in public spaces isn’t wildly different from what’s already come to be expected from smartphones.
However, given how similar they appear to analog glasses and the ability to cover the recording light, it makes the act of public recording via glasses far more surreptitious, and thus concerning.

With smartphones, it's easy to see from the user's body language - holding the phone out in front of them - that they are recording. There are no overt signals displayed by wearers of smart glasses during image or video capture, which fuels a sense of unease about the technology in general.
A quick search online for "smart glasses privacy violation" yields a slew of complaints about the technology, often regarding behavior toward women and children.
There are also worries about how easily the devices can get past security checks, potentially providing opportunities to those who wish to cause greater harm than a mere blight on personal privacy.
A joint investigation by The Observer and BBC Radio 4 recently revealed how AI-enabled glasses went undetected through the airport-style security scanners used in the UK parliament.

The two news outlets found that a £60 ($78) pair of Chinese-made glasses bypassed the scanners and could be used to read upside-down documents on MPs' desks, recording data such as phone numbers and addresses to be accessed at a later point. ®

3b922deb03a7e9f1: The electronics industry faces a printed circuit board (PCB) shortage that could rival the pandemic-era chip crunch – with AI once again accused of hogging supplies.
The Global Electronics Association says demand is arriving "at a scale the supply chain was not built for," straining everything from glass fabric and resin to finished boards.

Its report, "The PCB Squeeze: A Wake-Up Call for Global Electronics," says AI servers need increasingly complex boards. While a typical PC board has about 12 layers of tracks, AI server boards can have 40 to 60 layers or more, and each additional layer requires more resin, copper foil, and laminate.
The supply of materials is set to be constrained through at least the first half of 2027, the report says, with meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028.
Programs to deliver PCBs for automotive, industrial, medical and even the defense industries are being crowded out as AI soaks up scarce capacity, it claims.

The association's North American figures show orders growing much faster than deliveries. PCB bookings rose 56.1 percent in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, while PCB shipments increased 13.3 percent.

Fabrication capacity is expanding, aimed at meeting the increased demand from the AI infrastructure sector, especially in Asia, where more than 90 percent of the world's boards are made. The report says that $10 billion has gone toward new PCB plants in Southeast Asia, and at least as much has been invested in China over the past three years, but the raw materials are themselves constrained.

It warns of lengthening lead times for those raw materials. Standard FR-4 laminate now takes six to eight weeks to ship, up from two to three weeks a year ago, while advanced low-loss laminates now take 14 to 18 weeks for delivery, for example.

Tightening supplies usually lead to price increases, and the report says that suppliers raised laminate costs by 30 percent in September, and that the price tag of some types of E-glass cloth for circuit boards has risen by 300 percent.
The report also puts copper prices up 37 percent over the past year. Concerns have been raised about copper supplies before, as The Register has reported multiple times.
The association compares the risk with the 2021 chip shortage, when disrupted supplies left manufacturers unable to secure even relatively mundane components.
New capacity is coming, but it is late and comes in dribs and drabs, according to the report, while AI demand just keeps on absorbing it as soon as it arrives.

The association's advice is for buyers to plan early, and to share realistic forecasts with suppliers rather than double-booking. Board makers should qualify alternative suppliers of materials such as laminate and copper foil before shortages bite, but it warns against stockpiling beyond real need, which adds to forward-buying pressure.

But it would like governments to step in, of course, by tracking board and material lead times with industry and offering tax incentives for investment in advanced PCB and substrate manufacturing equipment.

The wish list also includes state investment in research and development plus qualification of new alternative materials. It would like to see loan guarantees and grants to protect critical programs and small fabricators, structured so as to sustain new capacity if forward buying unravels and demand corrects in 2027.

"Yes, we are seeing constraint in upstream materials and have been reporting it for the past couple of quarters," said Cori Masters, senior research analyst director for Supply Chain Operations at Gartner.

"In addition, AI datacenter infrastructure build out is moving capacity support to high-layer count PCBs which increase throughput time and decreases availability of line utilization for more traditional PCB products," she told The Register. ®

Most Iranian airlines largely stopped flying to Malaysia in 2022 due to US sanctions on refuelling Iranian planes.

On Sept 8, the US imposed sanctions on dozens of companies in the UAE, Britain, Malaysia, Turkey and Kazakhstan it said were supporting Iran's aviation sector to move weapons, personnel and illicit cargo.
The following day, Iran Air officials met with Malaysia's ambassador to Iran to discuss resuming direct flights between Iran and Kuala Lumpur.
'Doing our part'
Both Malaysia and Singapore implement UN Security Council sanctions on Iran.

The Singapore government said in a statement it "is firmly committed to doing our part" and "preventing bad actors from abusing our corporate vehicles", citing its efforts to strengthen vigilance in the maritime and financial industries this year.
The Malaysian government did not respond to requests for comment.

9be98e73c6c88adf: It’s been a tumultuous year for math. Big open questions that have occupied mathematicians for decades are now being solved in a matter of hours by artificial intelligence agents that companies deploy by the thousands to work on a single problem in tireless lockstep.  AI’s relentless rise is raising existential questions for the field: How will the tools affect humans’ understanding of mathematical concepts? In the face of AI’s brute-force productivity, will mathematicians still have jobs? And what will all this mean for mathematics as an intellectual pursuit?  At MIT, mathematicians grappled with these and other questions at a panel discussion on Monday titled “AI and Society: The Future of Math.” Leading mathematicians from MIT, Harvard University, Northwestern University, and New York University — each experts in their respective fields — sat down for a conversation that touched on the quality of AI math, how AI is challenging long-established research norms, and the evolving opportunities for mathematicians, whether they embrace the machines or remain “AI vegans.” The wide-ranging discussion, which took place in a packed lecture hall in MIT’s Building 3, was moderated by science writer Kevin Hartnett, author of “The Proof in the Code,” and featured Jacopo Borga, the Cecil and Ida Green Career Development Assistant Professor of Mathematics at MIT; Michael Hopkins, the George Putnam Professor of Pure and Applied Mathematics at Harvard University; Bryna Kra, the Sarah Rebecca Roland Professor of Mathematics at Northwestern University; and Tristan Buckmaster, professor of mathematics at New York University's Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences. As the panelists shared their various and at times conflicting perspectives on AI’s impact, one thing was clear: “Math has changed more in the last two months than in the last 100 years,” said Kra, who cautioned that AI’s power will change what it is to be a mathematician and what it will take to advance human knowledge in meaningful ways. “It’s like the first sentence in ‘A Tale of Two Cities’: ‘It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.’ It’s a really exciting moment … and also scary.” AI’s sprint Artificial intelligence has made steady strides over the last decade thanks in large part to mathematicians themselves, who out of curiosity have been honing AI models to solve problems with known solutions. These early exercises proved successful, most notably in 2025. That summer, at the International Mathematical Olympiad, Google DeepMind’s AI models achieved gold-medal status by quickly finding solutions to most of the problems that were posed to the world’s best high school mathematicians.  Around that same time, other mathematicians found that some AI systems could solve problems with known solutions, but in ways that were slightly improved compared to the solutions that human mathematicians had derived.  In 2026, AI’s power took a quantum leap. In several instances, scientists found that models could solve open-ended research questions — mathematical problems that had no known answer. Then, in September, OpenAI made a field-shaking announcement: The company focused thousands of its AI agents on a singular challenge, and after 88 hours, the agents produced a proof related to the Navier-Stokes equation — a Millienum Prize Problem that is one of seven unsolvable mathematical Holy Grails.  OpenAI’s sudden interest in the Navier-Stokes challenge coincided with work by Tristan Buckmaster, one of the panelists. After a year of progress, he and his collaborator, at rival AI behemoth Anthropic, were on the cusp of solving the problem when OpenAI made its announcement. OpenAI’s sprint to be first to the proof opened up a huge debate, about whether proper credit was given, whether the mathematicians’ data was leaked, how the AI agents arrived at their solution, whether that solution makes any meaningful sense, and above all, how AI will change mathematical research.  A month later, the company doubled down, releasing 722 manuscripts, organized into categories that ran the gamut of mathematical topics. The manuscripts claimed to have used AI entirely to solve many of math’s major, unsolved problems — an achievement that has widely been coined the “mathocalypse.”  But many mathematicians insist that it isn’t just about whether a problem can be solved, but also, how. And, they say, when they’ve looked into the details of AI proofs, it’s not clear how the agents arrived at their conclusions.  “The papers themselves are nonsense,” Hopkins said during Monday’s discussion, noting that AI-generated proofs contain “strange ideas.” He continued: “There still is a sense of AI math versus human math.” “For math to be important, it has to have human understanding,” Buckmaster added.  New norms For mathematicians like Kra, this moment in math’s history presents an opportunity to let go of certain long-held norms of mathematical research, such as competition among research groups and the prestige of being the first to prove an idea, also known as priority. “It shouldn’t matter that you’re first,” Kra said. “Speed should not be a priority. It’s not about the proof production anymore. We need to find other ways to assess understanding.” However, “We can throw away priority, but people are going to want to be pioneers,” Hopkins countered, noting the challenge that mathematicians will now face in making in-roads where AI has already clear-cut.  Kra, however, struck a hopeful counterpoint:  “You can be a pioneer in different ways, for instance in communicating [how a proof came to be],” said Kra, who helped this year to draft the Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics — a statement signed by mathematicians around the world that calls for action to address the risks that AI poses to mathematical research. “Communication of math is even more important now.”  Indeed, the panelists have already seen a subtle shift in what is expected of a mathematician, at all levels, from undergraduate students to early and established career mathematicians.  “The interview is becoming more important,” said Kra, noting that it’s no longer enough to accept, hire, or promote a mathematician based on ideas they have written or published — they have to also show that they understand and can explain those ideas to another person.  Human math AI is also making mathematicians question the role of academic journals, which have long been the benchmark for evaluating and validating mathematical advances. “Ninety percent of how we’ve judged [mathematicians] are through journals,” says Jacopo Borga, who is an early-career mathematician at MIT. “I’m not sure that’s how we should do this anymore. We should come up with a new metric and let it evolve.” Kra, who is a managing editor of a specialty journal, is seeing a huge increase in the number of papers submitted, primarily reporting results that were generated or assisted by AI. To deal with the deluge, that particular journal has had to hire an additional managing editor.  Where journal editors have traditionally prioritized publishing new proofs that push the field forward, Kra sees that, in response to AI “slop,” some publications are putting more value on exposition — the section of a paper that explains the reasoning behind a conjecture or proof. For now, humans have the advantage over AI in communicating mathematical ideas. “There’s a real art to exposition, if you can explain something in a clear and elegant way,” Hopkins echoed.  Kra noted that there are experimental journals coming online now, that are designed to highlight uniquely human contributions to mathematics. For instance, there are journals that publish expositions, such as papers that explain an old result in a new way that modern mathematicians can understand. “There is a lot of opportunity to curate and translate knowledge,” said Hopkins, who shared that one of his students has been working to prove a theorem from the 1970s. The original language and construction from that decades-old theorem, he said, was just as foreign as some of AI’s proofs today.  In noting novel approaches journals are taking in response to AI, Kra also mentioned Mathematical Discourse, a new peer-reviewed “video journal” that will feature videos of people giving talks about mathematical research. The journal’s preliminary site states that “giving a mathematical talk captures the human side of mathematics in a unique way, and supporting these human aspects of our discipline will be ever more important in the coming years.” “A new kind of mathematician” The rise of AI may be hitting especially hard for students, who are still learning the fundamentals in the presence of so many AI shortcuts.  “Mathematics is probably the slowest science you can do,” said Borga, to appreciative laughs from the audience. “Students today are bombarded by [conflicting messages of] what they should do, and are overwhelmed. We need to give them space to learn.” How they should learn could be a matter of personal belief.  “There is a big faction of my group who are ‘AI vegans’ [people who do not use AI], while others are using it,” said Hopkins, who is finding ways to support both groups. He also highlighted one particular student, who seemed to be a sort of “horse whisperer of AI.” This student has good mathematical instincts, Hopkins said, but struggles with execution. They are motivated by curiosity, rather than being first to a solution, and have a way of prompting AI to produce interesting insights.  “This may be a new kind of mathematician,” Hopkins said.  As AI forces the field of mathematics to adapt and change its centuries-long ways of pursuing knowledge, Borga and others see the moment as a new beginning, rather than math’s end. “The castle is collapsing,” Borga says. “There’s open ground to explore.” “AI is going to affect everyone (beyond mathematicians),” said Buckmaster, who urged students to stay the course “rather than escape or jump ship to another field. … Think of new ways to be creative and communicate your ideas,” he said. “Just do what you love.” The panel discussion, co-sponsored by the Department of Mathematics, is the first of a planned series hosted by MITHIC and SERC exploring how AI is reshaping our personal and professional lives.

7ed2d2b5505173bc: Microsoft has delivered its final scheduled non-security preview update of 2026 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2, with an updated Windows Search experience and a brighter Windows Hello for users who prefer darker rooms.

The optional KB5132057 update arrived on November 19, after this month's Patch Tuesday. Microsoft is skipping December's non-security preview because of reduced holiday operations, though that doesn't cancel the monthly security release. This last preview is quite a doozy.

Results appear faster with less clutter, the tool uses memory better, and files can be previewed directly in Windows Search.

We're less convinced by inline actions, which let users perform common tasks directly through Windows Search without opening Settings. 165fadc595acce83: Andy Burnham has attended his first EU-UK summit in Brussels with major agreements reached on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions. Ultimately though, the prime minister will have understood that this was merely the start of new political negotiations. Back home in the UK, he has started a “national conversation” on the future of UK-EU relations that gained momentum rapidly. Burnham held talks with European Council president Antonio Costa and president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen. Both Burnham and Costa come from sister social democratic parties and both are former mayors – Burnham of Greater Manchester and Costa of Lisbon. This could make for smoother meetings in future than in the months and years after the 2016 Brexit referendum. In the run up to the talks, the prime minister had repeatedly claimed that the Conservatives failed to get a good deal from the EU. As part of former prime minister Keir Starmer’s “reset” of relations with Europe, then-business secretary, Peter Kyle, and European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera signed a deal committing the UK and the EU to closer cooperation on trade. Like Costa and Burnham, Ribera is also from a European social democratic party (the Spanish Socialist Workers Party, or PSOE). Senior figures in Labour have long admired the electoral success of social democrats in both Spain and Portugal. When it comes to claims of the UK having had a bad deal, there is one explanation that is under-discussed. It has its roots in the internal party politics of the centre-right in Europe. Ahead of the 2009 European Parliament elections, the then-Conservative leader David Cameron decided to leave the European People’s Party (a bloc of centre-right pro-European parties). Cameron went on to set up a new right-of-centre eurosceptic faction with parties from Poland and the Czech Republic. But he underestimated how hurt highly influential EU figures like German chancellor Angela Merkel were by the move. So when it came to negotiating a better deal with the EU ahead of the 2016 referendum, Merkel and other figures had not forgotten Cameron’s betrayal. As such, they felt disinclined to meet him half way. Burnham is walking a fine line Youth mobility, migration, food exports and emissions are all important issues. But the broader discussion is increasingly about the politics around Brexit rather than the rights and wrongs of Brexit itself. The UK is not going to rejoin the EU in the near future. Burnham even said when standing in the Makerfield byelection that first and foremost he wants to sort the consequences of Brexit rather than necessarily the outcome. Now Burnham is increasingly focused on the claim that Brexit hasn’t worked for British voters – without saying it was completely wrong. He may understand that aiming to reverse Brexit in a binary way could simply open up new problems. It could even finish his premiership in the same way that it ended the tenures of multiple prime ministers before him. In contrast, however, Burnham understands that he has the political capital to discuss the downsides of Brexit. For now, at least, he can do this in a way that is unlikely to result in much political damage to his government. While not completely without risk, he has calculated that the benefits of discussing Brexit outweigh any costs. These costs could include the fragile “red wall” of Labour seats in northern England and the Midlands. The party knows all too well that this could flip to Reform UK the next time the country goes to the polls. But those voters who have already moved to Reform are something of a sunk cost for Labour. For now, it seems Burnham sees more advantages in drawing voters away from the Liberal Democrats and the Greens than he sees disadvantages in alienating supporters of Reform. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch appears to be sensitive to the fact that many people disapprove of how the Tories handled Brexit – whether they voted Remain or Leave. At the height of the Brexit chaos, however, Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester and so can revisit the issue in a fresh way, untainted by the Westminister turbulence of that time. His predecessor Starmer was frequently seen as being paralysed by caution. Burnham appears to know how to talk about difficult issues lightly and fluently – his own parliamentary seat overwhelmingly voted Leave in 2016. He may or may not truly want to see the UK rejoin the EU at some point – he has sometimes sent out mixed signals on the issue. But he certainly has the firm aim of removing the toxicity from the issue and having a “national conversation”. To do this, the prime minister will have to consider how Westminster relates to Brussels as well as how it relates to constituencies like his own in Makerfield. 449ce2f82209367a: A recent 'SNL' sketch called 'Sister' lampoons gender roles in caring for aging parents. NBCA “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “Sister” has gone viral. The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free? The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families. According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 63 million Americans provide ongoing care to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade. About 61% of these caregivers are women. As researchers who study aging, long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers initially have better health and financial status than noncaregivers. But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts. While societal gender expectations help explain why daughters often assume the bulk of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide. “Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch immediately went viral. Medicare doesn’t cover long-term care One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance with everyday activities. Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services. However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals or getting to the bathroom generally cannot rely on Medicare to pay for that assistance. Under Medicare’s home health benefit, limited personal care may be covered only when a patient also qualifies for skilled nursing or therapy services following surgery or a medical emergency and meets Medicare’s homebound requirements. This distinction has enormous consequences. Someone over 65 may have comprehensive coverage for medical treatment but little help with the daily tasks necessary to remain safely at home. And this care is expensive: The national median cost of a home health aide was approximately US$6,688 per month, while residing in an assisted living facility averaged $6,141 per month in 2025. For many older Americans, paying for the care they need is simply out of reach. A 2025 Harvard study found that 76% of households age 75 and older could not afford daily assistance from a home health aide after covering housing and basic living expenses. When paid care is unaffordable, those responsibilities frequently fall to relatives or, more rarely, close friends. Medicaid can help, but access is limited Medicaid, the public health insurance program for people who are low-income or have disabilities, is the country’s primary long-term care payer. Unlike Medicare, Medicaid can pay for personal assistance at home, including help with bathing, dressing and other daily activities. The program covered nearly two-thirds of U.S. home care spending in 2023. The divide between these programs dates back to 1965, when Medicare was created to cover medical care for older adults, while Medicaid was designed to provide health coverage for people with low incomes. Over time, Medicaid became the country’s main payer for long-term care as the need for these costly services grew. However, Medicaid eligibility generally requires meeting financial and other criteria that vary by state. Many older adults must exhaust most of their savings before qualifying for assistance. Even being eligible for the program doesn’t guarantee that all needed services will be readily available. States have considerable discretion over the home-based services they provide, and many eligible people spend more than a year on waitlists to get services. Who provides care in the meantime? As the sketch suggests, daughters are more likely to care for their aging parents. Visual Vic/Moment via Getty Images There’s a shortage of paid caregivers Having coverage, whether through Medicaid or the dwindling options available through private insurers to pay for long-term care, is only part of the challenge. Finding reliable help can be a struggle. The nation’s direct care workforce, which includes home health aides and personal care assistants, faces persistent recruitment and retention challenges. These shortages may get worse as immigration enforcement and deportations reduce the workforce – one-third of these workers are foreign-born. The median hourly wage for direct care work was $17.99 in 2025, only $2-$3 per hour more than what fast-food workers earned. Caregiving often has financial consequences When paid assistance is unavailable, insufficient or unaffordable, daughters and other relatives often fill the gaps by providing additional hours of care. Family caregivers may have to work fewer hours or quit their jobs. These decisions not only reduce their income right away, but also whittle down their retirement savings and can depress the Social Security benefits they get in the future. The federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave to care for certain family members, but the leave is unpaid. And caring for an older parent with chronic health conditions may continue for years after that leave runs out. Because women are more likely to provide family care, they also face disproportionate exposure to these employment and financial risks. Families often have to shoulder responsibility Over the past two decades, some states have begun to address these gaps. California, New Jersey and about a dozen other states, for example, have launched paid family leave programs. In New York and some other states Medicaid is compensating family caregivers. Washington state is helping finance long-term care coverage. In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris proposed expanding Medicare to cover more in-home assistance, an approach that would have addressed one of the main gaps in the current system. The Democratic presidential nominee’s proposal never moved beyond the campaign trail after Harris lost the 2024 election. “Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch makes light of an uncomfortable family dynamic, but the issue extends well beyond whether brothers and sisters divide responsibilities fairly. Government policies are behind why so much of that responsibility falls on families in the first place. When public programs do not cover the care older adults need, the need does not disappear. The work, and its financial and personal costs, simply shift to someone else. More often than not, that someone is a daughter. Jane Tavares receives funding from the RRF Foundation for Aging.
