48a4b14c4a193313: Philadelphia workers who work for a private company with more than 10 employees may be entitled to paid sick leave. andresr/E+ Collection via Getty ImagesWhat do you do when you wake up with a runny nose and a cough? If you work in Philadelphia, you might have the legal right to a paid sick day. There is no federal right to paid sick leave. However, Philadelphia, like a growing number of states and cities nationwide, requires certain employers to provide paid time off when workers get sick. In Philadelphia, these requirements apply to private-sector employers with more than 10 employees. In theory, under these laws, sick workers have time to recover and avoid spreading germs, and they don’t have to choose between a sick day and a paycheck. For immigrant workers, though, it may not be that easy. I study restaurant work, an industry that depends on the labor of people who are foreign-born. Philadelphia’s award-winning dining scene wouldn’t be the same without the creativity and hard work of people from countries such as Mexico, Honduras and Guatemala. I studied this industry during the COVID-19 pandemic by working in a restaurant from 2021 to 2022, as well as by interviewing restaurant workers, managers and owners from 2021 to 2024. Some interviews were also conducted by my then-fellow Temple University graduate students Andrew Chelius and Camila Franco Rodríguez. Philadelphia’s paid sick leave law has been around since 2015. During the COVID-19 pandemic, federal and local laws temporarily expanded those protections. The Families First Coronavirus Response Act, a federal law which was passed on March 18, 2020, and amended by the CARES Act later that same month, required private-sector employers with less than 500 employees to provide 80 hours of paid sick time each year, on top of their existing paid leave policies, to full-time employees. A 2022 temporary expansion of the local paid sick leave law in Philadelphia, meanwhile, required private-sector employers with 25 or more employees to provide 40 hours of additional paid sick leave to eligible employees. What I found, though, was that several factors could make it hard for workers to take advantage of these policies. Immigrant workers faced unique, additional barriers. ‘$300 for a simple flu’ Our interviews and my immersion in restaurant work showed me that even during a pandemic, restaurant workers had to deal with employers skirting the law or misunderstanding policies. Workers were also impacted by long-standing service industry norms that discourage calling in sick, even when they’re under the weather. Many bosses required doctor’s notes, too, before they paid out any sick time – as I heard from bosses themselves. The local law says, however, that employers may require “reasonable documentation” – but only after an absence of more than two days. Immigrant workers, meanwhile, experienced additional hurdles. Take the example of doctor’s notes. Seeing a doctor is more affordable when you have health insurance. If you’re an undocumented immigrant, getting health insurance is difficult and expensive. Undocumented people are not eligible for Medicaid and are excluded from the Affordable Care Act marketplace. Only a few states try to mend the gap by offering health insurance for low-income people ineligible for Medicaid. Pennsylvania is not one of them. Bill – a pseudonym, like the other participants’ names in this article – is originally from Mexico, and he was a server at an Italian restaurant in Philadelphia’s Center City during the pandemic. When he got sick, his attitude was: “Keep the money. Don’t pay me for sick days.” What kept Bill from claiming sick pay? His employer required him to turn in a doctor’s note before he could receive paid sick leave. However, Bill was undocumented and did not have health insurance. “I wasn’t going to go to the doctor and spend US$300-$400 for a simple flu,” he said. Gaps arise when restaurants have different policies for front-of-house workers, who interact with customers, than back-of-house workers, who staff the kitchen. Willie B. Thomas/DigitalVision Collection via Getty Images Different policies for back-of-house workers In the restaurant where I worked, meanwhile, it was harder for immigrant workers to get sick days than nonimmigrant workers, based on my observations and interviews. This was not necessarily due to ill will toward immigrant workers. But there was a stricter policy around paid sick leave in the kitchen, which was staffed mostly by immigrants from Latin America. The chef who managed the kitchen described his policy like this: “If you bring me proof that you went to the doctor, and the doctor gave you a day or two days of rest, OK, that’s fine.” Those days would be paid. In the customer-facing front of the house, though, where a different manager was in charge, workers – including me – weren’t told they needed proof. These workers were almost all nonimmigrants and mostly white. I heard from Socorro, a prep cook who worked at a different restaurant, that managers where she worked were stingier with sick days for kitchen workers than for servers. “The servers were given their sick leave days and paid them. They’d say, ‘Oh no, my head hurts. I’m not going to work.’ But we couldn’t. ‘Oh, your head hurts? You have to put up with it and come to work.” In that workplace, Socorro said, immigrants also mainly worked in the kitchen, while servers were mostly U.S.-born. Fear of retaliation Immigrant workers in Philadelphia restaurants – both those with and without legal status – also weighed the risks they could face if they asked for paid sick days. These were not risks their nonimmigrant co-workers generally worried about. Claudia, a restaurant worker from Mexico, worked with a local organization called El Comité de Trabajadorxs de Restaurante – the Committee of Restaurant Workers – to educate her peers about paid sick leave. She found that immigrants were really scared of losing their jobs if they spoke up for themselves. “The majority – 80% if not 90% – even if they know they have paid sick hours … they don’t ask for it,” she said. “They don’t claim it, because [they think], ‘Oh, I am an immigrant and they are going to fire me.’ Or, 'Where am I going to get another job?’” Healthy workers, healthy public My research suggests that immigrants in Philadelphia face a gap between the promise and the reality of the city’s paid sick leave policies. These barriers might also help explain gaps in paid sick leave access between foreign-born and U.S.-born workers in other places that require it, like New York City or California. Gaps in access based on immigration status are an equity issue. But beyond that, research suggests that everyone wins if it’s easier for workers to get paid sick leave. Paid sick leave makes for healthier workers, and healthier workers make for a healthier public. Read more of our stories about Philadelphia and Pennsylvania, or sign up for our Philadelphia newsletter on Substack. 6a2137afaca073ec: Some Windows 11 applications might fail to install or launch after Microsoft's November hotpatch, but not to worry: there's a Registry tweak to work around it.
Microsoft has confirmed it isn't administrators' imaginations. The November hotpatch is causing application errors, including in little-used and obscure apps such as Outlook.

Affected applications may fail during installation, launch, or use, displaying errors such as "ERROR_ALLOTTED_SPACE_EXCEEDED (0xC0000099)." Microsoft's investigation points to applications that load the 32-bit Windows Installer DLL, msi.dll. The problem is more common with 32-bit software, but can also affect 64-bit applications "under certain circumstances."

The workaround involves fiddling with the Registry on affected devices, so is not for the faint of heart and a backup is a good idea before diving in. Microsoft says the key "HotPatchTableSize" in the folder "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management" needs to be set to "2000" followed by a restart.
Just the thing to round out the week for administrators.

The issue affects the November hotpatch, not the standard monthly cumulative security update. "Devices which installed the November 2026 Windows monthly security update are not expected to be affected by this issue," Microsoft said.

Windows hotpatches are security updates that don't require a device restart (unless, as in this instance, administrators have to do so to address errors after a hotpatch is installed). Windows 11 hotpatching requires version 24H2 or later, an eligible subscription, and the necessary management and security configuration.

"Hotpatch update package size is significantly smaller than the standard cumulative updates," Microsoft said, and the goal is to "streamline the installation process and enhance compliance efficiency."
The offending hotpatch, KB5132043, was released on November 10. It followed the October 13 baseline, which was a prerequisite.
Microsoft made hotpatching the default in Windows Autopatch earlier this year. At the time, we asked: "What could possibly go wrong?"
Thanks to November's hotpatch, we have our answer. ®

e853741b74a166f4: Now that Ismail Lasim sudah buat pengakukan terbuka bahawa beliau tidak pernah letak jawatan menteri besar Negeri Sembilan, persoalan penting ialah siapa yang mengutus ‘surat peletakan jawatannya’ kepada Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan?
Persoalan ini amat penting kerana pada hemat saya pihak yang mengutus surat itu telah membohongi atau cuba membohongi Tuanku Muhriz Tuan Munawir.
Apa tidaknya kerana pihak itu telah memaklumkan perkara yang nampaknya tidak benar dan mahu baginda mempercayai isi kandungan surat itu mengenai peletakan jawatan menteri besar.

Orang atau orang-orang yang terlibat dengan penghantaran surat itu saya kira tidak sangka akan reaksi Yang Dipertuan Besar sebaik menerima surat itu. Atas kebijaksanaan Tuanku Muhriz, Istana Negeri Sembilan menegaskan (ketika itu) belum mengesahkan ketulenan surat itu meskipun menurut Setiausaha Agung BN Zambry Abdul Kadir ia telah ditandatangani Ismail.
Sebelum berbicara lanjut elok kita imbau kembali kenyataan Pengelola Bijaya Diraja Istana Negeri Sembilan Azizi Mohamad Ali yang dikeluarkan 17 Nov lalu berbunyi begini:
“Istana Negeri Sembilan mengambil maklum akan kenyataan Zambry Abdul Kadir, Setiausaha Agung Barisan Nasional berhubung peletakan jawatan Ismail Lasim sebagai menteri besar Negeri Sembilan.
Kenyataan itu dimuat naik di media sosial pada 10 malam 16 Nov dan kelihatan berdasarkan salinan surat peletakan jawatan yang berada dalam milikan beliau.
Surat peletakan itu telah dihantar ke Istana Hingap Seremban pada 12.16 pagi 17 November”.

Bagi saya ini amat janggal. Zambry telah menghebahkan ‘peletakan jawatan’ Ismail pada malam 16 Nov tetapi ‘surat peletakan jawatan’ Ismail dihantar ke Istana Hinggap hanya pada keesokan hari yakni 17 Nov.
Bukankah ini bermakna Zambry sudah mengumumkan peletakan jawatan Ismail long before Yang Dipertuan Besar dimaklumkan? Is this proper dalam urusan dengan istana?

Berbalik kenyataan Pengelola Bijya Diraja Istana Negeri Sembilan yang disebut tadi: “Surat itu diserahkan oleh seorang individu yang memperkenalkan dirinya sebagai Hamidi daripada firma guaman Shahrul Hamidi & Haziq"
Aneh. Jika saya mahu letak jawatan misalnya daripada syarikat tempat saya bekerja, saya akan umum sendiri my resignation. Bukan orang lain yang umum.
Dan surat peletakan jawatan akan saya serah sendiri kepada majikan bukan meminta pihak lain melakukannya.
Dalam kes ‘peletakan jawatan’ Ismail adakah ‘molek’ menyerahkan surat kepada Yang Dipertuan Besar menerusi third party? Dan tidak menghadap untuk mempersembahkan surat personally?

Ada lagi yang dihuraikan Pengelola Bijaya Diraja Istana Negeri Sembilan. Menurut beliau: “Pada jam 6.38 petang,semalam (16 Nov 2026 ) Setiausaha Sulit Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan telah menyampaikan kepada Ismail melalui aplikasi WhatsApp perkenan Tuanku Muhriz untuk menghadap seperti yang dipohon oleh menteri besar itu.
Perkara tu telah diakui terima oleh Ismail dan acara menghadap telah ditetapkan pada pukul 10 pagi Jumaat (20 Nov).
Perkenan untuk menghadap itu telah diberikan 80 minit lebih awal sebelum siaran media Zambry yang memaklumkan peletakan jawatan itu.
Aneh dan pelik. Ismail yang memohon menghadap bertindak ‘meneruskan hasrat letak jawatan’ (yang diumum Zambry) setelah tahu Yang Dipertuan Besar telah perkenankan permohonannya?

Berbalik pula kepada kenyataan setiausaha agung BN itu. Kata Zambry pengerusi gabungan itu Zahid Hamidi sudah menerima salinan suara peletakan jawatan Ismail yang diutuskan kepada Yang Dipertuan Besar.

“Pengerusi Barisan Nasional akan mengemukakan cadangan calon menteri besar yang baharu untuk dipersembahkan ke hadapan Duli Yang Maha Mulia Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilsn selaras dengan peruntukan Undang Undang Tubuh Kerajaan Negeri Sembilan”.

Zahid insisted Ismail resigned voluntarily. Beliau juga memberitahu media hanya satu nama akan dipersembahkan. Ini menurut saya tidak beri Yang Dipertuan Besar banyak pilihan. Atau tidak beri pilihan langsung.

Apa pun itu sudah tidak terpakai kerana hari ini Yang Dipertuan Besar bertitah supaya Ismail teruskan tugas sebagai menteri besar. Ini kata Ismail pada sidang medianya selepas menghadap Tuanku Muhriz.
Saya ulangi apa kata Ismail pada sidang media itu “Saya tak pernah setuju surat ini dihantar dan saya pun tak hantar sendiri surat ini kepada Tuanku. Saya hanya tahu melalui media sosial.”
Namun Ismail mengaku surat peletakan jawatan semenagnya ada dalam simpanan pimpinan parti namun tidak dinyatakan sebabnya.
Setahu saya ada parti mewajibkan Ahli Parlimen dan Adun yang mewaklinya menandatangnai surat melepaskan jawatan atau kedudukan dalam usaha memastkan mereka tidak lompat parti.
The pre signed resignation letter will be released in the event of crossing over to other parties. Ini amalan lazim sebelum ada anti hopping law.
Bagaimanapun boleh dirumuskan penjelasan Ismail diterima Yang Dipertuan Besar pada upacara menghadap semalam. Lantas baginda mahu Ismail kekal sebagai menteri besar.
Bagi saya episod Negeri Sembilan tamparan hebat kepada BN khususnya Umno yang selama ini megah mendakwa ia mempertahakan Raja-Raja Melayu dn kedaulatan Istana.
Di Negeri Sembilan tidak boleh dinafikan Umno mendekati (bersekongkol?) kumpulan yang cuba menurunkan Tuanku Muhriz daripada takhta dan gagal.

2b876ce610b840bc: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
What we learned when our Roundtables explored the quest to make minds immortal

To preserve our sense of self, some scientists are working on ways to keep our brains going—even beyond death. In their quest for cognitive immortality, these “mind savers” are exploring everything from head transplants and brain freezing to conscious software avatars.

In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtables event, senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado joined science editor Mary Beth Griggs to examine these ideas. After following the money, the science, and the philosophy, he came back part skeptical, part awestruck. Here’s a taste of what Antonio found—and what he made of it.

Not all the projects are quite what they seem: A $190 million US government program to develop replacement brain tissue is officially about treating stroke, but “it’s also a fig leaf for the actual ambition”: living forever.

AI could lead to convincing mind clones: Large language models are making it possible to build AI copies of people that act quite like the real thing. “This digital avatar might not be good enough for you, but what if it’s good enough for me?”
Immortality can be a hard sell: One company, Nectome, wants to preserve brains within 12 minutes of medically assisted death. “If you’re selling a hot product, this is not it.”
It’s not always clear what we’re trying to preserve: “I’m not even sure that I have a very good claim to be myself.”
There’s an upside to life as a brain in a jar: “You can surf the internet. I do that pretty much 12 hours a day, anyway.”
To find out which of these ideas might actually work, subscribers can now watch the full conversation on demand.

35d924813e8f8450: Global consultancy PwC says IT departments struggling to secure funding for ERP upgrades should make the expected benefits of AI part of their pitch.

The Oracle and SAP mega-partner told El Reg that a "clean core" – modern enterprise applications with fewer customizations embedded in the underlying system – makes deploying AI agents easier. Selling that prospect, rather than incremental improvements to existing processes, could help IT leaders justify a migration.

Oracle and SAP are both trying to persuade customers to move from established ERP systems to newer platforms. For SAP, that means S/4HANA, preferably in the cloud. For Oracle, it means Fusion Cloud Applications. Moving from ECC or E-Business Suite, respectively, can involve root-and-branch changes to technology and business processes, rather than a straightforward software upgrade.

Thousands of organizations still rely on these aging, often heavily customized systems. IT leaders struggle to justify a costly, time-consuming migration when the reward appears to be doing the same meat-and-veg business processes slightly better. For example, a survey of SAP users last year found that 95 percent said building a positive case for migration required substantial effort or was genuinely challenging.

Speaking to The Register, Jennifer Colapietro, PwC digital core modernization platform leader, said: "You're seeing it a lot more as part of the rationale for the business case for why they should upgrade, answering the question: 'Why now? What should we prioritize?' Certainly, AI and getting the value of AI, a key business case justification for that.

"Folks have budgets for ERP, but now [funding for transformation is] being split because they also have budgets for AI. But there's synergies across them. If you look at moving to a clean digital core ERP, that will help them to realize the AI value faster... be able to turn on AI and be able to start to automate a lot of the processes and implement the agents. That helps to build the business case."

SAP recently introduced Joule 2.0 while Oracle has announced Fusion Claw. With both of these new technologies, the vendors are promising customers they can build AI agents to automate business processes and perform some work that was previously done by humans. Colapietro argued that moving to more modern platforms makes deploying AI agents easier and more effective than adding AI capabilities around legacy systems.

"It is more challenging to apply AI to the older systems. We focus on the importance of a clean digital core as the foundation for getting the value and effectiveness out of AI and scaling AI responsibly. I think that's given," she said.

An ERP replacement isn't the only route to AI, however. European home improvement retailer Kingfisher – which owns the B&Q brand in the UK – eschewed SAP's overtures to upgrade its ECC system, despite encroaching deadlines. Mainstream maintenance for supported ECC 6.0 versions ends in December 2027, with optional extended maintenance through 2030 at a premium of two percentage points on the existing maintenance base.
Kingfisher opted instead for third-party support from Rimini Street, building an AI strategy around its existing ERP system using a combination of technology from Databricks and Google.
AI might help sell an ERP migration to the board. It doesn't make replacing the ERP system a prerequisite. ®

90752f7c49cc9934: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security.
The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data.
The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government.
The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters.
The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month.

A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers.

For Apple, a company that has long made privacy central to its marketing, and famously rejected an FBI order to break open an iPhone to assist a terror probe, being served the TCN meant it either had to somehow defy a legal order issued by the UK, or undermine the encryption technology that customers expected.

While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand.

At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens.
In August 2025, Gabbard announced that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to users in the US.

Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators.

Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless.
Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not.
What the judgment does not confirm
While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public.

"Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret in order to preserve national security and the public interest.

"We agree that it would be damaging to national security if all of the material (including the content of the technical capability evidence, and the evidence of Apple and the respondent) were publicly disclosed.

"That does not mean every detail must be kept secret in order to preserve national security. There may be some information that could be disclosed publicly without damaging national security. It is not, however, practical to determine the precise boundaries now."
The parties are working toward a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027. Apple's first challenge was dismissed following a "change in circumstances," and it filed a second claim in July 2026.
The Financial Times reported in October 2025 that the UK had replaced its original notice with a new order focused on British users.
The proceedings also include a separate challenge to the TCN regime brought by Liberty, Privacy International, and two individuals.

A government spokesperson said: "Terrorists, child abusers and organized crime groups cannot be allowed to operate beyond the reach of the law. The right to privacy is crucial but it should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public.

"A judge can authorize access to a criminal's home, a parcel they've sent, or a car they drive. The online world is no different. These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has direct access to a company's communications systems or data.

"Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so.
"Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies."
Apple did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

b6f28c6c829ce1b8: A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2.

The problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again."

Except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored."

Cross-device authentication lets users sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft says the issue affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID.
Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected.
An authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets.

Microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057, the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, users can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®

44d770d44f7e73b2: FRANKFURT, Nov 20 — German airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs as its turnaround efforts move slower than hoped, with the energy shock from the Iran war adding to headwinds, according to an internal letter seen by AFP on Friday.
The carrier embarked on a cost-cutting programme in 2024 to stem losses but the measures announced so far are “no longer sufficient”, according to the letter sent to staff.
During the first nine months of the year, the airline was losing on average €20 million (RM90.3 million) a month, it said.

“The year 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, the still very high fuel costs, nine days of strike action and our already very high cost base have intensified the situation,” the letter said.
Germany’s flagship carrier now plans to cut 1,000 full-time positions at the Frankfurt and Munich airports, amounting to around 2.5 per cent of its roughly 40,000 employees.

Lufthansa, which also operates carriers including Austrian, Swiss and Brussels Airlines, last year announced plans to cut 4,000 jobs across the whole group by 2030, mainly targeting administrative roles.
It was not immediately clear whether the cuts disclosed on Friday were included in this round of layoffs, or in addition. A Lufthansa spokesman declined to give further details.
Despite the woes of the flagship airline, the wider group is in good financial health.
It reported a 30-per cent jump in profits in the July-September period, beating forecasts, boosted by demand for premium tickets on long-haul routes.
But surging fuel costs since the start of the US war on Iran are weighing on the group, with its annual fuel bill set to come in two billion euros higher this year than in 2025. — AFP
cb6b8f7f209ece1b: HONG KONG, Nov 20 — Tech-rich Seoul, Tokyo and Taipei led losses across Asia on Friday as Anthropic’s sparkling debut failed to muster a recovery in sentiment towards the AI trade, with nerves frayed by worries over crisis-hit Nvidia, profitability and regulation.
After its record-breaking initial public offering, Claude-creator Anthropic soared 17 per cent on its first day as ordinary investors sought to grab a piece of the new kid on the block.
But the rally did nothing to drag other, more established firms higher as the uncertainty that has hung over the tech sector in recent months sapped confidence, sending Wall Street deep into the red.

Magnificent Seven members who led a scorching surge over the past two years continued a retreat that has characterised trade since the summer, as investors fret over AI profitability, eye-watering spending, rising borrowing costs and geopolitics.

Microsoft, Apple, Amazon and Tesla were all well down, along with Nvidia — which is battling to deal with the fallout from a spy scandal that has led to the resignation of pivotal leader Jensen Huang.
The losses continued on US futures markets, with Anthropic dropping more than four per cent.

Traders have also been spooked by the US Commerce Department’s move to close a loophole allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s powerful AI chips remotely, adding to worries that a new Democratic-led Congress will impose further regulations.
The selling followed through to Asia, where Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei — home to the region’s leading AI-linked firms — tumbled between five and 6.2 per cent.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 was dragged by losses of 11 per cent in Kioxia and 14.5 per cent in tech investor SoftBank, while TSMC shed 4.8 per cent and MediaTek tanked 10 per cent as Taiwan’s main stock market was dragged more than six per cent lower.
SK hynix and Samsung took the brunt as South Korea’s Kospi dived more than five per cent.
Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Bangkok, Jakarta and Manila also took a pummelling.
London, Paris and Frankfurt extended the losses at the open.
The flight from risk boosted the safe-haven yen, helped by a surge in Japanese inflation last month that stoked bets on another central bank interest rate hike.
US Treasuries were also boosted, with yields on most term-lengths dropping. Yields fall as demand sends prices higher.

“With volatility elevated, equity futures breaking support and high-beta assets under pressure, traders will increasingly look for signs of capitulation, stabilisation or a catalyst capable of reversing sentiment,” said Chris Weston at Pepperstone.
“The risk is that selling becomes self-reinforcing. As volatility rises, risk limits tighten, leveraged positions are reduced and systematic strategies can add to the pressure.

“Whether Anthropic’s IPO proves to be a defining moment for the AI trade remains to be seen. For now, the immediate priority is watching how markets settle into the weekend and whether buyers can regain control next week.”

Investors are keeping tabs on developments in the Nvidia case as California announced it was investigating whether the firm misled the public and investors about its chips ending up in China, despite federal export controls.
Huang resigned last week after reports alleged he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with a woman named Alice Huang who is a suspected Chinese spy.

Alice Huang, who is no relation, is the former director of Megaspeed, a cloud computing company based in Singapore that was investigated by local officials in 2025 over potential export control violations.
Jensen Huang has agreed to attend a closed-door questioning session about national security issues with Congressional officials on December 1.

Oil prices rose on worries about fresh violence in the Middle East and after the International Energy Agency (IEA) said the crisis in the Middle East had created the “largest threat” to energy security in history.
The IEA said in its annual World Energy Outlook that consumers were increasingly footing the bill as the world runs out of ways to absorb the impact of the conflict on energy supplies. — AFP
c1bc16b70ede5f6f: Canonical is targeting Ubuntu 28.04 LTS for the release of its immutable Core Desktop, with a stretch goal of making it the default download for Ubuntu 30.04.

Canonical's VP of engineering, Jon Seager, set out the timetable in his opening keynote at Ubuntu Summit 26.10. Yes, we know, we have heard this before: we reported on his plans last month. But this time, there's the beginning of a release schedule.

Seager said that Ubuntu Core is already out there in tens of thousands of IoT devices – which seems like a modest estimate to us, and to him too, as he quickly added "maybe more." Despite some noise a few years ago, though, what's still missing is the desktop version.
Seager's slides listed three bullet points: that Core Desktop will be "immutable," "composable," and "attestable."

As he put it, they are "taking the whole of the Linux operating system, and cramming the whole thing into snaps." Acknowledging that this is going to be wildly controversial, he said: "This is one for the Redditors."

He's right. There is a lot of resistance to snap, and in direct response, advocacy of the Red Hat-backed Flatpak instead – but we have seen almost none that is based on either system's technical merits. Much of that opposition concerns claims of one being more open than the other. We've looked at how both systems work, and our impression is that the implementation of snap is cleaner, simpler, easier to use, and more comprehensible. Snap does depend on systemd, which Flatpak does not – but only for now. Flatpak NG is in development and will also need everyone's favorite init system.
Ubuntu Core's immutability is not new technology: even Core 16 is now a decade old. It has supported in-place version upgrades since Core 22.

We have reported before that Canonical remains strongly committed to its packaging format, and that commitment seems stronger than ever. Seager continued: "Never has a model like snap confinement been more relevant… we're finally in a position where we can bring this to the desktop."

The core idea of an immutable OS is that "much more of the system is not writable at runtime," meaning that it "can't be messed with once the system has booted." He talked about the same three use cases we discussed last month. The "browser-centric machine" is the company's analog to Google ChromeOS, and he said that it's essentially ready now, suggesting that everyone listening probably has a family member whose computer is basically just a way to use a web browser.

The second was the dedicated games machine, which we interpret as a response to Valve's SteamOS. This edition, he said, would "boot straight to Steam," with "just enough of a shell to launch games." There's also an immutable "development workstation," and here, he offered the example of developers who need to work on some long-unsupported hardware or software, for whom an immutable OS means that you "can't brick your system by installing some weird old dependencies, unmaintained for 20 years."

Another important benefit is "atomic, transactional updates," which he said "brings enormous stability." The terminology comes from the database world: an atomic operation succeeds as a whole or is not applied. The aim is to avoid leaving the system stranded between incompatible package versions, with rollback providing a route back if an update causes trouble.
The "composable" part means assembling the OS from separately packaged components, from desktop environments to underlying services such as PipeWire and fingerprint-reader support.

Here, Seager used an example that spoke to us. He asked: "Ever installed something and watch as it spewed stuff all over your system?" Yes, we have, many, many times. You install one innocent-seeming little component, and it brings in a database, three new server components, and about half of a different desktop environment. We mentioned an example when we described how to customize Xfce a couple of months ago. That time around, in Debian, we found it was safe to install all packages starting with "xfce4-" except "xfce4-dev-tools." Most are tiny panel controls taking just hundreds of kilobytes, but the "dev-tools" package also pulls in several hundred megabytes of compilers, linkers, and other programming tools, totally unrelated to desktop layouts – and once installed, they're surprisingly tricky to remove again.

This is part of the appeal of a composable immutable OS: adding a component need not mean tangling its dependencies into the base system. But easier housekeeping isn't the only attraction. Canonical kept snap packages from its cancelled phone and tablet OS because snaps enable it to maintain a single package of, for instance, Firefox, which will work on all of its different OS versions that are still getting updates. Moving such important external dependencies into isolated snap packages makes it easier and safer to upgrade from one version of the OS to another. Complex sets of dependencies are the main point of failure of OS upgrades, especially when the OS has been used for a while.

This is very much not a solved problem. For instance, Debian version upgrades can be fraught – especially when the installation has decades of history behind it. Debian does at least support version-to-version upgrades. For many years and versions, RHEL did not – which is why we highlighted AlmaLinux's tooling for the task. Zorin OS added version-to-version upgrades in 16.3 just a few years ago. Linux Mint introduced its own upgrade tooling a few years earlier, although it still imposes restrictions.

It's a tough issue to crack. Major enterprise vendors discourage it, and phone OSes are all immutable. Helping with this problem is one of the main reasons snap packaging exists, while Flatpak is almost entirely irrelevant to it.

Seager also stated that Core Desktop would support "multiple desktops from the start." This will not be a GNOME-only project. Indeed, he specifically mentioned a KDE Plasma version, saying: "Plasma is great. People love it. We will have a KDE edition, with rolling Plasma. We will deliver upstream Plasma, as fast as we can." That sounds like a very welcome counterpoint to the LTS version of Plasma 6.6 in Kubuntu 26.04 whose announcement we covered back in August.

For the "attestable" line of the slide, he claimed that Core Desktop was "evolving the way we think about 'trust' on a machine. We have TPM, secure boot, TPM-backed Full Disk Encryption… but they're all bolt-ons." Core Desktop, he added, could "tie this into a hardware root of trust," delivering "verified system integrity." Canonical revived its TPM-backed full-disk encryption system back in 2025, and it arrived in Ubuntu 26.04. Back in January, systemd creator Lennart Poettering launched his startup Amutable, and earlier this month published a technical overview of its new immutable Linux. We suspect Canonical is watching closely, and that this is a hint in that direction.

We were also amused by Seager's mention of another rather niche distro: he said that Core Desktop would deliver "all of the joy that people derive from NixOS, for those with that perverse habit – but for everybody."

Daily preview installation images of Core Desktop will, apparently, be available very soon, in both GNOME and KDE flavors, and he warned that "there be dragons." (That may be a veiled nod to one of founder Mark Shuttleworth's other companies.)

After the promises made in 2023, we'll be watching that timetable closely. "I believe this is the future of Linux," Seager said, promising "a final version by 28.04, released alongside Ubuntu," adding that a "very stretchy stretch goal was by default for 30.04: download from ubuntu.com and you get Core Desktop – unless you ask for the other thing."
For those alarmed by that prospect, he had reassurance: "Ubuntu as you know it today is not going anywhere. There are no plans for the existing distro to go away."

Core Desktop wasn't even the main subject of his keynote. They followed a lengthy excursion into formal logic: definitions, proofs, invariants, and designing software whose behavior can be checked against precisely stated rules. The accompanying slides showed the logos of organizations working in this area, such as Hegel, Antithesis, and the Lean programming language. For now, an entire OS is much too big to formally verify, but subcomponents may be doable – and Canonical is starting with snapd.

He also expressed his satisfaction with the Stonking release, highlighting that it advanced Canonical's move toward Rust-based components, including Rustls and upki – noting that this proved very timely in the light of recent events. The release also delivered the newest available kernel, OpenSSL 4 – which he called a "huge change" – and official RISC-V images. He also called out the Myna speech-recognition feature, saying that it was all in-house, designed and shipped in six months by a team of "about two and a half people." It will form part of the company's plans for what it calls a context-aware desktop. ®
b6568a83ad3eb74a: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 20 — GBS Malaysia is targeting 50 companies for an artificial intelligence (AI) adoption programme that will allow businesses to test AI solutions through complimentary three-month proofs of concept before making longer-term investment decisions.

The PIKOM–GBS Malaysia AI Sandbox Programme covers four areas: customer experience, IT shared services, finance operations and general AI automation. Participating companies will identify business challenges, work with matched solution providers and evaluate results through a shared assessment framework.

Potential applications include customer service responsiveness, IT support, reporting, reconciliation, document processing and repetitive administrative tasks. The evaluation will also consider productivity, service quality, business outcomes and the implications of AI adoption for employees, data and governance.

Six solution providers are participating in the programme: Daythree AI Labs, Grafilab, Revolab.ai, Sabah Net, SHRDC and Talbotiq Technologies. Their expertise covers AI voice agents, operational intelligence, private AI, automation and workforce development.

Datuk Raymond Davadass, Chair of GBS Malaysia, said the initiative reflected the industry’s need to move beyond operational excellence and take on a greater strategic role in addressing business challenges.
“Malaysia must not be content with being where the world’s work gets done. We must aspire to be where the world’s business challenges get solved,” he said.
He said technology adoption should be measured by the business value it creates.
“AI is not our strategy. AI is an enabler of our strategy. The objective isn’t how much AI we deploy. It’s how much business value we create,” he said.

The programme was announced at the GBS Global Summit 2026, which marked the 20th anniversary of GBS Malaysia. Held under the theme “Borderless Intelligence: Connecting Minds. Empowering Business.”, the event brought together about 1,000 delegates from more than 35 countries, over 45 speakers, more than 40 exhibition booths and 75 supporting partners.
Malaysia’s GBS industry recorded 749 entities, representing a 66.8 per cent increase against the baseline, according to the GBS Malaysia Strategy Mid-Term Report 2022–2027, published in 2025.

Industry investments increased 13.5 times, from RM730 million in 2021 to RM9.87 billion in 2024. The sector also recorded 36,626 jobs created since 2021, as at mid-2025, while GBS market revenue was estimated at RM28.14 billion for 2025.
Raymond said the industry had demonstrated its ability to deliver operational excellence over its first 20 years, but its next phase would require greater strategic relevance.

He said collaboration between industry, government, academia and technology providers was important to Malaysia’s competitiveness and its ability to support increasingly sophisticated regional and global business mandates.

Meanwhile, PIKOM chairman Adjunct Practice Prof. Alex Liew outlined three priorities for Malaysia’s GBS industry: strengthening the delivery of higher-value services, helping people progress with the industry through skills development, and making collaboration a competitive strength.

“When an enterprise chooses where to locate its global services, it places confidence in an entire ecosystem: its people, infrastructure, tech providers and institutions. Our responsibility is to ensure that Malaysia continues to earn that confidence,” he said in his opening speech at the Summit.

Selangor Executive Councillor for Investment, Trade and Mobility Ng Sze Han, who officiated the summit, said, “Today, Global Business Services sit at the heart of digital transformation, innovation and economic growth. GBS will keep evolving with AI, automation and digital technology. The Selangor State Government will walk side by side with the private sector. We provide the infrastructure, we build the talent, and we keep Selangor a business-friendly place for your company to grow.”
GBS Malaysia also formalised a strategic Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Cyberview and launched a synthesis report prepared by Cyberview in collaboration with the industry body.

The collaboration featured alongside discussions on digital infrastructure and high-value industries, including a Cyberview side-track titled “Beyond Infrastructure: Powering the Next Wave of High-Value Industries”.

Other discussions covered enterprise transformation, workforce capabilities, cybersecurity, responsible AI and global investment. The agenda also addressed the need for practical reskilling, role redesign and leadership to prepare employees for changing work requirements.
The event concluded with a “Global Outlook 2027: Voices from the Floor” session, bringing together industry perspectives on priorities for the year ahead.
c1cb73c3d8571045: From Kua Kia Soong
The controversy over the RM1,000 land premium for the 99-year lease renewal of the Kuala Lumpur and Selangor Chinese Assembly Hall (KLSCAH) has become another occasion for racial politicking.
Some have portrayed the decision as an unjustified privilege for a Chinese organisation, while others have defended it as a concession to the Chinese community.
Both sides are missing the bigger issue: whether Malaysia genuinely respects its historical and cultural heritage or allows commercial development and political expediency to take precedence.

Established in 1923, KLSCAH is more than a Chinese communal building. It has played an important role in Kuala Lumpur's political, social and cultural history and has been used by Malaysians of different ethnic groups and political affiliations.
Its significance should be assessed in the context of national history, rather than reduced to the racial identity of its users.

The controversy also raises a more fundamental question: why is the preservation of historical buildings and cultural institutions in Malaysia so often treated as an inconvenience rather than a public responsibility?
Monorail and disregard for historical landmarks
Consider the fate of Kuala Lumpur's historic temples.

The Guan Yin temple, established in the 1890s or possibly earlier, is one of the city's historic places of worship. Located beside the Maharajalela Monorail station, its historical setting and architectural character are overshadowed by the surrounding concrete infrastructure.
The temple has survived fires, Kuala Lumpur's transformation and generations of change. Yet how much consideration was given to its historical setting when the monorail infrastructure was introduced?
Modern public transport is undoubtedly necessary. But must modernisation mean historical buildings are reduced to insignificant structures dwarfed by concrete and steel?
This is not an argument against public transport, but for intelligent urban planning that allows modern infrastructure and historical landmarks to coexist.
The Sydney Monorail, for instance, was decommissioned in 2013 and dismantled in 2014 as part of the city's transition to light rail.
Another new development now threatens the Guan Yin temple. The authorities should assess its impact on the historic precinct before any damage becomes irreversible.
The wider Chinese community should also be asking why more has not been done to protect such landmarks.
Kuala Lumpur is destroying its own history
The fate of other historical buildings in Kuala Lumpur should prompt reflection on our priorities.
Pudu Jail, built in 1895, was once among the city's most recognisable landmarks. Its imposing walls and famous mural formed part of Kuala Lumpur's physical and social history.
The prison complex was demolished in stages, with most of the buildings gone by 2012. Only sections of its exterior wall and entrance were retained.

Whatever one's views on the colonial prison system, Pudu Jail was part of our history. Its preservation could have provided an important historical and educational site. Instead, most of it disappeared.
Then there was Bok House, a neo-classical mansion built in 1929 by businessman Chua Cheng Bok along Jalan Ampang. It also housed the well-known restaurant Le Coq d'Or.

Despite appeals by heritage advocates, the mansion was demolished in 2006. The argument that it lacked sufficient historical value illustrated how little importance was attached to architectural heritage.
The Cathay cinema, another familiar Kuala Lumpur landmark, also disappeared in the name of urban redevelopment.
How many more buildings must we lose before we realise that a city is not defined merely by its shopping malls, luxury condominiums and skyscrapers?
The Sultan Abdul Samad Building, Central Market and historic buildings around Dataran Merdeka have fortunately survived.
But their survival should not be an excuse for complacency. They require continued conservation, proper maintenance and protection from insensitive development.
Malaysia's collective memory under threat
This is not simply a Chinese community issue.

Malaysia's heritage includes Malay villages, traditional wooden houses, mosques, Indian temples, colonial buildings, indigenous settlements, archaeological sites, historic cemeteries and natural landscapes.

The demolition of the Sri Uchimalai Muniswarar Temple in Rawang in February was another painful reminder of the vulnerability of places of worship with longstanding community ties. The temple was demolished after the landowner sought possession of the site.

The controversy over the 130-year-old Dewi Sri Pathrakaliamman Temple on Jalan Masjid India, Kuala Lumpur, also raised fundamental questions about how development should accommodate historic places of worship.

Although the authorities subsequently identified a replacement site, the episode showed how vulnerable such institutions can be when land ownership and development interests take precedence over historical continuity.

We should also remember the traditional Malay kampungs lost to urban redevelopment, indigenous communities displaced by development projects and historic landscapes sacrificed to commercial interests.
The heritage of the Orang Asli and indigenous peoples of Sabah and Sarawak deserves the same protection as Kuala Lumpur's old temples and shophouses.
A nation that remembers only the history of its politically powerful communities has a distorted understanding of itself.

Developers should be required to assess the historical, cultural and social significance of buildings and places of worship before obtaining development approvals. Where possible, they should preserve these sites in their original locations rather than treating relocation as the default solution.

In the latest KLSCAH controversy, critics who believe public institutions should not receive special consideration for heritage preservation must explain why the same principle should not apply to every other historic building, temple, mosque, church, traditional settlement and cultural institution in Malaysia.

Should a historic Malay institution be required to pay commercial land premiums even when its land is designated for institutional use? Should an Indian temple be denied consideration simply because its preservation benefits a particular religious community?
We must reject this absurd racial arithmetic.
The question is not whether KLSCAH is Chinese, Malay or Indian. It is whether the institution has historical, cultural and public significance that deserves protection.
Kua Kia Soong is a former MP and a former director of Suaram.

b7f674ad7efc71b2: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence giant behind Claude, has just pulled off the biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history. The company raised US$81 billion by listing on the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market, beating the previous all-time record of US$75 billion set by SpaceX earlier this year. Initially set at $US83, Anthropic’s share price soared to US$111 after its debut, briefly nudging the company’s value past US$2 trillion, before falling again as investors took profits. The blockbuster stock market listing comes at a nervous moment in the AI sector. Investors are increasingly questioning whether the huge sums of money being poured into the AI boom are justified, and many are reducing their exposure to technology stocks. Adding to this shakiness has been the shock departure of chipmaker Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, following an affair scandal. Anthropic’s debut certainly sets a benchmark for rival OpenAI, which still plans to go public. But we shouldn’t mistake investor enthusiasm in one company for a broader vote of confidence in the global AI industry. What does Anthropic’s performance tell us? One thing we can learn from this week’s result is that there is a huge amount of demand for Anthropic itself. Strong revenue was one factor. At the end of October, Anthropic’s annualised revenue run rate (an estimate of yearly revenue based on the previous month) was US$81 billion. But the company’s popularity likely also played a role. Claude is one of the most widely used AI tools around the globe. “Familiarity bias” is a well known phenomenon in investing. Intense demand meant many smaller investors missed out on getting shares ahead of the official listing. Last week, Bloomberg reported the share offering was about six times oversubscribed. According to the Wall Street Journal, only about 15% of available shares were ultimately allocated to retail investors. Is Anthropic’s huge valuation justified? Anthropic’s share price closed the day at US$97.17, up 17% from its IPO price, which values the company at US$1.76 trillion. That’s slightly less than where SpaceX landed at the end of its first day, at US$2.1 trillion. But it’s still a colossal figure, even accounting for the fact that Anthropic beat OpenAI to generating a quarterly operating profit earlier this year (before returning to an operating loss the following quarter). For Anthropic, like any company, going public should make it easier to raise large amounts of capital. That could be important for a company which has already made about US$900 billion in future spending commitments – mostly on computing infrastructure – between now and 2045. However, it’s important to look at how these commitments play out in the short and long term. About half of this spending is due by 2030. The near-term bill over the next 12 months is about US$70 billion, which is manageable with its current revenue run rate of US$81 billion. Other concerns may be more pressing. Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue rose 47% – which is strong – but this compares to a growth rate of 144% in the second quarter. This suggests a sharp slowdown in growth overall. Token prices have also been falling, driven in part by more competition from cheaper AI models. Also on revenue, the company has warned that some of its customers – “particularly early-stage and high-growth companies” – rely on external financing. This could reduce their spending with Anthropic if that financing dries up. What to watch after this public listing For any company, listing on a public stock exchange introduces much more scrutiny. Previously, the focus on Anthropic has centred on its technology and growth potential. Now, there’ll be a renewed focus on corporate governance. Beyond the financial metrics of revenue growth, profitability, cash flow and more, investors will now more closely scrutinise how management balances commercial returns with AI safety, privacy and social responsibility. Speaking just before the Nasdaq listing, Chief Executive Dario Amodei acknowledged people’s serious safety concerns: We have always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems. But he expressed faith in Anthropic’s ability to get the balance right: If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. Protesters staged major rallies outside the Nasdaq exchange’s New York headquarters and outside Anthropic’s San Francisco headquarters. They called for stronger government regulation and a slowdown or total pause on AI development. What does this mean for rival OpenAI? Another of the world’s major AI companies, OpenAI, had initially planned its own public listing this year. However, it has now ruled this out until 2027, citing safety concerns around the technology. Anthropic’s IPO creates both opportunities and challenges for its rival. On the plus side, Anthropic’s performance gives OpenAI and potential investors a yardstick – including financial performance benchmarks and lots of other useful information. But now that Anthropic has become a publicly listed company, this industry is about to come under even more intense scrutiny. If public sentiment about AI worsens between now and when OpenAI launches its IPO, it could pay a steep price. Angel Zhong does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
