24abcf689c6b9b5d: From Terence Netto
Former Sarawak DAP vice-chairman Wong King Wei has advised DAP to stay out of the Dec 12 Sarawak polls, citing the need for DAP to be friendly with the idea of state autonomy for Sarawakian parties.
Sarawakians want to assert the interests of their state after years of deferring to federal interests.
Decades-old reticence about their interests has in recent years been replaced by an assertiveness that Putrajaya cannot but respect.
The intensive battle between competing political coalitions in the peninsula makes the courtship of Sarawakian (and Sabahan) political parties imperative.
These days, the keys to Putrajaya, for peninsula aspirants, lie between Kuching and Kota Kinabalu.

Since the major Sarawakian parties have banded together into a fairly cohesive force in Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS), it does not make sense for DAP to be at cross-purposes with GPS components in the upcoming state polls.
As a single party, DAP may well emerge with the highest or second highest number of parliamentary seats in the next general election (GE16), which is due by February 2028.
No single party or coalition is expected to gain a simple majority in GE16.
This will require one or the other coalition in the peninsula to importune GPS to back them for the right to form the federal government.

DAP, as the anticipated holder of a sizeable number of seats in the peninsula, will be critical to negotiations with GPS, which is expected to sweep not only the state seats in the Dec 12 polls but also the parliamentary ones in GE16.
After seeing how the peninsula Malay vote is solidifying behind Umno and PAS-led Perikatan Nasional, DAP must think strategically about GE16.

Based on their performance in the Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka polls, DAP's Pakatan Harapan (PH) allies PKR and Amanah are struggling to make a dent in the Malay vote, and are no more confident of the non-Malay vote bank.
Fear of the evolving collaboration between Umno and PAS will keep the Chinese vote with DAP despite discomfort with DAP’s overly compliant attitude towards Anwar Ibrahim.

DAP secretary-general Loke Siew Fook, presently unencumbered by ministerial duties, will have more time to espouse the reforms championed by PH that have been neglected by Anwar's puzzling pussyfooting.
The path is open to a de facto premiership by Loke – by careful rhetoric and subtle gesture – given Anwar's continued tepidity in pursuing the reformasi agenda.
Nuanced rhetoric and statesmanlike gestures by Loke can restrain Sarawak DAP leader Chong Chieng Jen from remonstrating against a DAP decision to refrain from contesting in the Sarawak polls.

DAP should also signal to Rafizi Ramli’s Bersama to be realistic about its chances in GE16, which will require the PKR splinter to go only for the parliamentary seats – 10 at the most – that the Rafizi claque in PKR can win in GE16.
After two underwhelming outings in Johor and Melaka, Bersama ought to come down from the clouds and see that there is no point in overrating its chances.

So, it’s a rearguard action that DAP must undertake, running into GE16, to save what can be salvaged from the growing wreck of Anwar's myopia and Amanah’s failure to convince the Malays that moderate Islam is not a delusion but a viable proposition.
It’s the high road that beckons DAP which also happens to be the pragmatic road to take in the circumstances.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.

57de9e1d8f19559c: What began as a political impasse over the absence of a state executive council and the inability to convene the state assembly has descended into further chaos, with a new candidate for menteri besar proposed to the Yang Dipertuan Besar while the incumbent remains in office.

It is understood that during their meeting two days ago, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir allowed Ismail Lasim to continue serving as menteri besar. So why is Umno proposing another candidate for the ruler's consideration? Could Negeri Sembilan end up with two menteris besar?
So, what happens next in Negeri Sembilan?

Ismail and Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi have both expressed their desire to resolve this crisis, regardless of who instigated it, so that the state government can administer sans the unnecessary drama.
Now, I fully support what appears to be the sincerity of these two Malay leaders.
As I understand it, Ismail took the first step towards breaking the deadlock by withdrawing a letter seeking to remove Tuanku Muhriz as the state's ruler.
Ismail requested an audience with the ruler – said to be granted for Friday morning – while the 10 state executive councillors withdrew their court action and were ordered to pay legal costs.
The epilogue to this convoluted saga was fast approaching, and the public was prepared to move on to a new chapter.
But, alas, came an unexpected twist in this drama.
Umno announced that Ismail had resigned.
I initially assumed the resignation intended to reset relations between the politicians and the constitutional ruler, starting with the menteri besar's departure.
It sounded like a reasonable move. After all, Ismail and the 10 executive councillors had done plenty to incur the ruler's displeasure, which even I found unforgivable.
So it seemed encouraging that Umno wanted to put the past behind it and start afresh.

However, the Negeri Sembilan palace has yet to verify the Juasseh assemblyman's resignation as menteri besar. The comptroller of the Negeri Sembilan royal household said the supposed letter was sent only by an individual named Hamidi, who claimed to be from a law firm.
Under the state’s constitution, the menteri besar must submit his resignation to the Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, and it only takes effect with the ruler’s consent.
The palace's desire to verify the letter's authenticity certainly raises questions about it. At that point, Ismail seemed unsure which script he was supposed to follow.

Ismail's son spoke out, questioning the authenticity of the resignation letter and earning a rebuke from Zahid, who asked why family members were wading into the matter when it was an administrative issue.
Zahid has a point, but the letter itself remains perplexing.
And just as the public was trying to make sense of these conflicting scenarios, another unexpected development unfolded.
Tuanku Muhriz summoned Ismail for an audience ahead of schedule. Their meeting lasted an hour and a half.

We thought Ismail, who entered the palace as menteri besar, would emerge as an ordinary assemblyman, as Umno had announced. Instead, he walked out of the palace still holding the post of menteri besar!
So much for the audience with the ruler being the finale to this drama.
But Zahid remains adamant that only one name was submitted to Tuanku Muhriz for approval as the new menteri besar, even though Ismail is still carrying out his duties as instructed by the ruler.

For much of my life, I thought Anwar Ibrahim's imprisonment and black eye were part of the most unforgettable political saga I had ever witnessed. But I must admit, this drama is quite something, too.
What initially appeared to be a confrontation between Umno and the palace has turned into a power struggle within Umno itself.
Why is Zahid determined to replace Ismail, who now has the palace's consent to remain in office?

If Umno's top leadership wants to write another script, perhaps it should put it on hold for a year or two. Give the people of Negeri Sembilan some breathing space. fbe1739af67044ec: The app gives short, interactive lessons using quizzes, flashcards, and other easily accessible formats in three languages
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot of views of VotEDU on the App Store. Fair use.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Moldova is a relatively small post-Soviet state with a population of three million people. A landlocked country, it has a long border with war-torn Ukraine and Romania; with the latter, it shares the same official language. The territory that is now Moldova was once part of the Russian Empire, and later the Soviet Union, and Russia has been meddling in its affairs.

Moldova has a large Russian-speaking population and a problematic unrecognized territory: Transnistria, which is basically controlled by Russia. It also has European aspirations and was officially named a candidate to join the European Union in 2022, after Russia invaded neighbouring Ukraine.

The country’s most recent parliamentary elections were held in September 2025, and despite the record influx of Russian disinformation and other meddling, elections were recognized as fair and democratic by the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OCSE) observers. The pro-European Party of Action and Solidarity (PAS) won the elections with a small majority.

The initiative supported by Digital Spark is an app called VotEDU, which answers basic questions about the democratic institution of elections for high school students in Moldova. It does so through short, interactive lessons using quizzes, flashcards, and other easily accessible formats in three languages: Romanian, Russian, and English, and is the subject of this Spotlight story.
Global Voices interviewed the app’s developer, Vlad Garbuz, about the impact of Digital Spark and his initiative.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project.

Vlad Garbuz (VG): I started VotEDU, an independent civic-education project in Moldova, to help young people understand democracy before they vote for the first time. The idea began at the VOTech hackathon in Moldova. I joined Digital Spark because I wanted to turn it into a tool that students could use in everyday life and teachers could bring into class. The project helped me build the app and begin testing it with the young people it is meant for.
GV: What issue or challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

VG: Young people meet politics every day through their feeds, long before they enter a polling station. In Moldova, many young people encounter misleading claims online. Yet many have very few easy ways of asking questions about elections and getting the answers they can understand.

That made me wonder how civic education could reach young people in the spaces where they already spend their time. VotEDU was the answer. It puts short lessons, simple explanations, and activities on their phones, so they can learn at their own pace.
GV: What are the key changes or activities that you implemented during your participation in the project?

VG: During Digital Spark, VotEDU developed into a civic-education app with nine units, 28 short lessons, quizzes, interactive activities, and a glossary of 136 civic terms. The content is available in Romanian, Russian, and English. All of the lessons have been reviewed for accuracy and political neutrality. Student privacy guided the app’s design. A short guide was also prepared for teachers.

VotEDU was represented at Moldova Digital Summit 2026, where several educators expressed interest in trying it in schools. The app is now being piloted with high school students in Moldova through its web version. It is also available on the App Store, with the Google Play version coming soon.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your beneficiaries and the community you serve? Please provide examples.
VG: Teacher feedback has highlighted the need for digital tools alongside Moldova’s electoral education textbook. VotEDU brings these topics into a format students can explore on their phones.

High school students in the pilot program are using the app and sharing feedback. The feedback tells us how easy the information was to access, as well as appreciation of the app’s design, quizzes, and illustrations. Together with teachers’ suggestions, this feedback is helping improve the content in the app and making it a better user experience.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed?

VG: I have learned that the design of a civic tool is part of its message. If an app is hard to understand, available in only one language, or careless with privacy, it may leave out the very people it hopes to reach.

Building VotEDU has made me more careful about how I explain civic topics. Each lesson needs to be accurate and fair, while still being simple enough to use on a phone. I now think more about whether young people feel comfortable asking questions and forming their own views, not just whether the information is online.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?
VG: The lesson I will carry forward is to start earlier. Young people should have a chance to understand democracy before an election campaign is asking for their attention.

I have also learned that a good idea needs to be tested with the people it is meant to help. Building VotEDU was only one part of the work. Now students are using it and telling us what they think. Their experience will help us see what works, what is still unclear to students, and what needs to change.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built?

VG: I will continue the pilot program and use feedback from students and teachers to improve VotEDU. I plan to bring it to more schools, including rural schools, and use short questions before and after the lessons to see what students learn.

In October 2026, I also demonstrated VotEDU at MEGAPHONE & e-Society in Skopje. I showed how digital tools can make civic education more useful and engaging for young people, and inspire others to try similar ideas. VotEDU is a project that can be adapted for different countries and topics. Making the project public and accessible is one of my objectives to ensure anyone can easily build something that will bring benefits to their local community.
Written by Daria Dergacheva
1fd2d6e1dc2cfd95: Donate to our Digital Communities Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!
Originally published on Global Voices
Images via Canva and public domain.

Digital communications sparked new ways of forming communities: communities that spanned vast distances; that offered asynchronous interaction, innovative forms of constructing identities, and potentially enormous reach. These communities have provided connection for people who are isolated or marginalized, built powerful groups around both professional interests and unusual hobbies, and facilitated astonishing feats of knowledge-sharing and organizing, from Wikipedia to academic sub-field networks to hobby groups and fandoms.

But digital communities bring new challenges as well, from questions of moderation to questions of ownership. Almost all of them are built on the backbone of infrastructure owned by Big Tech — hardware at a minimum, usually several layers of software as well.

This is a risky place to put trust. Witness the sudden devastation when a platform is bought and sold, and what was accessible and inclusive becomes hostile; or the sudden change-to-terms-of-service maneuver, when a company leverages the trust of its users to exploit them for their sellable data. Increasingly hollowed-out echo chambers — toxic or just obliviously navel-gazing — make digital communities difficult and often dangerous to navigate. The proliferation of targeted ads, the risks of rapidly spreading mis- and disinformation, and, more recently, the insertion of large language model bots all illustrate this.

Sometimes it feels like it’s impossible to resist the tidal wave of AI slop and bot content and the all-pervasive mistrust of information engendered by the sheer amount of misinformation and disinformation we have seen produced this decade. But there are still ways to organize digitally.

The same social media that is polarizing Indian society is where young people have organized and continued to organize to resist the authoritarian Modi government. In Brazil, supporters of President Lula ran an organic, human-driven campaign that successfully beat algorithms weighted toward his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the October 2026 election. LGBTQ+ people in hostile environments often only have online spaces to find community and solidarity. People everywhere are rewilding the internet, reclaiming, reviving, and rebuilding communities everywhere in defiance of faceless, consolidated power.

In this month’s spotlight, Global Voices, in partnership with Ranking Digital Rights, will explore the multiverse of digital communities — starting with our own. We want to highlight specific communities, the tools and tactics they use to organize, resist, and overcome the algorithmic pressure from tech platforms, and show how digital communities thrive and persist the world over, defying overwhelming power asymmetries and rejecting pressure to accept the defaults.

20007bd249cf3ed0: From P Sundramoorthy

The Kuala Lumpur police chief's recent directive for policemen to fire when they encounter threats, including situations where they have doubts or feel threatened, raises an important question about the use of firearms by law enforcement in a civil democratic society.
The statement followed a serious incident in Gombak where a police officer suffered severe injuries in a machete attack.

Understandably, the safety and security of policemen must never be compromised. Officers who put their lives at risk to protect society deserve institutional support, protection and the authority to respond effectively to dangerous situations.
However, the broader question is whether a shoot-first approach is consistent with the principles of democratic policing.

Criminologically, policemen operate in unpredictable and potentially dangerous environments. They are expected to protect the public, prevent crime and enforce the law, sometimes while making split-second decisions. Their right to self-defence must be recognised and the government must provide the appropriate training, equipment and support.

Nevertheless, the authority to use firearms carries exceptional responsibility. In democratic societies, the determining factor should not simply be whether an officer feels threatened, but whether the threat is sufficiently immediate and serious to justify lethal force.
Differences in threats
There is an important distinction between a perceived threat, an actual threat and an imminent threat to life.

An officer’s subjective apprehension cannot, by itself, automatically justify discharging a firearm. The nature of the threat, the individual’s conduct, available alternatives and immediate danger to others must be objectively assessed.
International standards, particularly the United Nations Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials, emphasise necessity, proportionality and restraint.

Firearms should be used only in exceptional circumstances, particularly where there is an imminent threat of death or serious injury and less extreme measures are insufficient. The preservation of human life must remain paramount.

A policy that encourages officers to shoot whenever they experience uncertainty or apprehension could have unintended consequences. It may increase unnecessary fatalities, undermine public confidence and expose officers and the police institution to legal or disciplinary scrutiny.
Excessive or disproportionate force can weaken police legitimacy, public cooperation and effective crime prevention.
Equipping our police force

This does not mean expecting officers to hesitate when confronted with an immediate and potentially fatal attack. They must instead be equipped to make lawful and proportionate decisions under pressure.

Police services in established democratic societies generally emphasise structured use-of-force frameworks that incorporate de-escalation, conflict management, communication and alternatives to lethal force wherever practicable.
For Malaysia, this discussion should encourage greater transparency concerning police standing orders, firearms policies and procedures governing the discharge of weapons.
Public confidence requires firearm incidents to be documented and investigated without fear or favour, with independent scrutiny where death or serious injury occurs.
Accountability, however, must not become a mechanism for discouraging officers from taking necessary action when their lives or the lives of innocent members of the public are in immediate danger.
Police officers and other law enforcement personnel have a legitimate right and responsibility to protect themselves and the public.

When confronted with an imminent and serious threat, particularly an armed attack capable of causing death or grievous injury, they must have the authority and confidence to act decisively, including using lethal force where it is legally justified and necessary.
They should not be expected to expose themselves or innocent people to avoidable danger because of uncertainty about their authority to defend life.

Continuous training in firearms and the use of lethal force is essential. It must not be treated as a one-off exercise during basic training but be ongoing, regularly assessed and updated to reflect changing criminal threats, operational realities, technological developments and international best practices.

The SOPs governing firearms and lethal force must also be reviewed periodically and updated whenever necessary. They should clearly explain the circumstances in which firearms may be used, officers’ responsibilities, reporting requirements and post-incident procedures.
Ambiguous instructions place officers and the public at risk; clear, practical guidance is indispensable.

Ultimately, protecting police officers and protecting the public are not competing objectives. They are complementary responsibilities of a professional law enforcement service. Officers must not be expected to sacrifice their lives unnecessarily, nor should the public face an unrestricted use of lethal force.
The question is therefore not simply whether police should shoot or not. It is whether the circumstances legally, reasonably and objectively justify lethal force.

In a civil democratic society, officers must be decisive when confronting genuine and imminent threats to life, while restraint, professionalism, continuous training and accountability remain integral to the exercise of their authority.
The legitimacy of policing depends not merely on the ability to use force but on knowing when its use is justified and when it is not.
P Sundramoorthy is a criminologist at the Centre for Policy Research at Universiti Sains Malaysia.

62626f8cbcfd5bbe: Over the past decade, MIT researchers have developed aerial microrobots with bumblebee-like speed, agility, and durability, for tasks like precision agriculture or search-and-rescue. But these featherweight microrobots couldn’t carry the electronics needed for navigation, forcing them to remain connected to a motion-capture system in the lab. Now, the researchers have designed a flapping-wing microrobot with onboard sensors and computation, which can follow a complex trajectory and land precisely on a sunflower outside the lab’s motion capture environment. While the robot is still connected to an offboard power source, this demonstration highlights the potential of aerial microrobots to be used for precision agriculture in the future.  For instance, flying microrobots could weave through a field of almond trees or blueberry bushes to carefully pollinate delicate blossoms in regions where natural pollinator populations have been decimated by habitat loss. They could also hover near plants without causing damage, monitoring crop health and spotting pests before they become widespread. To enable onboard sensing and computation, the researchers developed a method to expand the artificial muscles that power the robot’s wings, increasing the net payload so the tiny robot could carry the necessary electronics. They also designed a sensor suite that can rapidly estimate the robot’s position and orientation without relying on an offboard motion capture system, and a miniature electronics package to securely hold the tiny computational components on the nimble vehicle. “This is a really important milestone for the research community. This is the first demonstration of an aerial microrobot that is sensory and compute autonomous. There are many situations, like pollination or industrial surveillance, where you can’t use a larger robot. Small-scale robots are uniquely positioned for these types of tasks, and if this thread of technology becomes successful in the future, it could be very promising,” says Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-corresponding author of a paper on the robot. He is joined on the paper by co-lead authors and MIT graduate students Yi-Hsuan (Nemo) Hsiao, Quang Phuc Kieu, and Zhongtao Guan; co-corresponding authors Jonathan P. How, a Ford Professor of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS) and the Aerospace Controls Laboratory (ACL) at MIT; Elizabeth Farrell Helbling, an assistant professor at Cornell University; and others at MIT. The research appears today in Science Robotics. Increasing the payload The MIT researchers previously developed a swift, agile aerial microrobot with four wings, each powered by a set of soft actuators, or artificial muscles, that flap the wings rapidly so the bot can perform detailed maneuvers.  The robot, roughly the same size and shape as a microcassette, weighs less than a paperclip. To bring this tiny robot closer to real-world applications, the researchers need it to carry the additional weight from electronics for onboard sensing and computation, while still being fast, maneuverable, and robust to collisions. In this research, they developed a method to scale up the artificial muscles without hampering the robot’s performance. They carefully tuned the radius and length of the soft actuators, increasing their size by 50 percent while boosting the robot’s net lift forces by 46 percent.  “It is very difficult to scale up the actuators without causing the output power of the system to go down, which reduces the lift forces. We tuned the geometry of the robot very precisely so lift proportionally increases with the additional actuator weight,” Chen explains.  They were able to achieve a lift-to-weight ratio of 1.9, giving the robot more than enough lift force to carry the onboard electronics package they developed, which weighs only 244 milligrams.  The tiny electronics package contains the sensors, and microcontroller needed for onboard sensing and computation.  The researchers incorporated an inertial measurement unit to estimate attitude, an optical flow sensor to estimate lateral flight speed and position, and a time-of-flight sensor to measure height. But without the precision of the attached motion capture system, the robot does not know its absolute position, causing it to drift off course. Speedy sensing To overcome this challenge, the team designed a sensing algorithm to calculate the robot orientation, angular velocity, and position extremely quickly, simplifying the calculations to reduce the computational cost. They found that estimating position continuously at a faster rate yielded higher performance than a more accurate, slower estimation. “We spent a lot of time optimizing the selection of the sensors and position estimators so the robot would have very low drift. Our robot can now fly with positional accuracy that is comparable to flying with offboard cameras,” says Hsiao.  They integrated the sensors and computing components into a tiny electronics package, which they attached to a fiberglass substrate so it wouldn’t be thrown off by vibrations of the robot. “When you are talking about a computer which is that small, everything must be thought through carefully. There are so many factors to consider; it must do both perception and control, while fitting onto the robot and running fast enough that the vehicle will remain stable during flight,” How says. They tested the offboard computation capabilities of the aerial microrobot through a series of flight demonstrations, including hovering at different heights and following point-to-point trajectories. The robot maneuvered quickly and precisely, with positional errors of only a few centimeters. In addition, they demonstrated the robot’s potential for artificial pollination by using a joystick to send high-level position setpoints, guiding the aerial vehicle around several plants before carefully landing on a sunflower.  “This is quite difficult to do, even if you do have a motion-capture system,” Hsiao says. The researchers analyzed the vehicle’s power expenditures and found the electronics only consume about 6 percent of the total power, with the rest fueling the robot’s artificial muscles and wings.  They identified ways to further reduce power consumption from the electronics. This would allow for the addition of more components, like a camera that would enable the robot to recognize objects. The researchers are now working toward two goals: putting a camera onboard for autonomous object recognition and obstacle avoidance; and integrating power electronics and batteries onto the tiny robot, which would enable untethered flight in an outdoor environment.  This research was funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), U.S. Office of Naval Research, U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and a Zakhartchenko Fellowship.

528841cbf861a044: Most staples for Thanksgiving, including potatoes and cranberries, haven't jumped in price this year. Noah Samuel Franz on UnsplashInflation-weary Americans have at least some good news to cheer this holiday season: The cost of a basic Thanksgiving meal has stabilized. A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people clocks in at US$78.93, approximately 0.4% less than in 2025, according to the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute. That’s because most staples haven’t seen a sharp jump in prices. Americans are still justified in feeling stressed about high grocery bills, but it’s because of the cumulative effect of rising prices in recent years. While inflation has slowed since its peak of more than 9% in 2022, the cost of a Thanksgiving meal is roughly 25% higher than it was before the COVID-19 pandemic began. I’m an agricultural economist who has been studying the many drivers of food inflation. What’s key to remember is that inflation data tells us how quickly prices are increasing, not whether prices are returning to previous levels. So even modest price jumps today are layered on already-elevated prices. Here’s what Americans can expect when they go shopping for Thanksgiving, from turkey to dessert: Go for frozen turkey Stable frozen turkey prices have played an important role in keeping overall holiday meal costs close to last year’s levels. The average advertised price for a frozen turkey over 16 pounds (about 7 kilograms) was $0.96 per pound, essentially unchanged from the $0.97 per pound in the same period last year, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Turkey Report, published on Nov. 13, 2026. These prices reflect the typical discounts leading up to Thanksgiving, when retailers often cut turkey prices as part of their holiday promotions. It’s a different story with fresh turkey prices, which are about 11% higher than a year ago, according to the Department of Agriculture data. So shoppers seeking a fresh bird may face a higher grocery bill. A longer-term trend is that turkey consumption has gradually declined over time. As a result, the cost of Thanksgiving depends on much more than turkey prices alone. This is where side dishes come in. Frozen turkey is among the Thanksgiving staples that haven’t seen big price jumps this past year. AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh A mixed picture for side dishes Mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce and sweet potato casserole are among the dishes that a frugal shopper might consider. Sweet potatoes are 12.5% cheaper year on year, and cranberry prices have dropped 4.8%, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Grocery Store Specialty Crops data. Potato prices, meanwhile, have been stable, increasing just 1.1% over the past year, according to September’s consumer price index, the most recent month of full data. If you’re considering mac and cheese, the costs of the main ingredients should balance out: Pasta and cornmeal prices are 4.3% higher year on year, while cheese is 3% cheaper. Prices for fruits and vegetables, however, have mostly ticked upward and are 3.9% higher than a year ago. That includes green beans, which are 2.2% more expensive. Prices for fresh apples are up 7.5%, and up 2.6% for lettuce. More broadly, higher prices for some fresh vegetables reflect the cost pressures facing food production. Farmers are grappling with high fertilizer, fuel and transportation expenses, not to mention tariffs in certain sectors. Of course, Thanksgiving isn’t complete without regional traditions. Sauerkraut is a popular side dish for turkey in the mid-Atlantic states, but fans will have to pay substantially more. Cabbage is about 30% more expensive year on year due to weather shocks and pest outbreaks that have reduced supply. Sauerkraut, a popular side dish in mid-Atlantic states, is likely to be pricier amid higher cabbage prices. Kelsey Todd on Unsplash Don’t forget dessert Americans might also find some sweet relief in prices for popular desserts. Some key baking staples became more affordable. Butter prices have fallen 10.3% over the previous year, while flour is down by 1.1% and sugar by 1%, according to the September consumer price index data. But some of the biggest savings come from eggs, where prices have dropped sharply. Like the turkey industry, egg production was hard-hit in 2022 by a highly pathogenic avian flu outbreak, which reduced supplies and pushed prices up. Since then, producers have rebuilt flocks and expanded production to grow supply. Egg prices are now 20.3% lower than a year ago. Where consumers will shell out more is milk, up 2.3%; canned fruit, up 2.3%; and frozen bakery products, up 1.3%, according to the consumer price index data. Pumpkins for pie-making will cost 2% more than last year. So keep all this in mind if you plan to bake a pie. And if you opt for a store-bought pumpkin pie, expect to pay about 2.5% more. Where other savings can be found Shoppers looking for alternatives to turkey could head to the poultry aisle. Prices for whole fryer and roaster chickens are anywhere from 7% to 20% lower than a year ago, according to USDA grocery store price data. Consumers can also take advantage of Thanksgiving promotions offered by grocery retailers. Several major retailers offer complete Thanksgiving meal baskets for less than $40, which can translate to approximately $3.50 to $4 per person. Among major retailers, Walmart is advertising its Thanksgiving basket for 10 people at $35, Aldi at $39 for 10 people and Target at $30 for six people. Although the contents vary, these meal packages generally include Thanksgiving favorites such as turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce, and ingredients for green bean and potato side dishes. Inflation remains at the top of consumers’ minds, and it isn’t expected to ease anytime soon. But in the case of Thanksgiving, shoppers can find at least some relief as they seek out staples for their feast. 03692ec60cac1bbf: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”

In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.

Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.

A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.

Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.)

The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.

Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.

But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows, has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack, arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. In response, Wiltschko says that “human perception isn’t a workaround for AI”. “Language models learn from what people have written. Our model learns from what people smell. Smell is ultimately a human experience, so the model has to learn from humans to bridge chemistry and perception. That’s what lets it predict how people will experience a scent as well as the human nose does.”

Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.

But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”

In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies.
For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.

“There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. “So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”

461a1fe87414da12: A teacher who believes a student’s term paper may have been written by a large language model (LLM) can use a tool for detecting artificial intelligence-generated text to help confirm their suspicions. But the teacher may want to think twice before putting all their trust in the detector.  Researchers from MIT and Cornell University showed that such detection tools, which are AI models themselves, can be fooled by AI-generated text disguised to appear as if it were written by a human. Detectors can also fail to identify AI text due to natural shifts in writing habits over time or the emergence of new LLMs. In a new paper, the researchers demonstrated how a special training technique makes an AI detector more accurate and resilient to deception, even as human and AI writing constantly changes. They employed a method called test-time adaptation, which allows a deployed detection model to learn from new, unlabeled data by adjusting its inner workings on the fly. In this way, the model adapts to unseen inputs without being retrained from scratch. In experiments, a commercial detector could only identify about 27 percent of AI-generated text that had been disguised, while the new approach achieved 93 percent accuracy. This method could help educators, editors, publishers, and hiring managers flag LLM-generated writing that people try to pass off as human-written. It could also be used by cybersecurity experts to prevent email phishing scams or identify search engine optimization fraud. “There are many high-stakes contexts where people really care about the identity of the author, from scientific publishing to short story competitions. We’ve shown that test-time adaptation allows your AI detector to be much more robust, even with continual adversarial behavior by AI users,” says study co-author Manish Raghavan, the Drew Houston (2005) Career Development Professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management, who also holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). He is joined on the paper by lead author Kevin Ren, graduate student at Cornell Tech, and senior author Nikhil Garg, an assistant professor at Cornell Tech. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. Duping the detectors The proliferation of LLMs that generate human-like text has led to a plethora of commercial AI-detection tools to help people identify whether a piece of writing was authored by a human. But these detection tools can fail when the text they evaluate significantly differs from the text they were taught to identify. This is known as a distribution shift. Detector developers typically train their models by gathering text from the internet that they know to be either AI- or human-generated. They train the model to tell the difference.  However, once the detector is released, people might change the way they write or the way they use AI to generate text.  For instance, a human in 2030 may write about different topics using new analogies that weren’t common for someone writing in 2010. A detector trained with 2010 data might be unfamiliar with this new writing style and incorrectly mark human-written text as AI-generated. The release of a detection model also creates a cat-and-mouse game between its developers and users who want to bypass it. These individuals can run AI-generated text through an automated “humanizer” software tool that modifies it to appear human-written to the detector. “After the company releases a model, a bunch of ‘humanizers’ pop up to try to beat it, so the company tries to incorporate this humanized text into their training so the detector can identify it, and so on. It’s like rinse-and-repeat. The cycle can go on forever,” says Ren. The researchers explored whether test-time adaptation (TTA) can make an AI detector resilient to these distribution shifts. Adaptation in action In TTA, instead of freezing the model so it can’t change during deployment, researchers allow that model to adapt itself to incoming data after it has been released. For an AI text detector, these data are new pieces of text uploaded by users.  These data are unlabeled, so the detector developers don’t know which data were written by humans versus AI models. But these new data represent contemporary human and AI writing — exactly what the developers want the model to be able to predict.  With enough examples, the detector learns to identify patterns to determine which data are AI-generated and which are human-generated. The researchers studied TTA by creating datasets to contain a certain amount of AI-generated and human-generated text, but they don’t provide those labels to the model. They also used LLMs to generate some examples that resemble text written by AI to specifically evade a detector.  Then they performed the TTA training process and tested the model on ground-truth data. In experiments designed to mimic the natural shift in human language over time, a detector that used TTA was 85 percent accurate, while traditional methods only achieved 73 percent accuracy. And when it came to writing designed to thwart detection tools, existing methods could only identify about 27 percent, while TTA enabled the model to catch more than 93 percent of disguised text. “TTA has the potential to really help deployed AI-detection models in terms of being able to proactively address this iterative ‘gaming’ behavior by adversarial AI users,” Ren says. Adapting to shifts in human writing behavior is a more difficult TTA problem, since the shifts are slower and occur in more subtle ways, he adds. The researchers caution that TTA may not always be an effective solution as future LLMs produce more natural-sounding language and it becomes harder to find verifiable human text to use for training. “It isn’t entirely clear if this will be a solvable problem,” Raghavan says. “There are some big, open questions about how you should think about science, writing, and art in a world where it is infeasible to tell the difference between human-generated content and AI content.” In the future, the researchers want to explore similar strategic domains where TTA could be useful and build better benchmarking tools to help engineers improve these AI detection models in a dynamic fashion. This project used API credits provided by Pangram to use their AI text detectors.
4510621dd9db4cda: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI, on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.

Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”

Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”

Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”

Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”

How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.

The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.
Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”

Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.

Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?
Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.
b3b92e37dd213603: From Mazli Noor

China’s industrial growth and capabilities have been a lesson in economic singlemindedness unmatched in recent history. Much as we might admire it, however, we must recognise that China’s industrial overcapacity has direct – and not necessarily all positive – implications for Malaysia’s own.

While lower-priced inputs bring significant short-term gains to consumers and producers alike, the consistent and prolonged import pressures they create can also pose long-term structural challenges for Malaysian industries, businesses and the broader Malaysian macroeconomy.

Overcapacity cannot be measured by any one given statistic, nor can undue trade or pricing practices be construed as a deliberate act of dumping simply based on volume or import trends. They are as contentious as they are opaque, as precedents brought to the World Trade Organisation have shown.

A significant portion of the trade deficit stems from an increasingly integrated supply chain, where raw components are assembled or finished in Malaysia for onward export to third-party markets. Regardless, the investment, trade and industry ministry (Miti) has been sufficiently concerned to initiate a detailed product audit that aims to differentiate between legitimate industrial inputs and imports that effectively constitute dumping, which might threaten the operational viability of local factories.

Goods from China now account for an estimated 26% to 27% of Malaysia’s total imports. The last full year figures from 2025 put Malaysia’s trade deficit with China at between RM146 billion and RM163.4 billion. This has widened markedly in 2026, with the first-nine-month deficit at RM191.5 billion, or 70% more than in the same period a year earlier.

By contrast, Malaysia recorded a 2025 trade surplus with the US of RM100 billion to RM101.5 billion. The comparison becomes even more vivid when we consider that Malaysia’s total trade surplus grew by 115.7% year-on-year to RM232.4 billion in the first nine months of 2026.

A deficit does not mean that all imports are harmful. The figures do, however, make it crucial that we keep a close eye on local producers, and how the country’s future investment and production capabilities are affected.

The widening influx of lower-cost manufacturing inputs from China has seen local firms simply unable to compete. Domestic factories in the iron, steel, plastics, chemicals and textile sectors have been compelled to scale back production. The dwindling orders mean machinery and labor operating at well below optimal levels, pushing up marginal costs and placing downward pressure on overall productivity.

The steel industry provides a clear example. The Malaysian Iron and Steel Industry Federation reports domestic crude steel capacity utilisation of just 39.1%, compared with a global average of 75%. A Miti anti-dumping investigation found utilisation in galvanised steel at 65% – well below the 80% considered sustainable.

Similarly, SMEs are facing inordinate pressures: local SMEs struggle to compete with not just the more competitive prices but a broader and deeper catalogue of products from China, which benefit from scale, integrated supply chains and, in many cases, wide-ranging subsidies and state support. Sectors such as retail, food and beverage, construction, mechanical workshops and steel have registered the hardest hits.

The influx of well-capitalised foreign businesses has also driven up commercial property rents significantly, crowding out local merchants and vendors already dealing with regulatory and compliance expenses. Nor does the increased commercial activity benefit domestic job markets – many Chinese operators utilise "enclave supply chains" where they bring in their own capital, raw materials and workforce directly from home, limiting whatever spillover effects might have been factored in before.

With negligible to no uptake on local procurement, skills development, technology transfer or jobs creation, the domino effect this creates reverberates across Malaysia’s industrial landscape, posing a very real threat of premature deindustrialisation, i.e. the erosion of manufacturing just as we look to build a more resilient base of higher-productivity activities. The priority should be to deepen local capabilities, not increase dependence on imported products and components.

The last few years have also seen Malaysia grow increasingly exposed to China’s own trade disputes. The US, in particular, and Western markets in general, have been trading tariffs and punitive measures with Beijing across a host of industries, from farming to electronics to rare earths and semiconductors. Ironically, Malaysia’s place in China’s supply chain means it now faces the same scrutiny, but without a place at the table, placing its own access to other export goods and markets at risk with little recourse.

Lower prices are not, by themselves, evidence of unfair competition. Cheaper goods and services have given households much more affordable choices, with Chinese e-commerce platforms, retailers and brands expanding the range of products available to consumers. The concern is whether the competition is sustainable and fair, and whether consumers’ immediate savings come at the expense of local production, investment and reliable supply chains.

Malaysia should respond firmly and on the basis of evidence while honouring its trade commitments. The aim is to deal with unfair practices, secure greater benefits from foreign investment and help viable Malaysian businesses improve productivity. It should not be to insulate local firms from competition.

Miti should first make trade remedies faster and more effective. Reform of the Countervailing and Anti-Dumping Duties Act 1993 should allow investigations to proceed efficiently and duties to be imposed when evidence establishes dumping, subsidisation and injury under the relevant rules. Decisions must be timely and transparent, and ordinary price competition should not be a reason to qualify for protection.

Foreign investors should be mandated to build stronger links with Malaysian businesses. Local content and procurement expectations, designed in line with international obligations, can encourage the use of local suppliers, skills development and technology transfer. Supplier development programmes can help Malaysian firms meet the quality, scale and reliability standards major investors require.

Product standards and customs checks also need to keep pace with cross-border trade. Sirim and the customs department should strengthen risk-based inspections, including of goods sold through cross-border e-commerce. Imported products must meet safety and quality requirements, while origin declarations and product classifications must be accurate. The same standards should apply to local goods.

Support for SMEs should be directed strictly towards investment that raises productivity. Under the New Industrial Master Plan 2030, grants and financing can help smaller firms adopt automation, artificial intelligence and digital systems, strengthen quality control and develop new products. Tie support specifically to explicit improvements in operational or technical capabilities.

Malaysia also needs to move away from business models built on abundant, low-cost foreign labour. Reducing reliance on foreign workers will take a credible productivity strategy built around strategic input from employers, rather than ad hoc restrictions that leave firms unable to operate. Predictable labour policies, investment in automation, technical training and better management can raise output per worker. Workers, in turn, need opportunities to develop the skills required for higher-value jobs.

No single measure will be enough. Trade remedies cannot make firms more productive – investment incentives are worthwhile only if they help build local capabilities, and automation will not deliver much without finance, skills and reliable infrastructure.

Malaysia needs to turn today’s trade and investment flows into stronger domestic productive capacity across all sectors. That means monitoring imports accurately, enforcing trade rules, securing meaningful local participation in investment projects and helping firms move into higher-productivity – and higher wages – activities.
This is the only way that Malaysia can hold its own in a world dominated by China’s industrial might.

bccee91cf8115d86: Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company's vision for its new "frontier ecosystem," announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as "the new OS for work."

The announcement is a striking inversion of how we've traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun.
